course.title: Accounting: Reading the Numbers of a Business
course.description: Read a company's balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement and notes, and judge from them whether the business is healthy, where its cash is going and which figures to distrust.
course.audience: A capable adult who has never studied accounting. They are comfortable with percentages and ratios, they may own shares or work for a business, and they want to read an annual report for what it shows. Australian companies report under AASB standards, which are IFRS, so the course uses IFRS terms and Australian examples. It does not teach bookkeeping, tax or personal finance, and it does not repeat Economics or Decision Theory.

paragraphs: Read a company's balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement and notes, and judge from them whether the business is healthy, where its cash is going and which figures to distrust.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash flow statement and say how each figure in one shows up in the others.
You'll be able to explain, from a company's own reconciliation, why a profitable business can run short of cash.
You'll be able to say when revenue and costs are counted, and which parts of a profit figure rest on estimates.
You'll be able to judge whether a low current ratio, a high gearing figure or a very high return on equity is a warning or a feature of the business.
You'll be able to find what you need in the notes of an Australian annual report and read a policy, an estimate and a going concern note for what they commit the company to.
You'll be able to spot the common warning signs, say what to check next, and say what a price-to-earnings ratio and a free cash flow figure do and do not tell you about value.

modules.title: The three statements
modules.description: What a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash flow statement each show, how one transaction touches them, and how to read a real company's set.

modules.title: Accruals: why profit is not cash
modules.description: Why profit and cash differ, when revenue and costs are counted, and which parts of profit are estimates.

modules.title: Working capital and liquidity
modules.description: How cash cycles through stock, customers and suppliers, and whether a business can pay what it owes.

modules.title: Ratios and what they hide
modules.description: Margins, turnover and returns on equity and capital, read for what each says and what each leaves out.

modules.title: Reading a whole report
modules.description: The notes, the warning signs of trouble, and a short look at how a business is valued from its numbers.

concepts.title: Asset
concepts.summary: Something the business owns or controls, such as cash, stock, equipment or a right to use a leased store.

concepts.title: Liability
concepts.summary: Something the business must pay or deliver later: suppliers, loans, leases, unearned revenue and provisions.

concepts.title: Equity
concepts.summary: What is left of the assets after the liabilities are deducted. It is measured at recorded cost and is not a bank balance or a sale price.

concepts.title: Current and non-current
concepts.summary: Current means expected to turn into cash, or to be paid, within the next year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer.

concepts.title: Double entry
concepts.summary: Every transaction is recorded as equal and opposite entries, so the accounting equation stays in balance.

concepts.title: Debit and credit
concepts.summary: The left and right sides of an entry. They are not good and bad: a debit increases an asset and a credit increases a liability.

concepts.title: Profit flows into equity
concepts.summary: Profit adds to retained earnings, and retained earnings are part of equity, so an event that changes profit also changes equity.

concepts.title: Provision
concepts.summary: A liability recorded for a cost that has been incurred and will be paid later, such as underpaid wages.

concepts.title: Gross profit
concepts.summary: Revenue less the direct cost of the goods sold. What counts as direct differs between companies.

concepts.title: Operating profit (EBIT)
concepts.summary: Profit before net finance costs and tax. Woolworths calls it EBIT and Lovisa calls it operating profit.

concepts.title: Significant items
concepts.summary: Costs or gains a company sets apart so that trading results can be compared. The label is the company's own, because IFRS allows no 'extraordinary' items.

concepts.title: Earnings per share
concepts.summary: Profit attributable to shareholders divided by the number of shares.

concepts.title: Operating cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash from the day-to-day activities of the business: receipts from customers less payments to suppliers, employees, interest and tax (under the layout both companies use).

concepts.title: Investing cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash spent on or received from long-term assets and investments, such as stores, equipment and businesses.

concepts.title: Financing cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash from or to the people who fund the business: borrowing and repaying, lease principal, dividends and share issues.

concepts.title: Lease principal
concepts.summary: The part of each lease payment that repays the lease liability. Both companies report it in financing, so operating cash flow is higher than it would be if rent were an operating cost.

concepts.title: Accrual accounting
concepts.summary: Revenue is recorded when delivered and expenses when received, whether or not cash has moved.

concepts.title: Reconciliation of profit to operating cash flow
concepts.summary: A table starting at profit and adding or subtracting non-cash items and changes in working capital to reach operating cash flow.

concepts.title: Non-cash expense
concepts.summary: An expense deducted in profit with no cash leaving, such as depreciation. It is added back; it is not a source of cash.

concepts.title: Growth consumes cash
concepts.summary: A firm that sells more on credit and carries more stock must fund the gap between paying for goods and being paid.

concepts.title: Revenue recognition
concepts.summary: Revenue is counted when control of the goods or services passes to the customer, in the amount the business expects to be entitled to.

concepts.title: Contract liability
concepts.summary: Cash received for an obligation not yet met, such as gift cards and loyalty points. It becomes revenue as the obligation is met.

concepts.title: Matching
concepts.summary: Costs are put in the same period as the revenue they helped earn.

concepts.title: Revenue that rests on estimates
concepts.summary: Where revenue depends on a measure of progress or a forecast, as with unbilled work in progress, the estimates are what a reader should question.

concepts.title: Depreciation
concepts.summary: Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its estimated useful life. It is an allocation of cost, not a measure of market value or of cash.

concepts.title: Change in estimate
concepts.summary: A new estimate of life or residual value changes the depreciation from that date on; past charges are not restated.

concepts.title: Lower of cost and net realisable value
concepts.summary: Stock is carried at the lower of what it cost and what it is expected to sell for, less selling costs.

concepts.title: Impairment
concepts.summary: A write-down when an asset's recoverable amount is below its carrying amount. It reduces profit and the asset with no cash leaving.

concepts.title: Working capital
concepts.summary: Current assets minus current liabilities. Less than zero is a working capital deficiency, or a net current liability.

concepts.title: Days of inventory, receivable and payable
concepts.summary: How many days of cost of sales, or of sales, the balance represents: stock over cost of sales, receivables over sales, payables over cost of sales, each times 365.

concepts.title: Cash conversion cycle
concepts.summary: Days of stock plus days of receivables less days of payables: how long cash is out before it comes back.

concepts.title: Credit terms
concepts.summary: A receivable period means little until it is set beside the terms the business gives, for example 30 days or the 24 days Woolworths gives business customers.

concepts.title: Current ratio
concepts.summary: Current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures accounting liquidity; acceptable levels vary by industry.

concepts.title: Quick ratio
concepts.summary: A stricter test that leaves out stock, so it counts only cash and near-cash against current liabilities.

concepts.title: Gearing
concepts.summary: Another name for leverage: how much of the funding is borrowed. The debt-to-equity ratio is one measure, and which debts count changes the answer.

concepts.title: Interest cover
concepts.summary: Operating profit divided by finance costs: how far profit could fall before interest could not be paid.

concepts.title: Margin
concepts.summary: Profit at some level divided by revenue: gross, operating or net. Each level answers a different question.

concepts.title: Asset turnover
concepts.summary: Revenue divided by total assets: how many dollars of sales each dollar of assets produces.

concepts.title: Return on assets from margin and turnover
concepts.summary: Net margin times asset turnover gives profit over total assets, so a thin margin can pay if the assets turn fast.

concepts.title: Classification of costs
concepts.summary: Which costs sit in cost of sales differs between companies, so gross margins are comparable only after checking.

concepts.title: Return on equity
concepts.summary: Profit divided by average shareholders' equity: profit per dollar of equity.

concepts.title: The DuPont split
concepts.summary: ROE equals net margin times asset turnover times accounting leverage (assets over equity).

concepts.title: Return on capital
concepts.summary: After-tax operating profit divided by average invested capital, where the capital comes from shareholders and from debtholders.

concepts.title: Thin equity
concepts.summary: A small equity base, from heavy borrowing, large payouts or reserves, makes ROE large without making the business better.

concepts.title: Notes to the statements
concepts.summary: Details that the face of the statements leave out: policies, breakdowns and estimates. They are part of the statements.

concepts.title: Critical accounting estimates
concepts.summary: The judgements the company says have the largest risk of a material change. Woolworths names leases, impairment of non-financial assets and provisions.

concepts.title: Going concern note
concepts.summary: The directors' statement that the business can pay its debts as they fall due, with reasons where the balance sheet looks tight.

concepts.title: Auditor's report
concepts.summary: An independent opinion giving reasonable assurance that the statements are not materially misstated. It is not a guarantee.

concepts.title: Quality of earnings
concepts.summary: How closely profit is matched by cash over several years.

concepts.title: Earnings management
concepts.summary: Using judgement in reporting or in structuring transactions to alter reported results.

concepts.title: Warning sign
concepts.summary: A pattern that calls for a question: profit and cash moving apart, receivables outrunning sales, estimates changing, debt reclassified, one-offs that recur.

concepts.title: Allowance for doubtful accounts
concepts.summary: A deduction from receivables for amounts not expected to be collected. It is an estimate, and it seldom matches the final loss.

concepts.title: Price-to-earnings ratio
concepts.summary: Share price divided by earnings per share: the number of years of current earnings the buyer pays for.

concepts.title: Free cash flow
concepts.summary: Operating cash flow after capital spending. It is the cash that can be paid to lenders and owners without harming operations.

concepts.title: Discounted cash flow
concepts.summary: A value found by estimating future cash flows and discounting them for the time value of money; the terminal value is often a large share.

concepts.title: Enterprise value
concepts.summary: The sum of the claims of all who fund the business, creditors and shareholders, so wider than market capitalisation.

lessons.title: Reading a balance sheet

lead.text: A balance sheet lists three kinds of things, and reading one starts with tagging each line as one of them. An **asset** is something the company owns or controls, such as cash, stock, equipment or the right to use a store. A **liability** is something it has to pay or deliver later, such as an amount owed to a supplier, a loan or a lease payment. **Equity** is what is left of the assets once every liability has been taken away, and it belongs to the owners.

Use the buttons to read Lovisa's balance sheet at 28 June 2026 one kind at a time. The report gives its amounts in thousands of dollars, so the 46,735 beside cash is $46.7 million. When you reach the equity view, notice that the total is exactly the difference between the first two totals: 696,037 less 618,076 is 77,961.

afterFigure.text: That leftover goes by several names. The report calls it both net assets and total equity, and other writers say net worth or capital, and all of them mean assets minus liabilities. Written as an equation, **assets = liabilities + equity**, it says that whatever the company holds was paid for by someone, and that only two groups of people could have paid: the ones it owes and its owners.

reveal.text: The three biggest liabilities are leases at $11,316 million, trade payables at $8,660 million and borrowings at $5,161 million. A reader who hears liability and thinks bank loan misses most of what Woolworths owes.

lead.text: Because equity is a share of the assets, we can ask how big the share is. For Lovisa it is 77,961 out of 696,037, about 11%. Of every dollar of assets, roughly 11 cents is left for the owners and 89 cents is covered by what the company owes, mostly under its store leases.

That slice is thin, and the later lessons on gearing and on return on equity come back to what a thin slice means. The habit to take from here is to turn the three totals into a share before reading anything else about a company.

reveal.text: Both companies are funded mostly by what they owe: more than four fifths of Woolworths's assets and about nine tenths of Lovisa's.

lead.text: Equity sounds like money, and it is easy to read it that way. Lovisa held $46.7 million of cash at the balance date and reported equity of $78.0 million, so the two figures are different sizes and measure *different things*. Equity is a *difference* between two totals. The assets behind it include stock, equipment and the right to use stores, and they are in use, not waiting in a bank account to be paid out.

Equity is not a price either. Accountants record an asset at what it cost and generally do not record later changes in what it could be sold for, so equity describes what has been recorded and says little about what the business is worth or what it will earn. One more limit is worth keeping in mind. A balance sheet is a snapshot of one date, while the income statement and the cash flow statement cover a period of time.

reveal.text: To learn what cash a company holds, read the cash line. To learn the owners' share, read the equity line. They answer different questions.

lead.text: Each side of the balance sheet is also split by time. A **current** asset is cash, or something the company expects to turn into cash or use up within the next year or its operating cycle, whichever is longer. A current liability is something it must pay within the same period. Everything else is **non-current**. The report lists the current items first, in rough order of how quickly they become cash, and then the rest.

Woolworths shows how the split reads. Its stock, cash and customers' debts are current, while its leased stores and property are non-current. On the other side, its trade payables are current and the long-dated part of its borrowings is not. The split matters because it sets what is due soon against what is available soon, and the later lessons on working capital show how to read the two bars side by side.

diagram.alt: Two bars to the same scale for Woolworths. Current assets total 7,691 million dollars and are mostly inventories, cash and receivables. Current liabilities total 13,686 million dollars and are mostly trade and other payables, provisions and lease liabilities.
diagram.caption: Both bars are drawn to the same scale. The report lists current items first on each side.

reveal.text: The same borrowings can appear on both lines, because each line holds the part due in its own period. A reader who looks only at the current line sees only the debt due soon.

lead.text: Both companies show a pair of lines that take a moment to read. Lovisa has a right-of-use asset of $356.8 million and lease liabilities of $419.0 million, made up of $87.8 million due within a year and $331.2 million due later. Woolworths has lease assets of $8,660 million and lease liabilities of $11,316 million, with $1,736 million current and $9,580 million non-current.

Why are there two lines? For years beginning on or after 1 January 2019, IFRS 16 asks a company that leases something for more than 12 months, other than a low-value item, to record the right to use it as an asset and its duty to pay for that right as a liability. The two lines describe one contract, so they appear together, and the liability is a real obligation even though no bank lent anything.

afterFigure.text: The size of the liabilities against equity is worth noticing. Lovisa's lease liabilities are more than five times its equity, and Woolworths's are more than twice its. A reader who skips the lease line misses much of what each company owes, and a later lesson on gearing returns to this.

diagram.alt: Two views, one per company. Each draws the lease asset as one bar and the lease liabilities as a second bar split into the part due within a year and the part due later. Lovisa: asset 356,846 and liabilities 87,829 plus 331,166, in thousands of dollars. Woolworths: asset 8,660 and liabilities 1,736 plus 9,580, in millions of dollars.

lessons.orientation: Read a balance sheet to say what a business owns, what it owes and what is left for its owners, and say what its figures leave out.
lessons.nextAction: Follow five events of an invented firm through the equation and say which of them change profit.

blocks.text: At 28 June 2026 Lovisa, which sells fashion jewellery from leased stores, held about $696 million of cash, stock, equipment and rights to use its stores. Every dollar of that was paid for by someone. Either the shareholders put the money in, or the company owes it to a supplier, a landlord, a bank or the tax office, and the balance sheet is the statement that sorts the one from the other.
A balance sheet answers that question line by line, and it helps to make a guess before we read one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a balance sheet, say who paid for a company's assets, and say what its figures leave out.
intro.whyItMatters: Every ratio and warning sign later in the course starts from these three groups, so reading them correctly comes first.

recap.keyIdea: A balance sheet lists what a company holds, what it owes and what is left for its owners at one date, and that leftover is a recorded difference, which says little about cash on hand or sale price.

blocks.text: You read Lovisa's balance sheet as $696 million of assets, $618 million of liabilities and $78 million of [[equity|What is left of the assets after all liabilities. Met in 'Reading a balance sheet'.]], and found that Woolworths's owners hold a similar thin share, about 14% of its assets. You saw that current items fall due or turn to cash within a year, that a lease shows up as an asset and a liability together, and that equity is recorded from cost at one date. It says little about cash on hand, sale price or earning power.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at how a single event, such as a loan or a sale, changes two lines at once and keeps the equation in balance.

lessons.title: Every transaction has two sides

lead.text: Every event a business records changes at least *two* things, and that is what keeps assets equal to liabilities plus equity after each one. The method is called **double entry**, and it writes down each transaction as two entries of equal size on opposite sides, so that the books balance. It is an old idea: Florentine bankers were already using it in a ledger of 1211, one of the earliest records we have.

Let's follow a joinery firm, invented for this lesson, that starts with nothing. In event one it borrows $50,000: cash, an asset, rises by $50,000 and so does the loan, a liability, and nothing in equity moves. In event two it pays $30,000 cash for a machine, so one asset falls and another rises by the same amount. In event three it buys $8,000 of timber on credit, so timber rises and so does what it owes its supplier, which the balance sheet calls trade payables. Use the buttons to see the whole balance sheet after each event.

afterFigure.text: The highlighted lines are the pair that changed, and the two totals match every time. A machine bought for cash does not make the firm any poorer or richer. Its cost reaches profit later, as the machine is used up, through depreciation, which a later lesson covers.

After buying a machine for cash: cash 20,000 and a machine of 30,000. After buying timber on credit: timber 8,000 and trade payables of 8,000. The two totals match each time, and the two lines that changed are highlighted.

steps.headline: A $20,000 job is done on credit, using $6,000 of the timber. What happens to the equation?

lead.text: Name the two things that change, then check which side of the equation each sits on.

workedSteps.text: The firm bills the customer, who has not paid. The customer now owes the firm $20,000, an asset called a receivable.
The job used $6,000 of the timber, so the timber asset falls.
Assets have risen by the difference between the two. Nobody new is owed anything, so liabilities have not changed.
Equity must make up the difference. The 14,000 is the profit on the job, revenue of 20,000 less the 6,000 cost, and it joins equity as retained earnings.
In event five the firm pays the supplier the $8,000 it owes. Cash and payables both fall, so profit does not change.
Check the totals. Assets are cash 12,000, receivable 20,000, timber 2,000 and machine 30,000. The loan is 50,000 and equity is 14,000.

diagram.alt: The same balance sheet after the last two events. After a $20,000 job on credit that uses $6,000 of timber: cash 20,000, receivable 20,000, timber 2,000, machine 30,000, a loan of 50,000, trade payables of 8,000 and equity of 14,000, with totals of 72,000. After paying the supplier $8,000: cash 12,000 and payables 0, with totals of 64,000.
diagram.caption: Equity has risen by the profit on the job, 14,000, and it does not change when the supplier is paid.

lead.text: Accountants write each of those pairs as a **debit** and a **credit**, and the two words cause more confusion than anything else in the subject, because in daily speech they sound like good news and bad news. In an entry they are only the two equal and opposite sides. All you need here is the one rule that Wikipedia's account of double entry gives: a debit to an asset increases that asset, and a credit to a liability increases that liability.

So the bank loan in event one is a debit to cash of 50,000 and a credit to the loan of 50,000, and the timber in event three is a debit to inventory of 8,000 and a credit to trade payables of 8,000. Each entry raises an asset and a liability together. Paying cash for the machine has its entries too. Reading them needs the rest of the bookkeeping rules, which a bookkeeper learns and a reader of statements can leave alone, because the equation already tells you what each event does.

reveal.text: Two events in the list, the wages owed and the mulch used, move profit with no cash at all. The customer's payment moves cash with no change in profit.

lead.text: Every event that changed profit so far also changed a customer's debt or used up stock. A cost can reach profit before any cash leaves, and Woolworths's report shows a large one. On 5 September 2025 the Federal Court of Australia gave a decision on the underpayment of award-covered salaried store team leaders. Woolworths reviewed it and recognised an additional provision of $710 million in the 2026 period: $406 million of further potential remediation, before income tax, and $304 million of interest, superannuation and payroll tax.

A **provision** is a liability recorded for a cost that has been incurred and will be paid later, and the entry has two sides. A liability rises by $710 million, and a cost of the same size is recognised in profit. No cash moves that day, and it goes out as payments are made.

afterFigure.text: The report adds that the provision is still growing: interest on it accrues at about $20 million every half-year until payments are made. The cost reached profit when the provision was recorded, so a cost can lower profit in one year and take the cash out in a later one.

diagram.alt: Two views of the Woolworths wage provision. When the provision is recorded, provisions (a liability) rise by 710 million dollars, profit falls by the matching cost, and cash does not change. When payments are later made, provisions and cash both fall and profit does not change.
diagram.caption: Cash leaves in the second view. The cost has already reached profit in the first.

lead.text: The opposite case is cash arriving before the work. Woolworths's trade and other payables come to $8,660 million, and the note behind the line splits them into trade payables of $6,302 million, accruals of $1,791 million and contract liabilities of $567 million. A **contract liability** is cash or other consideration received for something the company has not yet delivered. Woolworths's are mostly points in its Everyday Rewards program and gift cards.

When a customer pays for a gift card, the retailer has cash but has done nothing yet. It records cash up and a liability up, because it now owes goods, and the revenue follows as the card is used. The note says that nearly all of the amount at year end will become revenue in the following period.

Each later payment to staff takes cash and the provision down together, so profit is not touched a second time.

lessons.orientation: Read a transaction as two changes that keep the accounting equation in balance, and say which items move and whether profit changes.
lessons.nextAction: Read Woolworths's income statement from revenue down to profit and separate the one-off items from the rest.

blocks.text: A joinery firm borrows $50,000 from a bank, and the money arrives in its account the same afternoon. Its bank balance has jumped by $50,000, and it is natural to ask whether the firm has earned that much.

The answer depends on what else changed when the money arrived. Every event a business records changes at least two things, and which two they are tells us whether profit has moved, so we'll start with a guess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace an event through the accounting equation and say which items move and whether profit changes.
intro.whyItMatters: Cash and profit are different figures, and the two-sided entry is the mechanism that separates them.

recap.keyIdea: Every event changes at least two things so that the accounting equation stays in balance, and profit changes only when revenue or a cost is recorded, whether or not cash moves.

blocks.text: You followed five events of an invented joinery firm and saw that each changed two lines and left assets equal to liabilities plus [[equity|What is left of the assets after all liabilities. Met in 'Reading a balance sheet'.]]. The loan, the machine, the timber and the supplier's payment moved balance sheet lines only, and the job added a profit of $14,000 to equity. Woolworths's $710 million provision showed a cost reaching profit before any cash left, and its contract liabilities showed cash arriving before the revenue.

recap.nextHook: Next we read the income statement, where profits and costs are laid out layer by layer.

lessons.title: Reading an income statement

lead.text: An income statement covers a period of time, here the 52 weeks to 28 June 2026, and it works down from the top line by taking away one layer of cost at a time. Woolworths starts with revenue of $71,539 million. The cost of the goods it sold, $51,970 million, comes off first, and what remains is **gross profit** of $19,569 million, about 27 cents of each revenue dollar. The running costs of the business come off next, in branch expenses, administration and a line called other expenses, with a small amount of other income added. They leave earnings before interest and tax, or **EBIT**, of $2,407 million. Last come net finance costs and income tax, which leave a profit for the period of $1,152 million.

Each subtotal answers its own question. Gross profit says what the goods earned over what they cost, EBIT says what running the business earned before the cost of its funding and the tax, and profit says what was left at the end. Use the buttons to see the layers to scale, first from revenue to gross profit and then from gross profit down to profit.

afterFigure.text: Wikipedia calls this the multi-step layout, which starts with gross profit and then works through the operating expenses. Companies use the layout but name and order its layers in their own ways, as the next screen shows.

diagram.alt: Two views of Woolworths's income statement for the 52 weeks to 28 June 2026, in millions of dollars. The first draws revenue of 71,539, cost of sales of 51,970 and gross profit of 19,569 to scale. The second draws the layers from gross profit down to profit for the period of 1,152, passing EBIT of 2,407, with the other expenses line of 698 marked.
diagram.caption: Each view is drawn to its own scale. The first shows how much of revenue is left after the cost of sales, and the second how much of gross profit is left after everything else.

reveal.text: Profit for the period is the line at the bottom, and it is the profit that joins equity, as the profit on the job did in the last lesson.

lead.text: Lovisa's statement has the same shape in different proportions. Its revenue was $938.8 million and its cost of sales $163.4 million, so its gross profit was $775.3 million, about 83 cents of each revenue dollar against Woolworths's 27. Part of the gap is what each company counts as a cost of sales, a point the lesson on margins takes up.

Below gross profit Lovisa lists its costs one by one: salaries, property, distribution, depreciation and amortisation, impairment and other expenses. Its subtotal after them, **operating profit** of $158.2 million, sits where Woolworths's EBIT sits, before finance costs of $24.8 million and tax of $38.5 million. Profit after tax was $95.6 million. Depreciation and amortisation has a line of its own at $131.3 million, which is the yearly charge for the use of assets the company acquired earlier.

reveal.text: Several lines grew faster than revenue, among them salaries, other expenses and tax, which is why profit after tax rose only 10.7%.

lead.text: Woolworths's statement has a line of other expenses of $698 million, and its report ties that line to **significant items**: costs or gains that the company sets apart so that its trading can be compared from year to year. Before the items, EBIT was $3,105 million, and the items took off $698 million to leave the $2,407 million in the statement. After tax the items cost $461 million, which is the gap between a profit before them of $1,613 million and the profit for the period of $1,152 million.

The largest piece is in a note. On 5 September 2025 the Federal Court of Australia gave a decision about underpaid store team leaders, and Woolworths recorded an additional provision of $710 million, the entry traced in the last lesson. Smaller items in the note net against it, which is why the line shows $698 million.

afterFigure.text: The label belongs to the *company*. IFRS bars any item from being labelled extraordinary in the income statement, so a company that wants readers to look past a cost chooses a name of its own, and the reader decides how much weight the cost deserves.

lead.text: Profit is a total, and a company with more shares has more owners to share it. **Earnings per share**, or EPS, divides the profit that belongs to shareholders by the number of shares. Lovisa's note on the calculation uses $95.6 million of profit and an average of about 110.7 million shares, which gives 86.32 cents, against 78.12 cents in 2025. Profit rose 10.7% and EPS rose about 10.5%, because the share count barely changed.

Woolworths reported basic EPS of 93.2 cents against 78.9 cents, a rise of about 18%, and 130.9 cents before significant items. EPS is useful for comparing years because it still makes sense when a company issues new shares, which can raise profit while each share's slice shrinks.

reveal.text: A company that issues new shares changes the bottom of the fraction, so earnings per share has to be read together with profit.
Gross profit, by contrast, comes before the running costs, so Tessel's 600 is a much larger figure than its trading profit of 120.

lessons.orientation: Read an income statement from revenue down to profit, say where each layer of profit comes from, and separate a recurring result from a one-off item.
lessons.nextAction: Sort Woolworths's cash flows into operating, investing and financing and say what each shows.

blocks.text: Woolworths reported revenue of $71.5 billion for the year to 28 June 2026, and a profit of $1.2 billion. It is easy to read revenue as what a business makes and profit as the bonus on top, and the income statement is the statement that shows what stands between the two figures.
We'll read it from the top, one layer of cost at a time. First, make a guess at how large the gap between the two figures is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an income statement from revenue to profit, say where each layer comes from, and tell a recurring cost from a one-off.
intro.whyItMatters: A headline profit figure can include costs the company sets apart, and reading the layers shows what each headline includes.

recap.keyIdea: An income statement takes away one layer of cost at a time from revenue to profit, and a company's own label for a cost, such as significant items, says what it set apart and leaves you to judge whether the cost recurs.

blocks.text: You read Woolworths's statement from revenue of $71.5 billion down through gross profit, EBIT and finance costs to a profit of $1.2 billion, about 1.6 cents in each revenue dollar. Lovisa follows the same layers with a much higher gross profit and a depreciation line that grew faster than its revenue. Woolworths's significant items took $698 million off EBIT, the largest piece being the [[provision|A liability recorded for a cost that has been incurred and will be paid later. Met in 'Every transaction has two sides'.]] for underpaid wages. IFRS does not allow an extraordinary label, so a company's own label for a cost is a prompt to ask how often it recurs.

recap.nextHook: Next we read the cash flow statement, which follows the cash that the income statement does not.

lessons.title: Reading a cash flow statement

lead.text: The cash flow statement is about one thing, the cash that moved in and out of the business, and it sorts every movement into one of three groups. **Operating** cash flow comes from running the business day to day: receipts from customers, less payments to suppliers and employees, and, in the layout Woolworths and Lovisa both use, less the interest and tax paid. **Investing** cash flow is what is spent on, or received from selling, long-term assets such as stores and equipment. **Financing** cash flow moves between the business and the people who fund it: new borrowing and repayments, the principal part of lease payments, and dividends.

Each group answers its own question. Operating cash says whether running the business produces cash. Investing says what it cost to keep and grow the stores, and financing says how any gap was filled and what was paid out to lenders and owners. The figure draws Woolworths's three flows to scale.

afterFigure.text: The three flows add up to the $233 million rise in cash. Exchange rates took $11 million off the balance, so it went from $1,275 million at the start of the year to $1,497 million at the end.

diagram.alt: Woolworths's cash flows for 2026 in millions of dollars, drawn to scale from a centre line. Operating activities brought in 4,948 to the right. Investing activities took out 2,014 and financing activities took out 2,701, both to the left. The net increase in cash was 233.

reveal.text: Two lines are worth remembering. Lease principal is in financing, and the lease interest that goes with it is in operating, a split the lesson returns to.

lead.text: Woolworths made a profit of $1,152 million in 2026 and generated $4,948 million of operating cash, more than four times as much. The two statements measure different things. Profit counts costs when they are incurred, and it includes charges that need no cash that year. The largest is depreciation and amortisation, $2,984 million in 2026, the yearly charge for the use of assets the company acquired earlier. It lowers profit and sends no cash anywhere.

The cash flow statement follows the cash, so it leaves out such non-cash items, along with sales on credit that customers have not yet paid for. Operating cash came out $3,796 million above profit, and depreciation and amortisation accounts for nearly four fifths of that. The next lesson goes line by line through the reconciliation that links the two figures.

reveal.text: The rest of the gap, about $6 million, is the net effect of every other difference between profit and cash.

lead.text: How much of Woolworths's operating cash was left for its owners? Start with the $4,948 million. To keep its stores going it spent $2,435 million on property, plant, equipment and intangibles, and it repaid $1,298 million of lease principal. What remains is about $1,215 million, against dividends of $1,100 million, so the dividend was covered with little to spare. Woolworths also sold property for $348 million, and counting that would lift the figure to about $1,560 million.

The lease principal needs its own explanation. A lease payment has two parts. Interest on the lease liability, $586 million, is reported in operating activities, and the repayment of principal, $1,298 million, is reported in financing. So operating cash flow is struck *after* the lease interest and *before* the **lease principal**. Subtracting the principal, as we did here, is a reader's adjustment, and neither the standards nor the company ask for it. It puts a retailer that leases its stores on a footing closer to one that treats rent as a running cost.

lead.text: Two features of the layout can make operating cash flow hard to compare. The first is the lease. Both Woolworths and Lovisa report the principal part of lease payments in financing, so each company's operating cash flow is higher than it would be if rent counted as an ordinary operating cost. Lovisa's lease payments of $108.9 million in 2026 split into $89.2 million of principal, in financing, and $19.7 million of interest, which sits with the interest paid in operating.

The second is interest. IAS 7 lets a company put interest paid in operating activities or in financing activities, so two companies can classify the same payment differently. Before comparing the operating cash flow of two businesses, look for where each puts its lease and interest payments, and put them on the same footing. That is our own adjustment as readers, and the statements do not make it for you.

reveal.text: The adjustment can go either way: take the lease principal off the company that leaves it out, or add the lease payments back for the company that includes them. Either puts both on the same footing.
The same three subtotals can describe a business that pays its way or one that does not, and only the pattern across them tells you which.

lessons.orientation: Read a cash flow statement as three stories, from operations, investing and financing, and say what they show about how the business pays its way.
lessons.nextAction: Reconcile a profit to its operating cash flow and say which lines make cash run ahead of or behind profit.

blocks.text: A business that pays its own way brings in more cash from running itself than it spends on its stores, its lenders and its owners. Woolworths's cash flow statement for 2026 ends in three subtotals that let us test that: operating activities brought in $4,948 million, investing activities took out $2,014 million, and financing activities took out $2,701 million.
Before we read what is inside each one, work out roughly where those three figures leave the cash balance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a cash flow statement as three stories and say what each shows about how a business pays its way.
intro.whyItMatters: Profit can look healthy while cash is short, and the cash flow statement is where that shows up.

recap.keyIdea: A cash flow statement sorts cash into operating, investing and financing, and the pattern across the three, with the lease and interest lines read carefully, shows how a business pays its way.

blocks.text: You sorted Woolworths's cash flows by who the cash moved between, and found that its $4,948 million of operating cash, more than four times its [[profit|Revenue less costs for the period, as the income statement shows it. Met in 'Reading an income statement'.]], was lifted by non-cash charges. After the stores and the lease principal about $1.2 billion was left, close to the $1.1 billion paid in dividends. Lovisa's cash rose by only $6.5 million on $232.8 million of operating cash, because stores, leases and dividends took the rest, and where each company puts its leases and interest decides how to compare them.

recap.nextHook: Next we take the profit and the cash apart line by line, to see exactly why they differ.

lessons.title: Why profit is not cash

lead.text: Why would profit and cash differ at all? Because an income statement does not follow the money. Under **accrual accounting** a sale is recorded when the goods or the service are delivered, even though the customer has not yet paid, and a cost is recorded when the goods or the service are received, even though the supplier has not yet been paid. Wikipedia describes accrued revenue in just those terms: income recognised when a company delivers, before it is paid, and shown on the balance sheet as a receivable.

When the customer does pay, the income statement does not change, because the profit was already counted. Only the balance sheet moves: cash rises and the receivable falls. That one idea opens a gap between the two figures. Profit runs ahead of cash while customers owe more. Cash runs ahead of profit while the company owes more, or has charges that need no cash. The **reconciliation** in a company's report is the table that lists every item in the gap between profit and operating cash flow.

Woolworths's note 4.5 starts from a profit of $1,152 million and ends at operating cash flow of $4,948 million, and fifteen lines sit between the two. They fall into three blocks. The first holds non-cash items, $3,109 million in all, of which depreciation and amortisation is $2,984 million. The second holds changes in the balances that stand between sales and cash: stock, receivables, payables and provisions. Three of those five lines add cash and two take it away, and together they add $979 million. The third is two tax lines, which take off $292 million.

afterFigure.text: Each line explains part of the gap of $3,796 million, and the reconciliation is where a reader looks first when profit and cash disagree.

lead.text: There is a rule behind the signs. Start from profit, which counts a sale when it is made and a cost when it is incurred, and ask of each line whether the cash lagged behind that or ran ahead of it. When receivables rise, customers have been billed and have *not yet paid*, so profit holds revenue that is not yet cash and operating cash is lower by the rise. When stock rises, the firm has paid for goods that will not be a cost until they are sold, so cash is lower again. When payables rise, the firm has received goods or services that it has not paid for, so cash is higher by the rise, and a provision that is recognised and not yet paid works the same way. Depreciation is added back because it lowered profit while no cash left.

Woolworths's lines follow the rule. Stock rose and took $351 million off cash, while trade payables, provisions and other payables rose by $367 million, $652 million and $329 million, and put cash above profit by those amounts.

steps.headline: Harbour Print's profit is $48,000. What is its operating cash flow?

lead.text: Last year Harbour Print, an invented printer, was paid on delivery. This year it allowed 60 days to pay and its sales doubled to $600,000. Start from profit and make each adjustment in turn.

workedSteps.text: Start from the profit for the year.
Depreciation of $12,000 lowered profit and no cash left, so add it back.
Customers now owe about 60 days of sales. Receivables rose by about $100,000, so cash is lower than profit by that much.
Stock rose by $40,000, bought with cash and not yet sold, so subtract it.
Suppliers are owed $25,000 more, for goods received and not yet paid for, so add it.
Operating cash flow is about negative $55,000, against a profit of $48,000.

steps.headline: Larch Furniture's profit is $60,000. How does its operating cash flow compare?

lead.text: Larch Furniture is another invented firm. Its depreciation was $15,000, its receivables rose by $30,000, its stock fell by $10,000 and its payables rose by $5,000. Fill in the lines marked for you.

workedSteps.text: Start from the profit for the year.
Depreciation of $15,000 lowered profit, and no cash left. Decide what to do with it.
Receivables rose by $30,000, so customers owe more and cash is lower than profit.
Stock fell by $10,000, so the firm sold goods that it had paid for earlier. Decide which way that moves cash.
Payables rose by $5,000, so the firm received goods it has not yet paid for.
Put the lines together and compare the total with the profit of $60,000.

reveal.text: In 2026 the same line was about 79% of the gap, so the pattern repeats from one year to the next.

lead.text: Now turn the table round with Harbour Print's year. A firm that sells on 60-day terms still has to pay for its paper and ink and its wages when the work is done, and the customer's cash arrives two months later. Profit is recorded when the job is delivered, so it rises at once, while cash lags behind by 60 days. The bigger the firm grows, the more cash it has tied up in receivables and stock, and it must fund that gap from its own cash, from its suppliers or from a lender. Wikipedia's description of the cash conversion cycle makes the same point, as the time a firm goes without cash when it invests more in stock to expand its sales.

A textbook case, with an invented company, shows the pattern over three years: net income each year while receivables, stock and short-term borrowing all grew and the cash balance fell. Use the buttons to see when one job shows up in profit and when it shows up in cash.

afterFigure.text: A profitable firm can therefore fail for lack of cash, because someone has to pay the bills until the customers' money arrives.

lead.text: A common slip is to call depreciation a source of cash, because it is added back in the reconciliation. The add-back is a correction. Depreciation lowered profit and sent no cash anywhere, so to get from profit to cash it has to be put back. Wikipedia's account agrees: depreciation needs no current outlay of cash, so it is a non-cash expense that gets added back, and it does not bring cash in by itself.

The cash that pays for a business still comes from customers. A company with large depreciation and no customers would show an add-back and no cash at all. Woolworths's $2,984 million reflects the use of its stores' equipment, property and leased sites, and it is the main reason operating cash flow is more than four times profit.

reveal.text: When the buses are replaced, the purchase will appear in investing activities, which is where a company reports spending on equipment.

lessons.orientation: Explain from a company's reconciliation why a profitable business can run short of cash, and name the lines (receivables, stock, payables, depreciation, provisions) that account for the gap.
lessons.nextAction: Decide in which period a sale or a cost belongs, and say what sits on the balance sheet when cash and recognition do not coincide.

blocks.text: Harbour Print, an invented printing firm, makes a profit of $48,000 this year. It has repaid no loans and paid no dividends, yet its bank balance at the end of the year is lower than at the start. The firm is invented, and the pattern is common: profit and cash are measured in different ways, and in the same year they can move in opposite directions.

Woolworths shows the same gap on a large scale, with $1,152 million of profit and $4,948 million of operating cash flow. First, make a guess about how a profit and a falling bank balance can go together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain, from a company's reconciliation, why profit and cash differ, and name the lines that account for the gap.
intro.whyItMatters: A profitable company can run short of cash, and the reconciliation shows how before the bank balance does.

recap.keyIdea: Profit counts sales and costs when they happen and cash counts them when they are paid, so the reconciliation adds back non-cash charges and adjusts for receivables, stock, payables and provisions, and growth can use cash faster than profit supplies it.

blocks.text: You went through Woolworths's [[reconciliation|The table that starts from profit and ends at operating cash flow. Met in 'Why profit is not cash'.]], where depreciation and amortisation made up nearly four fifths of the gap between $1,152 million of profit and $4,948 million of operating cash flow. You applied the rule to Harbour Print, where a doubling of sales on 60-day terms turned a profit of $48,000 into a cash outflow of about $55,000. Depreciation is added back because no cash left, and it is not a source of cash.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at when revenue and costs are counted at all, since the timing rules decide how large a profit appears.

lessons.title: When revenue and costs count

lead.text: Woolworths's annual report says it recognises revenue from selling goods when control of the goods passes to the customer, measured at the amount it expects to be entitled to. Retail customers generally pay at the till, so for them the sale and the cash arrive together and the rule goes unnoticed. Business customers get credit terms, with payment generally due within 24 days, and for them the two dates come apart.

Counting an event when it happens, and not when the cash moves, is [[accrual accounting|Counting an event when it happens, whatever the timing of the cash. Met in 'Why profit is not cash'.]], and the moment a sale starts to count is called **revenue recognition**. In the figure the goods are delivered on 20 June, so the revenue falls in the year that ends on 28 June. At the year end the customer still owes the money, so the balance sheet shows a receivable, which is an asset.

afterFigure.text: When the cash arrives on 14 July the receivable turns into cash, and the cash adds nothing to revenue, because the sale was counted when control passed.

diagram.alt: A timeline from 20 June to 14 July with the year end on 28 June marked between them. Goods are delivered on 20 June, so the revenue is counted that day and falls in this year. At the year end the balance sheet shows a receivable. When the cash arrives on 14 July, the receivable becomes cash and no new revenue is counted.

lead.text: What changes when the thing sold is delivered over months and is not handed over at one moment? Suppose a gym sells a 12-month membership for $1,200 on 1 April, and its year ends on 30 June. The member has paid in full, yet only three of the twelve months have been delivered, so only three twelfths of the price, $300, is revenue for this year.

The other $900 is cash for months the gym still owes. It sits on the balance sheet as a [[contract liability|Cash received for something not yet delivered. Met in 'Every transaction has two sides'.]], the line that held Woolworths's gift cards, because the gym must either deliver those months or hand the money back, and it moves into revenue a month at a time as the months pass.

afterFigure.text: Move the year end along in the figure and the split moves with it. At 30 September six months are delivered and the liability has halved to $600, and once all twelve months are delivered the whole $1,200 is revenue and nothing is owed.

diagram.alt: A bar of twelve months starting in April, with the months delivered shaded and the year end marked. For a $1,200 membership at a year end of 30 June, three months are delivered, so $300 is revenue and $900 is a contract liability. At 30 September it is $600 and $600, and when all twelve months are delivered it is $1,200 and nothing is owed.

steps.headline: A yoga studio sells a six-month pass for $600 on 1 May, and its year ends on 30 June. How is the $600 shown at the year end?

lead.text: This is the gym's reasoning again with new figures. The first line is done, and the next two are yours.

workedSteps.text: The pass runs for six months, and May and June are delivered by the year end, so two of the six months are earned.
workedSteps.math: 2 of 6 months, one third of the price

workedSteps.text: Say which part of the price is revenue for this year.
The rest of the price was paid for months the studio has not yet delivered.
By the end of the six months the whole price has become revenue and nothing is owed.

lead.text: Woolworths has the same structure in a form you meet every week. When a shopper earns Everyday Rewards points, the policy treats the points as a separate promise: part of the price of the shopping is allocated to them and held back as a contract liability, and it becomes revenue only when the points are redeemed. Gift cards work the same way, because the cash arrives before the goods do.

The note on trade and other payables shows how much is held back. Contract liabilities were $567 million at the year end, mainly loyalty points, gift cards and data analytics and consulting services, and the note says substantially all of that revenue will be recognised in the following year. Set beside revenue of $71,539 million, that is less than 1%, so the timing effect is real but small for a company whose customers collect what they've paid for quickly.
Read the policy itself, and find where it says the points sit.

reveal.text: The policy puts the allocated part inside trade and other payables, which is the line the $567 million above came from.

lead.text: Behind every case so far sits one procedure, set out in IFRS 15, which has applied to reporting years starting on or after 1 January 2018. It has five steps in a fixed order, and the order matters because each step needs the one before it.

First identify the contract with the customer. Second, identify the **performance obligations** in it, which are the separate promises to deliver goods or services. Third, determine the **transaction price**, the amount the business expects to be entitled to, estimating it where part of the price is variable. Fourth, allocate that price across the promises according to what each would sell for on its own. Fifth, recognise revenue when each promise is met, which is when the customer obtains control, at a point in time for goods or over time for services.

You've seen the steps at work. Woolworths treats loyalty points as a second promise inside a shopping trip, which is the second step, and allocates part of the price to them, which is the fourth, so that part reaches revenue only at the fifth step, when the points are redeemed.
Put the five steps in the order the standard sets.

reveal.text: A contract with two promises is priced once and then split, which is why identifying the promises comes before the allocation.

lead.text: Costs follow the same logic. A cost is counted in the period whose revenue it helped earn, an idea textbooks call **matching**, and the cash for it can come before or after. Electricity used in June belongs to a year ending 30 June even when the bill arrives in July, and a year's insurance paid in April covers only part of this year, so the rest isn't a cost yet.

That gives four cases, and the figure sets them out. When the cash comes after the period, revenue leaves a receivable and a cost leaves an accrued liability. When the cash comes before, revenue leaves a contract liability and a cost leaves a **prepayment**, an asset the business holds until it uses what it paid for.

afterFigure.text: Wikipedia's article on revenue recognition calls accrued revenue an asset: income that is earned when goods or services are delivered, before the payment has arrived. Each of the four cases is a way of putting an item in the period where it happened.

diagram.alt: A table of four cells. When the cash comes after the period, earned revenue is a receivable, which is an asset, and a cost already used is an accrued cost, which is a liability. When the cash comes before, revenue still to be earned is a contract liability, and a cost not yet used is a prepayment, which is an asset.
diagram.caption: Revenue and cost, each with the cash coming after or before. Blue boxes are assets and orange boxes are liabilities.

lead.text: Sort six items by where they stand at a year end of 30 June.

reveal.text: In each case the question was whether the work, the use or the sale had happened by the year end.

lead.text: For a service delivered over time, IFRS 15 asks the business to choose a measure of progress, and a calendar is an easy measure for a gym. It is harder for a firm that does work for clients and bills them later, because the revenue and the **work in progress**, work done that hasn't been billed yet, then depend on estimates of how much is done and how much will be collected.

ASIC's 2016 statement on the legal services company Slater and Gordon shows where a regulator looks. Its inquiries into the 2014 and 2015 reports mainly concerned goodwill, the recognition of fee revenue and related work in progress, provisions against debtors, and the basis for classing work in progress as a current asset. On revenue it focussed on the accounting policies and on testing the estimates against historical data.
ASIC says it has neither approved nor disapproved the revenue basis, so its statement shows a reader where to look, which is at the estimates, and leaves open whether any figure was wrong.
Read what ASIC says its inquiries focussed on.

reveal.text: The statement points at the estimates and the policies, because those are what a regulator or a reader can test against what happened.

lead.text: One more choice sits inside the revenue line itself. A business that takes the risk of buying and selling goods may report the selling price as revenue and the cost of the goods as a cost. A business that acts only as an agent reports the fee it earns for arranging the sale, and not the full value of the transaction.

Wikipedia's account of Enron contrasts it with trading firms like Goldman Sachs and Merrill Lynch. Those firms followed the usual agent model and counted only their trading or brokerage fee as revenue, while Enron chose to count the full value of each trade. The article describes that merchant model as a much more aggressive reading of the rules. The practical test is the one you've just seen: ask who carries the risk of buying and selling, and read the revenue figure with that answer in hand.
Apply the test to a new pair of firms.

reveal.text: The test is about risk, so two firms can handle the same order and report very different revenue.

lessons.orientation: Decide in which period a sale or a cost belongs, and say what sits on the balance sheet when cash and recognition do not coincide.
lessons.nextAction: Say how much of a profit figure rests on estimates, and what changes when a useful life or a stock value changes.

blocks.text: A business customer takes delivery of groceries from Woolworths on 20 June 2026 and, like Woolworths's other business customers, pays on credit terms that its annual report gives as generally within 24 days. Woolworths's year ended on 28 June 2026, and in this case the cash arrives on 14 July.

So the goods were handed over in one year and the money came in the next, and the accounts have to say which year's revenue includes the sale. The rule they use explains a good deal of the gap between profit and cash that the last lesson began on.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which year a sale or a cost belongs to, and what the balance sheet holds when the cash arrives at a different time.
intro.whyItMatters: Revenue is the top line of every profit figure, so counting it early or late moves everything below it.

recap.keyIdea: Revenue is counted when control passes or as a service is delivered, and costs follow the revenue they helped earn, so cash and profit differ by a receivable, a contract liability, an accrued cost or a prepayment.

blocks.text: You placed a delivery, a gym membership and a loyalty point in time, and saw that the balance sheet carries the difference: a receivable when the cash comes later and a [[contract liability|Cash received for something not yet delivered. Met in 'Every transaction has two sides'.]] when it comes first. Costs follow the same logic through matching. A firm that only arranges a trade reports its fee and not the trade's value, and revenue that rests on an estimate of work done, as in ASIC's questions about Slater and Gordon, is where a reader should look hardest.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at how much of a profit figure rests on estimates: depreciation lives, stock values and write-downs.

lessons.title: Estimates inside profit

lead.text: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived asset over the years it is expected to be used. The simplest method, and the one Wikipedia calls the most often used, is straight-line: take the cost, subtract the value the business expects the asset to have at the end, called the **residual value**, and divide by the number of years it expects to use it, the **useful life**. For the machine in the opening that is $20,000 less $2,000, over five years, which is $3,600 a year.

Each year's charge reduces the asset's **carrying amount**, which is its cost less the depreciation charged so far, so after two years the machine is carried at $20,000 less $7,200, or $12,800. Depreciation allocates a cost over time. No cash leaves when it is charged, because the cash left when the machine was bought, and the carrying amount is not what the machine would sell for.

The useful life and the residual value are estimates made on the day of purchase, and they get revisited. When one changes, the charge is recalculated from that date over the remaining life, and no earlier year is touched. We call this a **change in estimate**.

For the machine, the carrying amount after two years is $12,800. With a new residual value of $5,000 and six years to go, the amount left to write off is $12,800 less $5,000, which is $7,800, and spread over six years it comes to $1,300 a year. The charge falls from $3,600 to $1,300, so profit is $2,300 a year higher than it would have been, and cash is the same as before, because nothing about the purchase changed.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the first two bars are the same under both estimates, because the past isn't restated, and the later bars are lower once the new estimate applies.

lead.text: On a real income statement the same decision can be large. Lovisa's depreciation and amortisation expense was $131.3 million in 2026, against an [[operating profit|Profit before interest and tax. Met in 'Reading an income statement'.]] of $158.2 million, so the charge is about 83% as large as the profit left after it. Lovisa says it writes off property, plant and equipment evenly over each asset's estimated useful life, and that it reviews the residual value, the life and the method at least once a year.

As a what-if, suppose the whole charge were 10% lower for any reason, such as longer lives. That is about $13.1 million, so operating profit would be about $13.1 million higher, a rise of about 8%, with no change in cash. The report doesn't split the charge between property, plant and equipment and other assets, so treat the 10% as a test of how sensitive profit is, and not as a forecast.

lead.text: Run the same what-if on Woolworths, whose report does split the charge.

reveal.text: The what-if moves profit by the change in the charge and leaves cash alone, whichever company it is run on.

lead.text: Stock gets the same kind of treatment. IAS 2 has a business carry its stock at the lower of what it cost and its **net realisable value**, which is the estimated selling price less the estimated costs of completing and selling it. When stock looks likely to sell for less than it cost, the write-down is an expense of the period in which it happens, and no cash leaves then, because the cash left when the stock was bought.

Woolworths's note shows the rule at work. Its inventories were $4,523 million, less a provision for obsolescence of $58 million, which leaves the $4,465 million on the balance sheet. Its policy carries the stock at whichever is lower, cost or net realisable value. The provision is a judgement about stock that won't sell at full value, and at about 1% of the stock it is a small one. Woolworths puts a cost on its stock with a formula called weighted average, which a worked example below compares with another formula.
Read one sentence from Lovisa's inventory note.

reveal.text: The write-down sits inside cost of sales, so it lowers gross profit in the year it is recognised, and the 2026 amount is about 41% above 2025's.

steps.headline: A bike shop buys 10 frames at $100 and later 10 frames at $120, and sells 10 frames at $200 each. How does the cost formula change its profit?

lead.text: The shop can't tell which frame went to which customer, so it needs a rule. Compare first in, first out with weighted average.

workedSteps.text: Revenue is the same under either formula, since ten frames were sold at $200.
First in, first out, called FIFO, assumes the first frames bought are the first sold, so the cheaper batch becomes cost of sales.
Weighted average spreads the cost of all 20 frames evenly, then charges ten of them.
FIFO shows the higher profit, and a higher value for the stock left on the shelf.
The cash is the same either way, so the $100 difference in profit is a $100 difference in stock.
workedSteps.math: $2,200 paid for frames, $2,000 received for sales

lead.text: Run the formulas the other way, with falling prices.

reveal.text: Which formula is higher depends on the direction prices move, and the cash is the same under every formula.

lead.text: A third judgement covers an asset that has lost value in a way straight-line depreciation doesn't capture. At each reporting date a business compares an asset's **recoverable amount**, which the textbook measures as its fair value less the costs of selling it, with its carrying amount, and writes the asset down if the carrying amount is higher. The loss is an expense called an **impairment**. It lowers profit and the asset together, it uses no cash that year, and later depreciation is revised to match the lower amount.

Lovisa's note on impairment shows how a charge can swing. It recorded a net impairment expense of $8,879,000 in 2026, against $858,000 in 2025, in stores in the Americas, Europe and Asia, which is more than ten times as much. In a reconciliation of profit to cash, an impairment is added back as a [[non-cash expense|An expense that lowers profit without any cash leaving in the year. Met in 'Why profit is not cash'.]], and the recoverable amount behind it is itself an estimate.
Apply it to a store whose trading has collapsed.

reveal.text: The write-down is the gap between what is carried and what can be recovered, and it hits profit in the period it is recognised.

lead.text: Sort the figures in a company's accounts by whether they are counted or judged.

reveal.text: A profit figure is a mixture of records and judgements, and the judged parts are where an estimate can move it.

lessons.orientation: Judge how much of a profit figure rests on estimates, and say what changes, and what does not, when a useful life, a cost formula or a write-down changes.
lessons.nextAction: Read working capital as a cycle of cash, stock and credit, and judge whether a low one is a warning or part of the business model.

blocks.text: A business buys a machine for $20,000, expects to use it for five years, and expects it to be worth $2,000 at the end. Spreading the $18,000 it will use up evenly gives a depreciation charge of $3,600 a year. After two years the owner decides that the machine will last six more years, and will then be worth $5,000.
Nothing physical has changed and no cash has moved. Yet the profit of every year from now on depends on that decision, which is a guess about the future that nobody can check for years.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how much of a profit figure rests on estimates, and what changes and what stays put when one of them changes.
intro.whyItMatters: Lovisa's depreciation and amortisation is about 83% of its operating profit, so a small change in an estimate moves the figure you're reading.

recap.keyIdea: Depreciation, stock values and impairments rest on estimates of life, price and recoverable value, so a change in an estimate moves profit and the carrying amount and leaves cash alone.

blocks.text: You recalculated a machine's charge after a [[change in estimate|A new estimate of life or residual value, applied from that date with earlier years unchanged. Met in 'Estimates inside profit'.]], saw that a 10% shift in Lovisa's depreciation would move its operating profit by about 8%, and read how stock and impairments are written down to a lower figure. In each case the cash left when the asset or the stock was bought, so an estimate moves the years in which the cost reaches profit, while the amount paid stays where it was. When you read a profit figure, ask which parts of it are counted from records and which are judged.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn to the balance sheet's current items and read working capital as a cycle of cash, stock and credit.

lessons.title: Working capital and the cash cycle

lead.text: **Working capital** is current assets minus current liabilities, the short-term resources a business holds less the short-term bills it owes. The main current assets are cash, receivables and stock, and the main current liabilities are payables, the current part of leases and borrowings, tax and provisions. When the result is below zero it is a working capital deficiency, or **net current liability**, and Woolworths's is $5,995 million: $7,691 million less $13,686 million.

The figure shows both sides to one scale. Stock is the biggest current asset at $4,465 million, and trade and other payables the biggest current liability at $8,660 million. Wikipedia points out that a company can hold plenty of assets and earn profits and still lack liquidity, if those assets can't easily be turned into cash, so the useful questions are how quickly the current assets turn into cash and when the current liabilities fall due.

afterFigure.text: The directors of Woolworths say they are satisfied that its cash reserves, expected operating cash flows and available facilities will let it pay its debts as they fall due. Dividing current assets by current liabilities gives the current ratio, which the next lesson uses, and a ratio under 1 describes the same position as a net current liability.

Current liabilities total $13,686 million, mostly trade and other payables of $8,660 million. Drawn to the same scale, liabilities are $5,995 million longer than assets.

lead.text: Read what Wikipedia says about a current ratio below 1, and find the kind of business it describes.

reveal.text: Cash that arrives before the bills do is the feature the extract describes, and Woolworths's note describes the same feature in its own words.

lead.text: Working capital is a snapshot, and to see how cash moves we count in days. Stock divided by the cost of sales it will be sold through, times 365, gives the **days of stock**. Receivables divided by revenue, times 365, gives the days a business takes to collect, and Wikipedia says days sales outstanding is better read as the days' worth of average sales you currently have outstanding. The same idea applied to suppliers, with trade payables over cost of sales, gives a rough count of the days a business takes to pay. That last count is this course's own shortcut, and it ignores accruals and other payables.

Put the three together and you have the **cash conversion cycle**: days of stock plus days to collect, less days to pay. It measures how long a business's own cash is out between paying for stock and being paid for the sale, because the days of supplier credit are days when someone else is funding the stock.

steps.headline: About how long is cash tied up in Woolworths's trading?

lead.text: This is a rough count from year-end balances, using the figures on the 2026 statements.

workedSteps.text: Days of stock: inventories of $4,465 million against cost of sales of $51,970 million.
Days to collect: trade receivables of $469 million against revenue of $71,539 million. Retail customers pay at the till, and business customers within about 24 days.
Days to pay: trade payables of $6,302 million against the same cost of sales.
The cycle adds the first two counts and takes away the third.
So customers' cash arrives about ten days before the suppliers' bills are due, which fits the reasons in Woolworths's own note. The count is rough, because it uses trade payables only.

steps.headline: Dunmore Tiles, an invented importer, holds 120 days of stock, takes 55 days to collect and pays its suppliers after 35 days. Who funds the gap?

lead.text: Dunmore has the opposite shape from Woolworths. The first and third lines are done, and the other two are yours.

workedSteps.text: Add the days the tiles sit and the days customers take to pay, to find how long it is from buying the stock to holding the cash.
Suppliers are paid on day 35. Say what that leaves.
So the cycle is the 175 days less the 35 of supplier credit.
Dunmore gives 30-day terms and customers take 55. Say what to check next.

lead.text: A count of days means something only beside the terms it is measured against. Woolworths gives business customers about 24 days and collects in about two, because most of its customers pay at the till. Dunmore gives 30 days and takes 55. Wikipedia says a high days sales outstanding may point to customers with credit problems or to weak collection work by the company, and that a low one may mean the credit policy is too tight and is hampering sales. A gap between the days and the terms shows where to ask, and the answer lies in the receivables themselves.

Last year Dunmore held 90 days of stock, took 40 days to collect and paid suppliers after 35, a cycle of 95 days. This year's 140 days comes from stock and collection both stretching while supplier terms stayed put, and someone has to fund the extra 45 days. The Lyryx textbook shows the same pattern in its own invented company, and reminds readers that ratios identify areas that need investigation and don't answer the question on their own.

afterFigure.text: In the two Dunmore views, the dashed orange stretch is the cash cycle: the days of tiles that nobody else is paying for. Woolworths's lower bar runs past its upper one, so it has none.

diagram.alt: Day counts drawn to scale for three cases. Woolworths holds about 31 days of stock, takes about 2 days to collect and pays suppliers after about 44 days, so its cycle is about minus 10 days. Dunmore Tiles this year holds 120 days of stock, takes 55 days to collect and pays after 35 days, a cycle of 140 days. Last year it held 90 days, took 40 and paid after 35, a cycle of 95 days.

lead.text: Read a negative cycle for a business that collects at the till.

reveal.text: A negative cycle is a statement about timing, and it holds only while suppliers go on giving those terms.

lead.text: Two firms have the same shortfall in working capital. Look at the shape of each cycle and at who funds it.

reveal.text: Judging a net current liability means asking what the cycle looks like and who funds it, before judging the figure itself.
