blocks.text: Woolworths's balance sheet shows current assets of $7,691 million and current liabilities of $13,686 million, so within a year it owes about $6 billion more than it holds in cash, receivables and stock. Its directors still sign the accounts as those of a going concern, a business expected to carry on, and the company explains the gap in a note of its own.
To judge a gap like that you need to know how cash moves through the business, and this lesson sets that out in days.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate a cash cycle from the statements, and say whether a low or negative working capital is a warning or part of the business model.
intro.whyItMatters: Woolworths runs with a $6 billion shortfall in working capital and explains why, so the size of the gap alone tells you little.

recap.keyIdea: A working capital below zero can be part of how a business trades, and the cash cycle in days shows whether its stock, customers and suppliers make it so.

blocks.text: Woolworths's note put its $5,995 million net current liability down to fast-turning stock and the timing of supplier payments, and the day counts bore that out with a cycle of about -10 days. Dunmore Tiles showed the opposite shape, with stock and collection days both stretching against fixed supplier terms and someone having to fund the gap. Before you judge a ratio, ask what the [[cash conversion cycle|Days of stock plus days to collect, less days to pay. Met in 'Working capital and the cash cycle'.]] looks like and who funds it.

recap.nextHook: Next we put ratios on liquidity and gearing, and look at what leases and classification can hide.

lessons.title: Liquidity and gearing

steps.headline: Can it pay what falls due?

lead.text: The **current ratio** is current assets divided by current liabilities, which Wikipedia describes as a check on whether a firm can cover its short-term obligations from what it holds. Woolworths's is $7,691 million over $13,686 million, about 0.56, and Lovisa's is $151.4 million over $185.5 million, about 0.82. Both are below 1, and the last lesson showed that this can be part of how a business trades. Lovisa's current liabilities include $87.8 million of lease liabilities due within the year.

The **quick ratio** is the stricter test. It leaves out stock, which Wikipedia says it doesn't treat as sufficiently liquid, so it sets only cash and near-cash against what is due. Woolworths's cash of $1,497 million and receivables of $1,046 million come to $2,543 million, about 0.19 of its current liabilities. Both ratios measure accounting liquidity, and neither says how fast the stock turns, which is why the cash cycle belongs beside them.

lead.text: Two firms share a current ratio but not their current assets.

reveal.text: The quick ratio is the check on what the current assets are made of.

lead.text: **Gearing**, also called leverage, is borrowing to fund the business. Wikipedia says borrowed money can produce large profits when the investment works out, and that when it doesn't the borrower may be unable to repay. A common measure is debt to equity, which compares the funds supplied by lenders with the funds supplied by owners, and which debts go into the top line is a choice that changes the answer.

Since annual periods beginning on 1 January 2019, IFRS 16 has made a lessee show a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for leases longer than 12 months, so a retailer's store leases sit on its balance sheet as liabilities. IFRS 16 itself says only that the liability is shown. Counting it as debt is this course's own reading, and the reason is that a lease is a fixed commitment to pay, much like a loan.

Woolworths's borrowings of $5,161 million over equity of $4,910 million are about 1.05, and with $11,316 million of lease liabilities added they are about 3.4. Lovisa's loans of $87.0 million over equity of $78.0 million are about 1.1, and with $419.0 million of lease liabilities added about 6.5.

afterFigure.text: The two companies look alike on borrowings and far apart once leases are counted, and Lovisa leans harder on its landlords than Woolworths does.

lead.text: Count the debts for a chain that has both loans and leases.

reveal.text: The leases are the larger part of what Hallam owes, so the figure that leaves them out is the one that misleads.

lead.text: Borrowing and leasing both bring a bill that falls due whatever the profit is. **Interest cover** is operating profit divided by finance costs, and the textbook reads it as showing how far operating income could fall before interest could not be paid. Woolworths's EBIT of $2,407 million over net finance costs of $829 million is about 2.9, so its operating profit could fall by about two thirds before it stopped covering the interest.

Finance costs include the interest on leases, which is why counting leases in gearing and in cover go together: in its cash flow statement Woolworths paid $586 million of lease interest against $236 million on its borrowings. A business with a thin margin can carry less debt than a rival and still have thinner cover, because its profit is a smaller cushion.

steps.headline: How far could Lovisa's operating profit fall before it stopped covering its finance costs?

lead.text: This uses the 2026 income statement and the lease note, in thousands of dollars.

workedSteps.text: Divide operating profit by finance costs.
Operating profit could fall to the size of the finance costs before the cover ran out, so find the share it could lose.
Most of the finance costs are lease interest, which the lease note puts at $19.7 million for the year.
Counting leases in both the gearing and the cover gives a consistent picture, and Woolworths shows the contrast.
workedSteps.math: Lovisa: gearing 6.5, cover 6.4. Woolworths: gearing 3.4, cover 2.9.

lead.text: A ratio is only as good as the lines that feed it. Wikipedia reports a finding by the Federal Court of Australia, in June 2011, that eight Centro executives and directors had breached the Corporations Act when they approved financial reports that gave no disclosure of billions of dollars in short-term debt. The sentence doesn't say how the debt was shown or how large it was, so use it for the principle: debt due within a year belongs in current liabilities, and a ratio built on a total that leaves it out looks safer than the firm is.

A ratio can also be correct and still not answer your question. Profit measures what a business earned, while gearing and interest cover measure whether it can pay what it owes, and the two can part company, as the next case shows.
Read two sources on one company, and say what they support together.

reveal.text: Profit and the ability to pay debt are different questions, and a reader needs the ratios for the second.

lead.text: Match each question a reader might ask to the ratio that answers it.

reveal.text: A ratio answers one question, so the first step in reading is to know which question you have.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a business can meet what it owes by reading the current ratio, gearing and interest cover together, and say what leases and classification can hide.
lessons.nextAction: Compare businesses by their margins and by how fast they turn assets into sales.

blocks.text: Woolworths's borrowings were $5,161 million at 28 June 2026, and Lovisa's loans were $87.0 million. Those sizes aren't comparable, so set each against the money the owners have in the business, the equity, which was $4,910 million for Woolworths and $78.0 million for Lovisa.

Wikipedia describes borrowing to invest as leverage, and says it can magnify profit but may leave the borrower unable to repay. Whether that risk is large depends on what is counted as borrowed, and on how well profit covers the cost.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read the current ratio, gearing and interest cover together, and say what leases and classification can hide.
intro.whyItMatters: Woolworths and Lovisa look alike on loans and very different once leases are counted, so which debts you count decides what you see.

recap.keyIdea: Each ratio answers one question: the current and quick ratios ask whether a business can pay what falls due soon, gearing asks how much it leans on borrowing and leases, and interest cover asks whether profit can carry the interest.

blocks.text: Woolworths and Lovisa looked alike on borrowings and far apart once leases were counted, and their interest covers of 2.9 and 6.4 times showed how much more room Lovisa's profit leaves. Centro and ABC Learning showed the limits of a ratio: it is only as honest as the lines that feed it, and a profit figure doesn't tell you whether debt can be paid. Read the [[interest cover|Operating profit divided by finance costs. Met in 'Liquidity and gearing'.]] and the gearing beside the liquidity, and choose the ratio for the question you have.

recap.nextHook: Next we compare businesses by their margins and by how fast they turn assets into sales.

lessons.title: Margins and turnover

lead.text: A **margin** is a profit divided by revenue, and it tells you how much of each dollar of sales is left once some costs are taken out. Which costs depends on the level. The **gross margin** takes out only the cost of what was sold, the **operating margin** also takes out the cost of running the business, before interest and tax, and the **net margin** takes out interest and tax as well, which is the profit margin Wikipedia describes as the percentage of profit earned for every dollar of revenue.

Woolworths's 2026 figures are a gross margin of 27.4%, an EBIT margin of 3.4% and a net margin of 1.6%, from gross profit of $19,569 million, EBIT of $2,407 million and profit of $1,152 million on revenue of $71,539 million. Lovisa's are 82.6%, 16.9% and 10.2%, from $775.3 million, $158.2 million and $95.6 million on revenue of $938.8 million.

afterFigure.text: Lovisa's margins are higher at every level. It keeps about three times as much of each sales dollar as Woolworths at the gross level and about six times as much at the net level.

lead.text: Read a firm whose margins moved in opposite directions.

reveal.text: Each margin is deducted at a different level, so a gain at the top can be lost lower down.

lead.text: A margin doesn't say how large the profit is beside what the business had to own to earn it. **Asset turnover** is revenue divided by total assets, the sales each dollar of assets produces in a year, and multiplying the net margin by it gives profit over total assets, because the margin is profit over revenue and the turnover is revenue over assets, so the revenue cancels. Wikipedia notes that return on sales doesn't account for the capital used to generate the profit, and the turnover puts that capital back in.

That settles the opening puzzle. Retailer A's 10% margin and 0.5 turns give 5%, and Retailer B's 2% margin needs 2.5 turns, five times as fast, to give the same 5%. A thin margin pays when assets turn fast, and a thick margin is needed when they don't.

afterFigure.text: The curve joins every mix of margin and turnover that earns 5%. The second view places the two real companies against it, with Woolworths below the curve and Lovisa above it.

steps.headline: What return on total assets do Woolworths and Lovisa earn, from their margins and turnovers?

lead.text: The figures come from the 2026 statements. Woolworths is in millions of dollars and Lovisa in thousands, and because each result is a ratio the units cancel.

workedSteps.text: Woolworths's net margin is its profit over its revenue.
Its asset turnover is its revenue over its total assets.
Margin times turnover gives profit over total assets, because the revenue cancels. The direct division agrees.
Lovisa's margin is 95,590 over 938,763, and its turnover is 938,763 over 696,037.
Woolworths's own report gives a return on funds employed of 16.4% before significant items. That is the company's own measure, and this lesson doesn't recompute it.

lead.text: Rank three firms by their return on assets, and not by their margins.

reveal.text: A ranking by margin and a ranking by return on assets can come out in opposite orders.

lead.text: Margins are comparable only when the same costs sit in the same lines. Lovisa's note says its cost of goods sold covers the supplier's price, shipping to its warehouse, shrinkage and obsolescence, and that its warehouse and outbound freight costs go under distribution expenses, outside gross profit. Its distribution costs were $22.2 million, about 2.4% of revenue, so a rival that put its warehouse and delivery costs inside cost of sales would show a gross margin as much as about 2.4 points lower for the same business.

Woolworths shows the same issue from another side. It reports $395 million of freight revenue inside cost of sales at the Group level, and its revenue figure excludes it. The safest comparison sits further down: by operating profit every cost has been deducted, wherever it sat above that line. So when two companies' gross margins differ, check what is inside cost of sales before drawing a conclusion, and compare operating margins.
Compare two sellers that file the same cost in different lines.

reveal.text: Where a cost sits moves the gross margin and leaves the operating margin alone.

lead.text: A margin can be reported before or after items a company calls [[significant items|Items a company reports separately from its underlying result. Met in 'Reading an income statement'.]]. Woolworths's EBIT in 2026 was $3,105 million before significant items and $2,407 million after them, a difference of $698 million, and in 2025 the difference was $569 million. That is an EBIT margin of 4.3% before and 3.4% after in 2026.

Items that appear in both years, each close to 1% of revenue, are hard to describe as unusual events. The company's figure before them is a fair place to start, and the figure after them is the one that includes everything that was charged, so a careful reader keeps both in view and asks whether the items are likely to come again.
Read the margin of a firm whose one-off costs return every year.

reveal.text: An adjusted margin is a best case when the adjustments recur.

lessons.orientation: Compare businesses by gross, operating and net margin and by asset turnover, and say what a margin cannot tell you.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether a high return on equity reflects a good business or a thin equity base.

blocks.text: Two retailers each earn a 5% return on their assets. The first keeps 10 cents of profit from every dollar it sells, and the second keeps only 2 cents. Both figures come straight from their income statements, and nobody has made a mistake.
A margin describes how much of each sales dollar is left as profit, and it says nothing yet about how many sales dollars each dollar of assets produces. To read a business you need both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compare businesses by their margins and their asset turnover, and say what a margin can't tell you.
intro.whyItMatters: Woolworths keeps about 1.6 cents from each sales dollar and Lovisa keeps about 10, and the margin alone doesn't say which earns more on its assets.

recap.keyIdea: A margin shows how much of each sales dollar is left at some level, and it has to be read with asset turnover and with what sits in each cost line, because the same return can come from a thin margin and fast turnover or a thick margin and slow turnover.

blocks.text: You computed three margins for Woolworths and Lovisa, then multiplied each net margin by [[asset turnover|Revenue divided by total assets. Met in 'Margins and turnover'.]] to reach a return on assets of about 3.4% for one and 13.7% for the other. You also saw that gross margins depend on where costs are put, which makes the operating margin the safer comparison, and that items called significant which appear in both years belong in any forecast.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at return on equity, and at how a thin equity base can make a return look better than the business is.

lessons.title: Return on equity and return on capital

lead.text: Maya's answer is the idea behind **return on equity**, or ROE: the profit that belongs to the owners, divided by the owners' equity. Equity is what remains of the assets once the liabilities are taken away, so ROE says how many dollars of profit each dollar of the owners' money produced.

Which equity should we divide by? Profit is earned across the whole year while equity moves, so the usual practice is to divide by the average of the opening and closing equity. Woolworths made $1,138 million for its own shareholders, and their equity went from $4,860 million to $4,795 million, an average of about $4,828 million, which puts its ROE at about 24%. Lovisa made $95.6 million on equity that went from $78.6 million to $78.0 million, an average of $78.3 million, so its ROE is about 122%.

afterFigure.text: Wikipedia says ROE is used mostly to compare companies in the same industry, and that 15 to 20% is generally considered good. Woolworths sits above that range and Lovisa far above it, which leaves a question about what each ratio is measuring.

reveal.text: Equity is the denominator, so two companies with the same trading can show quite different ratios.

lead.text: To see what a return on equity is made of, we can split it into three parts that multiply together, which is known as the **DuPont split**. The first part is [[net margin|The profit kept from each dollar of sales. Met in 'Margins and turnover'.]], the profit kept from each dollar of sales. The second is [[asset turnover|The sales made with each dollar of assets. Met in 'Margins and turnover'.]], the sales made with each dollar of assets, and you met both in the last lesson. The third is new. **Assets over equity**, which Wikipedia calls accounting leverage, says how many dollars of assets stand behind each dollar of the owners' money.

Multiply the three and the sales cancel, and so do the assets, which leaves profit over equity. The figure does it for Woolworths on average figures: 1.6 cents kept from each dollar of sales, times $2.10 of sales for each dollar of assets, times $7.00 of assets for each dollar of equity, which comes to about 24%.

afterFigure.text: The second view is a what-if and not a forecast. Keep Woolworths's shops, sales and profit as they are, halve its equity, and only the last box changes: assets over equity doubles to about 14 and the return jumps to about 47%. A real company that did this would pay more interest, so the true jump would be smaller, but the direction is the same, and nothing about the stores has improved.

diagram.alt: Four boxes joined by multiplication and equals signs: net margin, asset turnover, assets over equity and return on equity. For Woolworths the values are 1.6%, 2.1, 7.0 and about 24%. In the second view the equity is halved, assets over equity doubles to about 14 and the return becomes about 47%.

lead.text: Why is Lovisa's equity so small? A return above 100% needs equity that is smaller than one year's profit, and Lovisa's is: $78.0 million of equity against $95.6 million of profit. The first view of the figure shows one reason. Shareholders put in $215.7 million of issued capital, and a line called the common control reserve is negative $208.9 million, so those two lines together leave only $6.8 million. The label tells us little about where that reserve came from, and this lesson doesn't go into it. What matters for the ratio is what the line does, which is to cancel nearly all of the issued capital.

afterFigure.text: The second view shows the year. Lovisa earned $95.6 million and paid $88.6 million of it out as dividends, 93% of the profit, so almost nothing was left to add to equity, and equity ended the year at $78.0 million, a little below the $78.6 million it began with. A company that pays out nearly all of its profit never builds equity up behind it, so the ratio stays high.
Neither fact is a fault in the business. They explain why the figure sits above 100%, while the split showed that the shops themselves earn a good deal more per dollar of sales than Woolworths's do.

reveal.text: A very high return on equity points first at the equity: a small denominator, made small by payouts and by reserves.

steps.headline: Two invented retailers earn 20% on equity, with assets twice equity. What turnover does the one with a 2% margin need?

workedSteps.text: Write return on equity as net margin times asset turnover times assets over equity.
Divide both sides by the assets over equity of 2, to find what margin times turnover must be for both retailers.
Check the first retailer, whose margin is 10% and whose turnover is 1.
The second retailer's margin is 2%, so its turnover is the number that turns 2% into 10%.
Read the result in cents. The first retailer keeps 10c of each dollar of sales and sells a dollar's worth for each dollar of assets, while the second keeps 2c and sells five dollars' worth.

lead.text: Each retailer has assets twice its equity. The first has a 10% net margin and turns its assets over once a year, and the second has a net margin of 2%. The method is to find what margin times turnover must be, and then solve for the missing factor.

The split shows what drives a return on equity, and it shows why the ratio is awkward for comparing companies: its third factor depends on how a business is funded. Two companies with identical shops and sales can report different ROEs because one has borrowed more or paid out more.

**Return on capital** takes the funding out of the picture. It divides the after-tax operating profit by the capital that shareholders and lenders have put in. Operating profit is counted before interest, and the capital adds equity and debt together, so swapping one for the other changes neither the top of the ratio nor the bottom. Annual reports leave you to build it, and we will use a simple version at year end: operating profit less tax at the company's own rate, divided by equity plus borrowings plus [[lease liabilities|What a company owes under leases, such as its shop rents. Met in 'Reading a balance sheet'.]], less cash, since cash in the bank isn't being used to run the shops. Counting leases as capital is this course's own choice and the reports don't do it for you; it puts a company that rents its shops on the same footing as one that borrowed to buy them.

afterFigure.text: On this method Woolworths earns about 9% on its capital, or about 11% if its significant items are left out, and Lovisa earns about 21%. The gap of five to one in return on equity has narrowed to about two and a half to one, and Lovisa is still ahead, so its shops do earn more on the money in them. Woolworths also reports its own return on funds employed, 16.4% before significant items. The report gives the name and the figure but not the formula, so the figure can't be set beside ours. When you compare companies, use one method for all of them.

diagram.alt: How a rough return on capital is built for Woolworths and Lovisa, and how it compares with return on equity. After-tax operating profit is 1,757 million dollars for Woolworths and 112.8 million for Lovisa. Capital, equity plus borrowings plus lease liabilities less cash, is 19,890 and 537.2. Returns on capital are 8.8% and 21.0%, against returns on equity of about 24% and 122%.

steps.headline: Kestrel Cafés is invented and earns an operating profit of $4.5 million, taxed at 30%. What is its return on capital?

workedSteps.text: Take tax off the operating profit to find the after-tax operating profit.
Add up the capital that funds the business, and take off the cash.
Divide the after-tax operating profit by the capital.
Read it in cents. Kestrel earns about 17c a year on each dollar of capital, whether the dollar came from the owners, the bank or the landlord.

lead.text: Its equity is $8 million, its borrowings $6 million, its lease liabilities $9 million and its cash $4 million. The first and last lines are done, and the two in between are yours.

reveal.text: Before trusting a return, look at what it divides by. A figure that funding cannot move is the safer one for comparing businesses.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a high return on equity reflects a good business or a thin equity base, and use a return on capital to compare businesses fairly.
lessons.reviewLabel: Return on equity and return on capital
lessons.nextAction: Find a policy, an estimate and a going concern note in an annual report, and say what each commits the company to.

blocks.text: Lovisa earned $95.6 million for its shareholders in the year to 28 June 2026, and the owners' equity on its balance sheet stands at about $78 million. Divide the first by the second and the return is more than 100% in a single year. The same sum for Woolworths, which earned $1,138 million for its shareholders on equity of about $4.8 billion, gives about 24%.

A ratio of 122% beside one of 24% looks like a verdict on which business is better. Before taking it that way, we need to ask what the ratio divides by, because the owners' share of a business can be large or small for reasons that have little to do with how the shops trade.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to take a return on equity apart, say what a very high one is made of, and use a return on capital to compare businesses that are funded differently.
intro.whyItMatters: A return on equity is easy to find and easy to misread, because it depends on how the business is funded as well as on how well it trades.

recap.keyIdea: A return on equity compares profit with the owners' own money, so read its three parts and its denominator before trusting it, and compare businesses that are funded differently on return on capital.

blocks.text: You split Woolworths's return of about 24% and Lovisa's of about 122% into [[net margin|The profit kept from each dollar of sales. Met in 'Margins and turnover'.]], asset turnover and assets over equity, and found that Lovisa's much higher margin does most of the work while its equity, about a ninth of its assets, adds a smaller lift. That equity is smaller than a year's profit because Lovisa paid out 93% of its profit and carries a negative common control reserve. Built the same way for both, a return on capital shrinks the gap from about five to one to about two and a half to one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes through the notes to the statements, where a company says how its figures were put together and what they contain.

lessons.title: Reading the notes

lead.text: The notes are part of the financial statements. They don't repeat the balance sheet, the income statement or the cash flow statement. They give the details those leave out: the accounting policies a company followed, a breakdown of the larger lines, and the estimates behind the figures. Each line on a statement carries a note number in a column of its own, as Woolworths's revenue line does, and that number is the way to the note.

An annual report holds several kinds of writing, and each answers a different question. The statements give the totals. The notes say how the totals were built and what they contain. The auditor's report is an independent examiner's opinion on whether the statements are free of material misstatement. The directors' report sits alongside them and includes the remuneration report.

afterFigure.text: Woolworths states its basis in its first note: the report is prepared under the Corporations Act 2001 and Australian Accounting Standards, and it complies with IFRS as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board. That sentence tells you which rules were used to prepare the numbers. It says nothing about whether the business is sound.

The second view lists the three notes Woolworths names as critical estimates.

lead.text: The label on a statement names a group, and the note says what is inside it. Woolworths's balance sheet shows cash and cash equivalents of $1,497 million, which a reader would take as money in bank accounts. The notes qualify that. They say that $695 million of it, up from $684 million the year before, relates to receivables from credit card merchants, for electronic transfers and for card payments at the point of sale, and that the equivalent amount will be reclassified from cash to receivables in the 2027 financial period.

afterFigure.text: So $695 million of the $1,497 million, about 46%, is money owed to Woolworths from card payments, and the other $802 million is everything else in the line. Does that make the cash figure wrong? It doesn't, because the note says openly what the line contains. What you gain is the chance to decide whether the full figure suits the question you are asking.

lead.text: Every set of statements rests on estimates: how long an asset will last, how much of a debt will be collected, what a claim will cost to settle. A company doesn't have to give them all equal weight, and Woolworths picks out three. In its note on critical accounting estimates and judgements it says that the ones with a higher degree of complexity, or a significant risk of causing a material adjustment to the amounts in its statements, are in Note 3.5 Leases, Note 3.9 Impairment of non-financial assets and Note 3.12 Provisions.

That sentence works as a map. If you want to know where a company's figures could later turn out to be wrong, these are the notes to read first. The same paragraph adds that revisions to accounting estimates are recognised prospectively, which means a change counts from the year it is made onward and the earlier years stay as they were reported.

reveal.text: A provision is an estimate of a cost still to come, and Note 3.12 is where Woolworths explains its estimates of that kind.

lead.text: A company's statements are prepared on the assumption that it will carry on trading, and the **going concern note** is where the directors say whether they still think so. Woolworths's note says the directors expected, when they approved the report, that the group has enough resources to keep operating for the foreseeable future. Its current liabilities exceed its current assets by $5,995 million, so the note gives reasons: the fast-turning nature of its inventories, the timing of payments to suppliers, funds used for investments classed as non-current, and its current lease obligations. It ends by saying the directors are satisfied that cash reserves, expected cash flows from operations and available facilities will let the group pay its debts as they fall due.

What does a note like this commit the directors to? It is their own judgement, formed on the day they approved the report, so it is a statement they answer for and not a figure you can read off the balance sheet. It says what the judgement rests on, which here is cash, operating cash flows and facilities. And it explains anything that would otherwise look alarming, as the reasons do for a net current liability.

reveal.text: What a note commits the directors to is a judgement they stand behind, and what it rests on is the part you can test.

lead.text: An **audit** is an independent examination of a company's statements and of its internal controls. The textbook that describes it is careful with one word: an audit seeks reasonable assurance, not certainty, that the information is not materially misstated. It gives a reader some confidence that the statements are trustworthy, and it is not a verdict on the business.

The responsibility sits with the directors first. ASIC puts the main responsibility for a financial report on the directors, and names asset values, provisions, revenue from contracts with customers, capitalised spending and expected credit losses as the harder areas, which call for appropriate expertise. Two of Woolworths's three critical estimates, impairment of non-financial assets and provisions, come under the first two of those areas, so the company's own list and the regulator's point at the same places.

reveal.text: An opinion about the statements is a smaller thing than a verdict on the business.
A note that names its own support has told you where to look next.

lessons.orientation: Find what you need in an annual report beyond the three statements, and read a policy, an estimate and a going concern note for what they commit the company to.
lessons.nextAction: Read a set of statements for warning signs, and say what to check next without jumping to a verdict.

blocks.text: Woolworths's income statement for the year to 28 June 2026 opens with a line for revenue. The figure is $71,539 million, and a small number beside it, 2.1, points to a note. Behind that single total sit millions of sales, and each one had to be judged: has the customer taken the goods yet, is some of the money still owed back, is a loyalty point a discount or a debt?

The statement gives you the sum, and the notes say how it was put together. Much of what you need in order to judge a company's numbers sits in them, so it helps to know what the notes hold and how to find the right one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find your way around an annual report, read a note against the line it explains, and say what a policy, an estimate and a going concern note commit a company to.
intro.whyItMatters: The face of a statement gives a total, and the note says what the total is made of and how it was judged.

recap.keyIdea: The notes are part of the statements, and they say what each line contains, which estimates it rests on and what the directors commit to, so read the note before you rely on the line.

blocks.text: You found that Lovisa's receivables line holds only about a tenth in money customers owe, and that Woolworths's cash includes $695 million of card receivables, and in both cases the note changed how the line should be read. Woolworths names leases, impairment and provisions as its critical estimates, and its going concern note rests the directors' view on cash, operating cash flows and facilities. An audit gives [[reasonable assurance|Confidence that the statements are not materially misstated, which is short of certainty. Met in 'Reading the notes'.]] about the statements and is not a verdict on the business.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses what the notes show to read a set of statements for warning signs, and to decide what to check next.

lessons.title: Warning signs

lead.text: Profit counts a sale when it is made, whether or not the money has come in, and cash counts only the money. Over a few years the two should keep roughly in step, and how closely they do is called the **quality of earnings**. Add up Alder's three years and the profit comes to 46, while the cash that came in from operations comes to 12.

afterFigure.text: Where did the cash go? Most of that gap is sitting in receivables. In years two and three together, profit was 33 above operating cash flow, and receivables rose by 40, from 12 to 52, so Alder has been recording sales and waiting for the money. For a company growing fast on reliable customers that could be harmless. It is also what the early stages of a problem look like, and the figures alone can't tell you which.

diagram.alt: Paired bars for each of three years for Alder. Profit is 10, 15 and 21. Operating cash flow is 9, 6 and negative 3. Over the three years profit adds up to 46 and operating cash flow to 12.
diagram.caption: Profit against operating cash flow, in millions of dollars. The company is invented.

lead.text: Receivables show what customers owe, so a company whose receivables grow faster than its sales is either giving customers longer to pay or selling to customers who pay less reliably. Alder's revenue rose 1.7 times over the three years and its receivables 4.3 times. Divide receivables by revenue and multiply by 365 and you have the days of sales still uncollected: about 44 days in year one, 79 in year two and 112 in year three.

A balance sheet doesn't show receivables at face value. The company takes off an **allowance for doubtful accounts**, its estimate of the amount it doesn't expect to collect, usually worked out by ageing the receivables, since the longer an account has been outstanding, the less likely it is to be collected. The textbook that describes the allowance notes that it seldom matches what finally proves uncollectible. So when receivables outrun sales, two questions follow: how old the receivables are, and whether the allowance has grown with them.

reveal.text: Receivables that grow faster than sales have to be collected from someone, so how old they are is the first question.

lead.text: In 2016 ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, issued a media release on Slater and Gordon, a legal services company with businesses in Australia and the UK. It says ASIC had made inquiries about the firm's financial reports for the years ended 30 June 2014 and 30 June 2015, and that the inquiries mainly concerned four things: whether the goodwill of its Australian and UK businesses was recoverable, how it recognised fee revenue and the related work in progress, the provisions it held against debtors and disbursement assets, and the basis for classing work in progress and disbursements as current assets.

afterFigure.text: Every item on that list is a judgement: what an acquired business is worth, when a fee counts as earned, how much of a debt will be collected, when an asset will turn into cash. In the half year to 31 December 2015 the firm impaired goodwill, reduced the value of its work in progress when it adopted a new revenue standard, and increased its provisions against debtor and disbursement assets. ASIC then discontinued its inquiries into the two earlier reports.

diagram.alt: A four-row list of what ASIC's media release on Slater and Gordon describes: inquiries about the reports for the years to 30 June 2014 and 2015; part of work in progress and disbursements moved to non-current in the 2015 report; goodwill impaired, work in progress reduced and provisions increased in the half year to 31 December 2015; and inquiries discontinued.

reveal.text: A regulator closing its inquiries is a statement about the inquiries. It says nothing in favour of the accounts unless it says so.

lead.text: Two Australian cases from the lesson on liquidity and gearing show the warning sitting in the debt. In June 2011 the Federal Court of Australia found that eight executives and directors of Centro had breached the Corporations Act by signing off financial reports that failed to disclose billions of dollars of short-term debt. ASIC brought the action, and the court's finding was about what the reports said and left unsaid.

ABC Learning was highly profitable on the numbers: Wikipedia's account gives a net profit after tax of $52.3 million on revenue of $292.7 million in 2004/5, with rapid growth in the number of its centres. Profit then fell 42%, to $37.1 million, in the second half of 2007, and the company could not service its $1.8 billion of debt. It went into receivership in November 2008, with its auditors unable to sign off on its accounts. The profit figure said little about how much the company owed, which is why a reader needs the balance sheet and the interest cover next to the income statement.

reveal.text: An income statement says how the year went, and the balance sheet and notes say what is owed.

lead.text: Enron is the extreme case of the first pattern. According to Wikipedia's account, Enron used mark-to-market accounting for long-term contracts: once a contract was signed, income was estimated as the present value of the net future cash flow and recorded at once. The article says income could be recorded although the firm might never have received the money, which produced large discrepancies between reported profits and cash. Because that profit could not be counted again, new income had to be found from more projects each year to keep the growth going.

Two terms describe how a gap like this can arise. **Creative accounting** follows the letter of the accounting rules but departs from their spirit, in favour of the people who prepare the figures. **Earnings management** is the use of judgement in reporting, or in structuring transactions, to alter reported results, either to mislead some stakeholders or to influence outcomes that depend on reported numbers, such as a bonus. Wikipedia adds that research links large accruals and weak governance with earnings management, and accruals are what make profit differ from cash. That is why the first check on any set of statements is to set profit against cash.

reveal.text: Profit that runs ahead of cash year after year is the pattern to look for, and the cash flow statement is where it shows.

lead.text: None of these patterns proves anything. Creative accounting can follow the rules, and a debt that is hard to see or a sale counted early uses ordinary accounting, so a pattern is a reason to ask a question and not a verdict. ASIC says directors are primarily responsible for their financial report, and an audit gives reasonable assurance and not certainty, so the reader's own questions count.

Five checks, in this order, take you most of the way. Set three years of profit against operating cash flow. Set receivables against revenue. Look for write-downs and changes in estimates. See how debt is classified and what the notes say about it. And ask whether the same one-off charge turns up year after year. Woolworths's significant items were $698 million in 2026 and $569 million in 2025. That is only two years, too few to call a pattern, and the useful question is what the items are. Some patterns are normal: the going concern note you read in the last lesson gives a reason for Woolworths's net current liability, and a very high return on equity can come from thin equity.

diagram.alt: A table of five checks. Profit and cash: profit up and cash down, ask what absorbed the cash. Receivables: growing faster than revenue, ask how old they are. Write-downs: late, large or changing, ask which estimate changed. Debt: short-term debt hard to see, ask what the notes say. One-offs: the same item every year, ask what makes it one-off.

steps.headline: Brindle Ltd is invented. What do the first two checks show for its three years?

workedSteps.text: Check one: add up three years of profit and of operating cash flow.
Compare the two totals.
Check two: work out the days of sales in receivables for each year, receivables divided by revenue times 365.
Read the trend in the days.
Neither check raises a question. That does not show everything is well, because two checks can't rule out a problem, so the next step is the notes on policy changes and estimates.
workedSteps.math: No warning from two checks, so read the notes

lead.text: Its revenue over the three years is 200, 230 and 250, its profit 20, 24 and 27, its operating cash flow 22, 25 and 28, and its receivables 30, 34 and 37. The sums are done, and the readings are yours.

reveal.text: A change in estimate is a judgement. The check is how far it moves profit and whether the new figure is sound.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to spot the common warning signs in a set of statements, say what to check next, and say why a warning sign is a question and not a verdict.
intro.whyItMatters: Most problems show first in how profit, cash, receivables and debt move together, and the right response to a pattern is a question.

recap.keyIdea: A warning sign is a pattern that calls for a question, such as profit that does not turn into cash, receivables that outrun sales, estimates that move or debt that is hard to see, and the right response is to check the next thing and not to reach a verdict.

blocks.text: You set Alder's profit of 46 against operating cash of 12 and saw receivables rise 4.3 times while revenue rose 1.7 times. In Slater and Gordon, Centro and ABC Learning the questions lay in asset values, revenue, debt and how debt was shown, and ASIC's closing of its inquiries was not a clean bill. Wikipedia's account of Enron shows profit far ahead of cash at the extreme, which is why the five checks start by setting [[profit against cash|The gap between profit and operating cash flow. Met in 'Why profit is not cash'.]].

recap.nextHook: The last lesson turns to what a business is worth, and what a share price assumes about the earnings and cash behind it.

lessons.title: What a business is worth

lead.text: The **price-to-earnings ratio**, or P/E, is the share price divided by earnings per share. Wikipedia gives a plain reading of it: a share at $24 that earns $3 has a P/E of 8, so the buyer is paying for eight years of this year's earnings. Lovisa's figure for 2024 is $32.87 over 75.4 cents, about 44, and for 2026 it is $23.25 over 86.3 cents, about 27.

afterFigure.text: Does a lower P/E mean the shares are cheap? It doesn't. A buyer pays 27 years of today's earnings only if the earnings are expected to grow, and the ratio fell because the price fell faster than earnings rose. Buyers may expect slower growth, or they may doubt the earnings more, and the ratio doesn't say which. Wikipedia reports that investors often call a P/E of 10 to 20 fairly priced, and adds that it depends on the sector and the business. Lovisa's was above that range in each of the five years.

lead.text: Profit isn't cash, and what owners and lenders can eventually be paid is cash. **Free cash flow** is the operating cash flow left after the spending a business has to make to carry on. Wikipedia describes it as the part of cash flow that can be taken out and paid to lenders and shareholders without causing problems in operations. It differs from profit because it counts spending on equipment and changes in working capital, and it leaves out non-cash charges.

The statements don't print it, so you build it. For Woolworths, operating cash flow was $4,948 million, its payments for property, plant, equipment and intangibles were $2,435 million, and it repaid $1,298 million of lease principal, which sits under financing but is the cost of keeping its stores. That leaves about $1,215 million. Treating lease principal as a cost is the reader's adjustment, as in the cash flow lesson, and the report does not do it for you.

afterFigure.text: Set that against Woolworths's profit of $1,152 million and the $1,100 million it paid in dividends. Free cash flow is a little above both, so the dividend was covered by the cash left after the shops and the leases.

lead.text: A balance sheet records what a business has done, and a price says what buyers expect it to do, so the two can be far apart. Assets are recorded at cost, changes in their market value are generally not recorded, and nothing on the balance sheet records a business's earning power. Lovisa's equity is $78.0 million. Divided by about 110.7 million shares, the number implied by its profit and its earnings per share, that is about $0.70 a share, against a price of $23.25, which is about 33 times as much.

afterFigure.text: Which of the two is the value of the business? Neither. The balance sheet figure leaves out earning power. ASIC cautions that a share price is not the value either: a price reflects trades in small parts of a business, a whole business may sell in a thin market, and a buyer may expect gains from combining it with its own. ASIC says a company's market capitalisation will generally not be an appropriate fair value for its underlying business, though it can be a cross-check.

reveal.text: A gap between price and equity per share is a question about earnings, and it is not by itself a verdict.

lead.text: A **discounted cash flow** valuation estimates the cash a business will produce in future years and discounts each year's cash, because money that arrives later is worth less than money in hand now. Wikipedia describes it as a method that values a security, project, company or asset with the time value of money built in. The forecast usually covers a few years in detail and then adds a continuing value for everything beyond, called the **terminal value**.

afterFigure.text: The figure uses an invented business expected to bring in $100 million a year for 30 years. Discounted at 8% a year its cash is worth about $1,126 million today, and at 10% about $943 million, which is 16% less for a rate only two points higher. At either rate more than half of the value comes from after year five. Wikipedia says terminal value is often a large share of the total and is highly sensitive to growth and discount rate assumptions. The arithmetic of a discounted cash flow is exact, and the answer is only as good as the forecast and the rate behind it.

diagram.alt: Bars showing the present value of an invented business that pays 100 million dollars a year for 30 years. At 8% a year the blocks of years 1 to 5, 6 to 10, 11 to 20 and 21 to 30 are worth about 399, 272, 311 and 144, a total of about 1,126. At 10% they are worth about 379, 235, 237 and 91, a total of about 943.
diagram.caption: Each bar is the present value of a block of years. Use the buttons to compare an 8% rate with a 10% rate. The business is invented.

reveal.text: Most of the value of a long forecast sits a long way off, and that is where a change of rate bites.

lead.text: A share price covers only the shareholders' claim, and a business is funded by lenders too. **Enterprise value** is the sum of the claims of everyone who funds it, creditors and shareholders, and Wikipedia calls it more comprehensive than market capitalisation, which reflects only common equity. A simple way to understand it is to imagine buying the whole business: you would pay the shareholders for their shares, settle with the lenders, and receive the business's cash, so cash is taken off. In outline, enterprise value is market capitalisation plus debt, less cash.

That puts a heavily borrowed company and a debt-free one on the same footing. The reports we have used print a share price and not a market capitalisation, so the questions here use invented companies.

reveal.text: Enterprise value is what the whole business costs, and it counts every claim on it.
A price is a view of future earnings and risk. The ratio shows the view, and growth, risk and cash are what you ask about next.

lessons.orientation: Read a price-to-earnings ratio, a free cash flow figure and an enterprise value for what they say about a business, and say why accounting profit alone does not give its value.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a set of statements for what they show: how a business is funded, whether its profit turns into cash, which figures rest on estimates, and what a price assumes.

blocks.text: Lovisa's annual report gives a share price of $23.25 for 2026, against earnings of 86.3 cents for each share. For 2024 it gives $32.87 and 75.4 cents. Earnings per share went up by about 14% and the price went down by about 29%.

Earnings rose and the price fell, so something changed in what buyers were willing to pay for each dollar of profit. A price and a profit each say little alone, and the relation between them, with the cash behind the profit, is something the statements can help us read. None of it gives a business's worth outright, but it shows what a price is assuming.
