intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a price-to-earnings ratio, free cash flow and enterprise value, and say what a share price assumes about a business.
intro.whyItMatters: These measures turn a share price into questions about growth, cash and risk that the statements can help answer.

recap.keyIdea: A price-to-earnings ratio, free cash flow, equity per share, a discounted cash flow and enterprise value each turn a price into a question about growth, cash and risk, and none of them gives a business's worth on its own.

blocks.text: You saw Lovisa's P/E fall from about 44 to about 27 as its earnings rose, and Woolworths's come to about 43 on its statutory earnings and about 31 before significant items. Woolworths's free cash flow of about $1,215 million covered its dividend, while Lovisa's, about $85 million, fell a little short of its own. Equity of $0.70 a share against a price of $23.25 sets cost against expectation. A [[discounted cash flow|A value found by discounting forecast cash for the time value of money. Met in 'What a business is worth'.]] value moves a good deal with its rate because so much of it lies far ahead, and enterprise value counts the lenders' claims as well as the shareholders'.

questions.prompt: Lovisa holds about $696 million of cash, stock, equipment and store rights. Who do you think paid for most of it?
hints: Lovisa leases its stores and has loans. Who is owed the money in those arrangements?
Think of the two ways money can be put in, and which one a store lease and a loan belong to.

acceptedIdeas: Mostly the people it owes, with shareholders paying for about a tenth
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mostly the people it owes, with shareholders paying for about a tenth

choices.label: Shareholders paid for nearly all of it, and the company owes almost nothing to anyone
Shareholders and the people it owes each paid for roughly half of it
Mostly the people it owes, with shareholders paying for about a tenth

questions.onCorrect: The owners' share is about $78 million of $696 million, around 11%. Most of what Lovisa holds is covered by amounts it owes, and the largest are the payments due under its store leases.

misconceptions.feedback: Almost nothing owed would mean no store leases and no loans. Lovisa has both, and each is an amount owed to someone other than its shareholders.
An even split would leave the owners with roughly $350 million at stake. Count how much Lovisa owes for its leases before settling on that.

questions.prompt: These ten lines come from Woolworths's balance sheet at 28 June 2026. Which group does each one belong to?
hints: Ask of each line whether it is something the company holds, something it must pay, or part of the owners' share.
A line can mention equity in its name and still be an asset. Think about where the report places it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assets: inventories, lease assets, trade and other receivables and the equity-method investments. Liabilities: trade and other payables, lease liabilities, provisions and borrowings. Equity: retained earnings and contributed equity.

items.label: Inventories
items.explanation: Stock on hand is something the company holds, and the report lists it among the current assets.

items.label: Lease assets
items.explanation: The right to use leased stores is an asset, the other half of the lease pair.

items.label: Trade and other receivables
items.explanation: Money that customers owe the company is something it holds a claim to, so it is an asset.

items.label: Investments accounted for using the equity method
items.explanation: The report lists it among the non-current assets, whatever the word equity in its name suggests.

items.label: Trade and other payables
items.explanation: It is what the company owes its suppliers and others for goods and services.

items.label: Lease liabilities
items.explanation: It is the obligation to make lease payments, the other half of the lease pair.

items.label: Provisions
items.explanation: A provision is an amount the company expects to pay later, so it is listed among the liabilities.

items.label: Borrowings
items.explanation: Loans are amounts owed to lenders.

items.label: Retained earnings
items.explanation: Profit kept in the business belongs to the owners, so it sits in equity.

items.label: Contributed equity
items.explanation: It is the money shareholders put into the company, and it is part of equity.

questions.onCorrect: Assets are what the company holds, liabilities what it owes, and equity the owners' share. Where a line sits in the report shows which, and a word in its name can mislead.

questions.prompt: Woolworths has total assets of $34,065 million and total liabilities of $29,155 million. Roughly how much of its assets is left for the owners, and what does that show?
hints: Equity is what is left of the assets once the liabilities are taken away. Work out roughly how much that is.
Compare the leftover with the $34,065 million of assets. Is it closer to a tenth, a third or a half?

acceptedIdeas: About 14% of its assets, because creditors paid for most of what it holds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 14% of its assets, because creditors paid for most of what it holds

choices.label: About 1% of its assets, because liabilities nearly match what it holds
About 14% of its assets, because creditors paid for most of what it holds
About 40% of its assets, because owners paid for a large part of what it holds
About 70% of its assets, because owners usually pay for most of what it holds

questions.onCorrect: Equity is $4,910 million, about 14% of $34,065 million. Lovisa's 11% and Woolworths's 14% are both thin slices.

misconceptions.feedback: A 1% share would be about $340 million. The gap between assets and liabilities is more than ten times that.
A 40% share would need liabilities of about $20,000 million. The statement shows $29,155 million.
A 70% share would leave the creditors with under a third of the assets. Here they paid for most of them.

questions.prompt: A reader sees Woolworths's equity of $4,910 million, next to cash of $1,497 million, and says the owners could take $4.9 billion out of the business tomorrow. Which reply fits the balance sheet?
hints: Compare the two figures in the question. If equity were cash, how large would the cash line be?
Think about what a supermarket's assets are made of: shelves of stock, stores, equipment and leases the business needs to keep trading.

acceptedIdeas: Equity is assets less liabilities as recorded, and most of those assets are in use
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equity is assets less liabilities as recorded, and most of those assets are in use

choices.label: Equity is assets less liabilities as recorded, and most of those assets are in use
Equity is cash held on the owners' behalf, so $4.9 billion is there to be withdrawn
Equity is the market price of the business, so a buyer would pay about $4.9 billion

questions.onCorrect: Equity is a recorded difference between two totals, and the assets behind it are mostly stock, stores and equipment still in use. Nothing in the statement sets that amount aside as cash.

misconceptions.feedback: The balance sheet shows cash of $1,497 million, well under the equity figure. Equity is calculated as a difference, so it does not describe a cash balance.
Assets sit on the balance sheet at what they cost, and later changes in what they could be sold for are generally not recorded. Equity therefore says little about a sale price.

questions.prompt: Woolworths lists borrowings of $401 million among its current liabilities and $4,760 million among its non-current liabilities. What does the split tell you?
hints: Current means expected to turn into cash, or to be paid, within the next year or so.
Think of the two lines as the same loans sorted by when each part is due.

acceptedIdeas: About $401 million falls due within the next year and the rest falls due later
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $401 million falls due within the next year and the rest falls due later

choices.label: The $401 million is interest owed on the loan and the $4,760 million is the amount borrowed
The larger amount comes second because it is the one the company repays first
About $401 million falls due within the next year and the rest falls due later

questions.onCorrect: Current liabilities fall due within the next year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer. The $401 million is the part of the borrowings due soon, and the rest is due later.

misconceptions.feedback: Both lines are borrowings. The split sorts them by when each part is due, and interest would be a separate matter.
The order follows timing and not size. Items due within the year come first, whatever their amounts.

questions.prompt: Kessel Books, an invented bookshop chain, signs a ten-year lease on a new store. What does its balance sheet show once the lease starts?
hints: The standard on leases applies to any lease of more than 12 months.
Ask what the company gets from the contract and what it must pay for it. Each answer is a line on the balance sheet.

acceptedIdeas: A right to use the store, and a matching obligation to make the lease payments
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A right to use the store, and a matching obligation to make the lease payments

choices.label: Nothing yet, because the rent is recorded only as each payment falls due
A right to use the store, and a matching obligation to make the lease payments
The whole store as an asset owned outright, paid for with the owners' money
A bank loan for the full price of the store, with the store itself as the asset

questions.onCorrect: Under IFRS 16 a lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for a lease of more than 12 months. The two describe one contract, so they appear together.

misconceptions.feedback: A ten-year lease is longer than 12 months, so the contract is recorded when it starts. A lessee shows both the right it holds and the payments it owes.
Kessel Books does not own the store. It holds a right to use it, and the payments it has agreed to make are a liability.
A lease liability is the obligation to make the lease payments. It is not a bank loan, and the company has not borrowed the price of the building.

questions.prompt: Two invented retailers each hold $10 million of assets. Firm A owes $9 million and Firm B owes $4 million. Each then writes $2 million off its assets after a fire. Which description fits?
hints: Liabilities do not change when an asset is written off. Equity is what is left, so it takes the whole loss.
Work out each firm's assets after the fire and compare them with what it owes.

acceptedIdeas: Firm A's remaining assets no longer cover what it owes, while Firm B's still do
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Firm A's remaining assets no longer cover what it owes, while Firm B's still do

choices.label: Both are hit equally, because each firm lost the same $2 million of assets
Firm A's remaining assets no longer cover what it owes, while Firm B's still do
Firm B is hit harder, because it has more equity there to be lost
Only Firm A is hit, because Firm B's liabilities absorb the loss in its case

questions.onCorrect: Firm A has $8 million of assets against $9 million owed, so its equity is gone and more. Firm B has $8 million against $4 million owed and keeps $4 million. The same loss falls harder on the thinner slice.

misconceptions.feedback: The dollars lost are equal, and the effect is not. Liabilities are fixed, so equity takes the loss, and Firm A has little equity to take it.
Firm B has more equity, and that is why it can absorb the loss. Compare what each firm has left after the fire with what it owes.
Writing off an asset does not reduce a liability. Equity, the leftover, takes the whole loss in both firms.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Bakehouse, an invented company, sorts its balance sheet lines by timing. Which are current and which are non-current?
hints: Ask of each line whether it will be turned into cash, used up or paid within the next 12 months.
A loan can appear in both groups, because the part due soon is current and the rest is not.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Current: flour and sugar, money cafes owe, amounts owed to the supplier and the loan instalment due in six months. Non-current: the ovens, the rest of the loan, the right to use the shop and the lease payments due later.

items.label: Flour and sugar in the storeroom
items.explanation: Stock is expected to be used up within the year.

items.label: Money cafes owe for bread, due in 30 days
items.explanation: Customers' debts due within 30 days will be collected within the year.

items.label: Amounts owed to the flour supplier, due in 30 days
items.explanation: A liability due within the year is current.

items.label: The loan instalment due in six months
items.explanation: The part of a loan that falls due within 12 months is current.

items.label: The ovens
items.explanation: Equipment is used over several years, so it is non-current.

items.label: The rest of the loan, due over four years
items.explanation: It falls due after the next 12 months.

items.label: The right to use the shop under a ten-year lease
items.explanation: The right lasts well beyond the year.

items.label: Lease payments due after the next 12 months
items.explanation: Only the part due within the year is current.

questions.onCorrect: A line is current when the cash comes in or goes out within the next 12 months, and it is non-current when it lasts or falls due later. One loan can have a part in each group.

questions.prompt: Dune Coffee Roasters, an invented company, bought its roastery for $2 million many years ago, and similar buildings now sell for about $5 million. Its balance sheet shows total equity of $3.4 million. A friend says that is what the owners' share is worth today. What is the best reply?
hints: Think about what number goes on the balance sheet when a company buys an asset.
The statement generally does not record later changes in what an asset could be sold for.

acceptedIdeas: Assets are recorded from what they cost, so equity does not follow building prices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assets are recorded from what they cost, so equity does not follow building prices

choices.label: The roastery is an asset, so its rising market price is added to equity each year
Equity is the cash in the bank, so $3.4 million must be sitting in the account
Assets are recorded from what they cost, so equity does not follow building prices
The balance sheet shows liabilities at market price, which cancels the higher value

questions.onCorrect: Accountants record an asset at its cost and generally do not record later changes in market value. The $2 million building stays at a cost-based figure, so equity measures what has been recorded.

misconceptions.feedback: Changes in market value are generally not recorded, so the higher price does not flow into equity.
Equity is the difference between assets and liabilities. It is not a cash balance, and the cash line is separate.
Liabilities are amounts owed, and nothing about a rise in a building's price changes what the company owes.

questions.prompt: Quill Stationers, an invented company, publishes only its balance sheet at 30 June. According to the source, which question can that statement alone answer?
hints: The source says the balance sheet applies to a single point in time.
Profit, cash collected and sales are all measured over a period, and a snapshot cannot show a period.

acceptedIdeas: How much Quill owed its suppliers at the end of 30 June
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much Quill owed its suppliers at the end of 30 June

choices.label: How much profit Quill earned over the whole of the year
How much cash Quill collected from customers during the year
Whether Quill's sales were higher than they were the year before
How much Quill owed its suppliers at the end of 30 June

extracts.text: Of the four basic financial statements, the balance sheet is the only statement that applies to a single point in time of a business's calendar year.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Balance sheet" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: A balance sheet gives the position on one date, so it can say what was owed on 30 June. Profit, cash collected and sales all cover a period, and they come from the other two statements.

misconceptions.feedback: Profit is measured over the year, and that is the job of the income statement. A snapshot of one date cannot show it.
Cash collected over the year is a flow, shown in the cash flow statement. The balance sheet shows only balances at the end.
Comparing sales across years needs the income statement. The balance sheet has no sales line.

questions.prompt: A joinery firm, invented for this lesson, borrows $50,000 and the bank pays it into the firm's account. What happens to the firm's profit?
hints: Ask whether the firm has done any work or sold anything yet.
Think about the two things the bank's payment changes. One is an amount the firm holds, and the other is an amount the firm owes.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing changes, because cash and a loan both rise by $50,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing changes, because cash and a loan both rise by $50,000

choices.label: It rises by $50,000, because cash arrived in the bank account
It falls by $50,000, because the firm now has a debt to pay back
Nothing changes, because cash and a loan both rise by $50,000

questions.onCorrect: Cash, an asset, and the loan, a liability, both rise by $50,000, and nothing in equity moves. Borrowing makes the firm able to spend, and it does not make the firm richer.

misconceptions.feedback: Cash did arrive, and a debt arrived with it. Profit comes from revenue less costs, and the firm has recorded neither yet.
The debt is real, and so is the cash that came with it. The two offset each other, so nothing in equity moves.

questions.prompt: A landscaping firm, invented for this lesson, pays $12,000 cash for a new mower. How much does the purchase itself lower profit?
hints: Ask which two lines changed when the cash was paid. Did anything in equity change?
Cash fell by $12,000, and something else rose by the same amount.

acceptedIdeas: Not at all on the day, because the cost reaches profit later as the mower is used
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not at all on the day, because the cost reaches profit later as the mower is used

choices.label: By the full $12,000, because $12,000 of cash left the business on the day it was spent
By $6,000, because only half of the price counts as a cost in the first year
Not at all on the day, because the cost reaches profit later as the mower is used

questions.onCorrect: The purchase swaps cash for an asset, so assets are unchanged in total and equity does not move. Profit falls as the mower is used up, through depreciation, which a later lesson covers.

misconceptions.feedback: Cash fell by $12,000, and the mower, an asset, rose by $12,000. Profit measures revenue less costs, and the purchase has not yet been used up.
No part of the price is a cost on the day. The mower is an asset, and profit falls as it is used.

questions.prompt: Why does equity rise by $14,000 and not by the $20,000 the customer owes?
hints: Compare what the firm gained on the job with what it used up to do it.
Equity is what is left of assets after liabilities, so ask which assets changed.

acceptedIdeas: The $6,000 of timber used is a cost, so only the difference reaches equity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $6,000 of timber used is a cost, so only the difference reaches equity

choices.label: The $6,000 of timber used is a cost, so only the difference reaches equity
Equity rises only when the customer pays, so nothing is recorded until then
The timber was bought on credit, so $6,000 is still owed to the supplier

questions.onCorrect: The receivable adds $20,000 of assets, and the timber used takes $6,000 away. Liabilities are unchanged, so equity rises by the $14,000 difference, which is the profit on the job.

misconceptions.feedback: Equity rose on the day the job was done, whether or not the customer had paid. The receivable is an asset, and the revenue is counted when it is earned.
The supplier is still owed $8,000 for all the timber, and that sits in payables whether the timber is used or not. The $6,000 is the part of the timber that the job used up.

questions.prompt: Kell Landscaping, another invented firm, has nine events in its year. Which of them change profit, and which move balance sheet lines only?
hints: Profit changes only when revenue or a cost is recorded. Ask of each event whether it records either.
Moving cash in or out does not change profit when the other side of the entry is an asset or a liability.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changes profit: finishing the job, using the mulch and recording wages owed. Balance sheet only: the loan, the trailer, the mulch bought on credit, the customer paying, paying the supplier and the advance payment.

items.label: It borrows $40,000 from a bank
items.explanation: Cash and a loan both rise, and no revenue or cost is recorded.

items.label: It buys a $9,000 trailer with cash
items.explanation: One asset replaces another, and the cost reaches profit later.

items.label: It buys $3,000 of mulch on credit
items.explanation: Stock and payables both rise, so nothing is a cost until the mulch is used.

items.label: It finishes a $15,000 job and bills the customer
items.explanation: Revenue is recorded when the work is done, even though the customer has not paid.

items.label: It uses $1,500 of the mulch on that job
items.explanation: Using stock is a cost of the job, and the stock asset falls.

items.label: It records $2,000 of wages owed for the last week of June
items.explanation: A cost counts when it is incurred, whether or not cash has gone out.

items.label: The customer pays the $15,000 it owed
items.explanation: Cash rises and the receivable falls, and the revenue was counted earlier.

items.label: It pays the mulch supplier the $3,000 it owed
items.explanation: Cash and payables both fall.

items.label: It receives $5,000 from a customer for work to be done next month
items.explanation: Cash and a liability rise, and no revenue is earned yet.

questions.onCorrect: Profit moved only where revenue or a cost was recorded: the finished job, the mulch used and the wages owed. Borrowing, buying an asset, paying a debt and collecting a debt only moved balance sheet lines.

questions.prompt: A theatre company, invented for this lesson, takes $240 in advance from a customer for a season ticket covering six shows that have not yet been staged. Which pair of changes does it record that day?
hints: Has the theatre staged any show yet, or only taken the money?
Cash received before the work is done creates something the company owes.

acceptedIdeas: Cash rises by $240 and a contract liability rises by $240, with no revenue yet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cash rises by $240 and a contract liability rises by $240, with no revenue yet

choices.label: Cash rises by $240 and revenue rises by $240, because the theatre has been paid
Cash rises by $240 and a contract liability rises by $240, with no revenue yet
Cash rises by $240 and a receivable falls by $240, because the customer owed that sum
Cash rises by $240 and inventory falls by $240, because the tickets were stock

questions.onCorrect: The theatre owes six shows, so cash and a contract liability both rise by $240. Revenue is recorded as each show is staged.

misconceptions.feedback: Revenue is recorded when the work is done. On the day of sale the theatre has only taken money for shows it still owes.
The customer paid in advance and owed nothing before, so no receivable existed to fall.
A season ticket is a promise of shows later. It does not remove anything from stock on the day it is sold.

questions.prompt: Harlow Cafes, an invented chain, is told in May to repay staff $2 million of underpaid wages, to be paid next year. Its year ends on 30 June. What does the year-end show?
hints: The cost has been incurred even though the cash has not left. Ask where the other side of the entry goes.
Compare with Woolworths's $710 million provision: when did the cost reach profit, and when does the cash go?

acceptedIdeas: A $2 million liability is recorded and profit is lower, though no cash has gone yet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A $2 million liability is recorded and profit is lower, though no cash has gone yet

choices.label: Nothing yet, because the wages will be recorded when the cash is paid next year
A $2 million liability is recorded and profit is lower, though no cash has gone yet
Cash is lower by $2 million and profit is lower by $2 million, because the wages are owed
Profit is lower by $2 million but no liability is shown, because nothing has been paid

questions.onCorrect: A cost the company has incurred is recorded when it arises, with a liability for what it will pay. Profit falls this year, and the cash leaves next year as payments are made.

misconceptions.feedback: Waiting for the cash would leave this year's profit too high. The cost arose this year, so it counts this year.
Cash has not gone out, so it has not fallen. The other side of the entry is a liability.
Every entry has two sides. A cost recorded without cash going out means a liability has risen.

questions.prompt: Orchard Tutoring, an invented company, records this entry: debit Cash $3,000, credit Contract liabilities $3,000. What happened?
hints: A debit to an asset raises the asset, and a credit to a liability raises the liability. Say which two lines rose.
Cash is an asset. What kind of liability is a contract liability?

acceptedIdeas: It was paid $3,000 for tutoring that it has not yet given
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It was paid $3,000 for tutoring that it has not yet given

choices.label: It borrowed $3,000 from a bank and put the money in its account
It gave $3,000 of tutoring, and the customer paid on the spot
It was paid $3,000 for tutoring that it has not yet given
It paid a supplier $3,000 that it owed from an earlier month

questions.onCorrect: Cash and a contract liability both rise, so the company has been paid for work it still owes. The liability becomes revenue as the tutoring is given.

misconceptions.feedback: A loan would be a credit to a loan account, not to contract liabilities. Contract liabilities are for work still owed.
Tutoring given and paid on the spot would record revenue. This entry records a liability, so the tutoring is still to come.
Paying a supplier would lower cash and lower the amount owed, and here cash rises.

questions.prompt: A signmaker, an invented firm, finishes a $9,000 job on credit using $4,000 of its own stock. Which pair of changes keeps its equation in balance?
hints: Count what the firm gained and what it used up. Which total moves?
Nothing new is owed to anyone, so decide whether liabilities can change.

acceptedIdeas: Assets and equity both rise, by the profit the job leaves after its cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assets and equity both rise, by the profit the job leaves after its cost

choices.label: Assets rise by $9,000 and equity rises by $9,000, ignoring the stock used
Assets rise and liabilities rise, because the customer now owes the firm
Assets rise by $9,000 and equity is unchanged, because the customer has not paid
Assets and equity both rise, by the profit the job leaves after its cost

questions.onCorrect: The receivable adds $9,000 of assets and the stock used takes $4,000 away, so assets and equity both rise by the $5,000 profit. Liabilities do not change.

misconceptions.feedback: The stock used is a cost, so equity rises by the profit and not by the price of the job.
A customer's debt is an asset, the firm's claim on the customer. Liabilities are what the firm owes, and they have not changed.
Equity rises on the day the work is done, because revenue is recorded when it is earned and not when the cash arrives.

questions.prompt: Six events happen at Paige Printing, another invented firm. Which two kinds of item change in each?
hints: Name the two lines that change in each event, then ask which group each line belongs to.
Revenue earned with no cost to set against it raises equity directly.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two assets: the printer and the customer paying the bill. An asset and a liability: the loan, the paper on credit and the advance payment. An asset and equity: the design paid for on the spot.

items.label: It borrows $20,000 from a bank
items.explanation: Cash rises and a loan, a liability, rises.

items.label: It buys a $5,000 printer with cash
items.explanation: Cash falls and the printer, another asset, rises.

items.label: It buys $2,000 of paper on credit
items.explanation: Stock rises and payables, a liability, rise.

items.label: A customer pays a $7,000 bill it owed
items.explanation: Cash rises and the receivable falls.

items.label: A customer pays $4,000 on the spot for a design that used no stock
items.explanation: Cash rises and revenue joins equity as profit.

items.label: It is paid $6,000 for a job to be done next month
items.explanation: Cash rises and a contract liability rises.

questions.onCorrect: Each event changes exactly two things, and the equation holds after all six. Only the design paid for on the spot raised equity.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's revenue for the year to 28 June 2026 was $71,539 million, and its profit was $1,152 million. Roughly how much of each revenue dollar did it keep as profit?
hints: Compare the two figures. Profit is a small number beside revenue.
A cent is a hundredth of a dollar. Is the ratio nearer a hundredth, a tenth or two fifths?

acceptedIdeas: About 1.6 cents of each dollar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1.6 cents of each dollar

choices.label: About 1.6 cents of each dollar
About 16 cents of every dollar
About 40 cents of every dollar

questions.onCorrect: Profit was about 1.6% of revenue. The rest of each dollar went on the cost of goods, running costs, finance costs and tax.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make profit about $11,500 million. Profit is $1,152 million, a good deal smaller.
Forty cents would leave profit at about $28,600 million. The statement shows $1,152 million.

questions.prompt: Put these lines of an income statement in the order they appear, from the top.
hints: Each line is the one above with a layer of cost taken away.
Finance costs come off before tax, and tax is the last layer taken away.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Revenue comes first, then gross profit after the cost of goods, then operating profit after the running costs, then profit before tax after finance costs, and profit for the period after tax.

questions.onCorrect: The statement works down from revenue by taking away one layer of cost at a time: the cost of goods first, then the running costs, then finance costs and tax.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's revenue rose 17.6% in 2026 and its profit after tax rose 10.7%. Four of its costs, in $ million for 2025 and 2026, were: cost of sales 143.5 and 163.4; property expenses 49.4 and 56.0; distribution costs 21.3 and 22.2; depreciation and amortisation 108.6 and 131.3. Which statement is best supported?
hints: For each line, compare the 2026 figure with the 2025 figure as a share of the 2025 figure.
Revenue grew 17.6%. Only costs that grew faster than that held profit growth below revenue growth.

acceptedIdeas: Depreciation and amortisation grew fastest, and faster than revenue grew
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Depreciation and amortisation grew fastest, and faster than revenue grew

choices.label: Cost of sales grew fastest, because it is the largest of the four lines
Depreciation and amortisation grew fastest, and faster than revenue grew
Property expenses grew fastest, because the rent on stores rises with sales
Distribution costs grew fastest, because freight is the cost that follows sales

questions.onCorrect: Depreciation and amortisation rose about 21%, faster than revenue's 17.6%, so it weighed on profit growth. Cost of sales rose about 14%, property about 13% and distribution about 4%.

misconceptions.feedback: A large line is not always a fast one. Cost of sales rose from $143.5 million to $163.4 million, a smaller percentage than revenue grew.
Property expenses rose from $49.4 million to $56.0 million, about 13%, which is slower than revenue.
Distribution costs rose from $21.3 million to $22.2 million, only about 4%.

questions.prompt: One headline says Woolworths's profit rose 21% in 2026, and another says its profit before significant items rose 17%. Which reading is best?
hints: Work out which costs each figure includes. Which of the two leaves out the significant items?
Ask what a reader wants to know: how the business traded, or what was recorded for the year?

acceptedIdeas: Both are right, because the two figures answer different questions about the same year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both are right, because the two figures answer different questions about the same year

choices.label: Only the first matters, because a cost the company recorded is a cost whatever it is called
Both are right, because the two figures answer different questions about the same year
Only the second matters, because significant items are not real costs and can be left out
Neither can be used, because the company chooses which costs to set apart as significant

questions.onCorrect: The 21% figure is profit as recorded, and the 17% figure sets significant items aside to show trading. Each is a true figure, and a reader needs to know which question each answers.

misconceptions.feedback: The first figure does include every recorded cost, and it is useful. Alone, though, it cannot show how trading changed apart from the items the company set aside.
A significant item is a cost the company recorded, such as the $710 million wage provision. It is left out of one figure to show trading, and it is still a cost.
Both figures can be compared with the same figure a year earlier. What matters is knowing what each figure includes.

questions.prompt: Last year Marlow Tools, an invented company, earned $40 million on 100 million shares. This year it earned $44 million, and it now has 125 million shares. What happened to earnings per share?
hints: Earnings per share is profit divided by the number of shares. Check what happened to each part.
Profit rose by a tenth. Did the number of shares rise by more or less than that?

acceptedIdeas: It fell, because shares grew by more than profit did
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fell, because shares grew by more than profit did

choices.label: It rose by about 10%, because profit rose by about 10%
It rose, because there are more shares to share in the profit
It fell, because shares grew by more than profit did
It cannot be judged without knowing the dividend paid

questions.onCorrect: Profit rose by 10% while the share count rose by 25%, so each share's slice shrank from 40 cents to about 35 cents. Per share, the company did worse even though its profit grew.

misconceptions.feedback: Profit did rise 10%, but the share count rose by more than that, and earnings per share depends on both.
More shares means the profit is divided among more owners. Each share's slice gets smaller unless profit grows as fast.
The dividend is a separate decision. Earnings per share depends only on profit and the number of shares.

questions.prompt: Tessel Homewares, an invented chain, shows gross profit of 600, operating costs of 480, trading profit of 120, interest paid of 30, tax of 27 and net profit of 63. Which line of Woolworths's statement does its trading profit match?
hints: Match by position. Which costs come off before the trading profit, and which come off after it?
Trading profit comes before the interest and the tax. Which Woolworths line comes before net finance costs and income tax?

acceptedIdeas: EBIT, because it sits before the finance costs and the tax
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: EBIT, because it sits before the finance costs and the tax

choices.label: Gross profit, because it comes first after the cost of sales
Profit before tax, because it sits just above the tax line
EBIT, because it sits before the finance costs and the tax
Profit for the period, because it is the last profit figure

questions.onCorrect: Trading profit comes before interest and tax, which is where EBIT sits. Companies name their layers differently, so read what a subtotal is taken before and after.

misconceptions.feedback: Gross profit sits above the operating costs. Tessel's trading profit comes after them.
Profit before tax comes after the interest, and Tessel's trading profit comes before it.
The last profit figure comes after both interest and tax. Tessel's trading profit comes before them.

questions.prompt: A company shows a $50 million cost in its income statement under the heading 'extraordinary items', so that readers will treat it as a one-off. What does the source say about this under IFRS?
hints: Read the sentence for what it says may be presented as extraordinary.
The source does not say there are conditions under which the label is allowed.

acceptedIdeas: No item may be presented as extraordinary in the income statement under IFRS
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No item may be presented as extraordinary in the income statement under IFRS

choices.label: The heading is allowed when the directors explain the cost in the notes
The heading is allowed for any cost that is unusual and unlikely to happen again
The heading is required for any cost above a set size, so that readers can find it
No item may be presented as extraordinary in the income statement under IFRS

extracts.text: No items may be presented in the income statement as extraordinary items under IFRS regulations or (as of ASU No. 2015-01) under US GAAP.

questions.onCorrect: The sentence says IFRS allows no item to be shown as extraordinary in the income statement. Companies that want to set costs apart use labels of their own, such as significant items, and the reader decides how much weight they deserve.

misconceptions.feedback: The source states no condition under which the label is allowed. An explanation in the notes does not change that.
The source says no items, so unusual costs are not an exception.
Nothing in the source requires the label. It says the opposite, that none may be presented that way.

questions.prompt: Marlin Foods, an invented company, reports significant items of $40 million, $52 million and $47 million in its last three years, each described as one-off. How should a reader treat them?
hints: Count how many years the company has set costs aside. Can a one-off cost happen three years running?
The label is the company's own. Look at what the figures say about how often it is used.

acceptedIdeas: Treat them as a regular cost of this business and read profit before and after them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treat them as a regular cost of this business and read profit before and after them

choices.label: Ignore them, because the company has described each one as a one-off
Treat them as a regular cost of this business and read profit before and after them
Add them back every year, because a cost described as significant is never part of trading
Reject the statements, because IFRS does not allow a company to report significant items

questions.onCorrect: A cost set aside every year is part of what the business costs to run, so profit after the items matters as much as profit before them.

misconceptions.feedback: The label is the company's description. Three costs in three years suggest a cost that keeps coming back.
A cost that recurs may belong to the business, so adding it back every year can flatter the result.
IFRS bars the heading extraordinary in the income statement. It does not bar a company from describing items as significant.

questions.prompt: Pennant Outfitters, an invented retailer, has six costs. Which come off before EBIT, and which come off after it?
hints: EBIT means earnings before interest and tax. Which two items are named in that phrase?
Costs of running the stores reduce EBIT, and the cost of funding the business and the tax come after it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Before EBIT: the stock sold, store wages, depreciation of fit-outs and head-office salaries. After EBIT: interest on the bank loan and income tax.

items.label: The cost of the stock it sold
items.explanation: It is the first layer, taken from revenue to reach gross profit.

items.label: Wages of the store staff
items.explanation: Running costs come off gross profit on the way to EBIT.

items.label: Depreciation of the store fit-outs
items.explanation: Wear on assets used in trading is a running cost, so it reduces EBIT.

items.label: Salaries at head office
items.explanation: Administration costs are running costs above EBIT.

items.label: Interest on its bank loan
items.explanation: EBIT is earnings before interest, so finance costs come off after it.

items.label: Income tax on the year's profit
items.explanation: EBIT is earnings before tax, so tax is taken from what remains.

questions.onCorrect: EBIT is struck after the cost of goods and the running costs, and before finance costs and tax. The running costs reduce it, and interest and tax come off what is left.

questions.prompt: Operating activities brought in $4,948 million, investing activities took out $2,014 million, and financing activities took out $2,701 million. Roughly how did Woolworths's cash change over the year?
hints: The three flows all come out of the same pool of cash. Which one is positive?
Take the two outflows off the inflow and see how much is left.

acceptedIdeas: It rose by only about $0.2 billion, once the two outflows come off
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rose by only about $0.2 billion, once the two outflows come off

choices.label: It rose by only about $0.2 billion, once the two outflows come off
It rose by about $5 billion, the whole size of the operating inflow
It fell by about $2.7 billion, the size of the financing outflow

questions.onCorrect: Cash rose by $233 million. Operations brought in nearly all of what investing and financing took out, so the balance barely moved.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the operating inflow. The investing and financing flows took cash out of the same pool.
That counts only the financing outflow. Operating activities brought cash in over the same year.

questions.prompt: These seven lines are based on Woolworths's cash flow statement for 2026, shortened a little. Which of the three sections does each one belong to?
hints: Ask whom the cash goes to or comes from: customers and the tax office, buyers and sellers of long-term assets, or lenders and owners.
Spending on stores is not a running cost of the year. It is spending on something that lasts.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operating: receipts from customers and income tax paid. Investing: payments for property, plant and equipment and proceeds from selling it. Financing: lease principal, dividends and proceeds from borrowings.

items.label: Receipts from customers
items.explanation: Cash from selling goods is the core of running the business.

items.label: Income tax paid
items.explanation: Both companies show tax paid in operating activities.

items.label: Payments for property, plant, equipment and intangibles
items.explanation: Spending on long-term assets is investing.

items.label: Cash from selling property, plant and equipment
items.explanation: Selling a long-term asset brings cash into investing.

items.label: Repayment of lease principal
items.explanation: Woolworths reports the principal part of a lease payment as a financing flow.

items.label: Dividends paid
items.explanation: Cash paid to the owners is a financing flow.

items.label: Proceeds from borrowings
items.explanation: New loans come from the people who fund the business.

questions.onCorrect: The three sections follow who the cash moves between: customers, suppliers and tax in operating, long-term assets in investing, and lenders and owners in financing.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's profit after tax in 2026 was $95.6 million, and its operating cash flow was $232.8 million. Its depreciation and amortisation was $131.3 million. Which explanation fits best?
hints: Compare the gap between the two figures with the size of the depreciation and amortisation charge.
A charge that lowers profit and sends no cash anywhere leaves operating cash higher than profit.

acceptedIdeas: The depreciation charge cut profit and sent no cash out, so it explains most of the gap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The depreciation charge cut profit and sent no cash out, so it explains most of the gap

choices.label: Customers paid far more than they were billed, so cash ran ahead of sales
The directors overstated the cash figure, since cash should never be larger than profit
Borrowings were counted as operating cash flow, which inflated the total
The depreciation charge cut profit and sent no cash out, so it explains most of the gap

questions.onCorrect: Operating cash flow was $137 million above profit, and depreciation and amortisation of $131 million accounts for nearly all of it. The charge reduced profit and no cash left.

misconceptions.feedback: The statement shows receipts from customers, and nothing there suggests they overpaid. The gap is close to the size of a non-cash charge.
Cash and profit measure different things, so one can exceed the other. A non-cash charge in profit is the usual reason.
Borrowings appear in financing activities, not in operating. The statement keeps them separate.

questions.prompt: Lovisa generated $232.8 million of operating cash flow in 2026, spent $58.5 million on investing and $167.7 million on financing, and its cash rose by only $6.5 million. What does the small rise show?
hints: Operating cash flow was collected, so look at where it went afterwards.
Look inside the financing outflow. It holds the lease payments and the dividends.

acceptedIdeas: Operating cash went on stores, leases and dividends, so the small rise says little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operating cash went on stores, leases and dividends, so the small rise says little

choices.label: The business was close to running out of cash, since the balance barely moved
Operating cash flow was overstated, since the cash balance did not rise by as much
Operating cash went on stores, leases and dividends, so the small rise says little
Customers were slow to pay, so the cash was not collected during the year

questions.onCorrect: The $232.8 million came in and was spent: $58.5 million on investing, and most of the $167.7 million of financing on lease payments of $89.2 million and dividends of $88.6 million. The small change in the balance reflects what was paid out.

misconceptions.feedback: A flat balance after large payments to owners and landlords is not a sign of trouble. The cash came in and went out.
The operating figure is cash that came in during the year. The balance rose less because other flows took cash out.
Operating cash flow already counts the cash collected from customers. Slow collection would show up as a smaller inflow.

questions.prompt: Ferris Stores and Gannet Stores, both invented, each report operating cash flow of $100 million. Ferris reports $40 million of lease principal in financing. Gannet, reporting under another rulebook, puts all of its lease payments inside operating cash flow. How should you compare them?
hints: Find where each company puts the cost of using its stores. Is it inside the operating figure or outside it?
To compare, both figures need the same items in them. Ferris's figure is before a cost that Gannet's figure is after.

acceptedIdeas: Take Ferris's $40 million of lease principal off its figure, or add Gannet's lease payments back
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Take Ferris's $40 million of lease principal off its figure, or add Gannet's lease payments back

choices.label: Compare the printed figures, because operating cash flow is defined the same way everywhere
Ignore operating cash flow and compare profit, since cash flow cannot be made comparable
Add the $40 million to Ferris's figure, since lease principal was left out of its operating cash
Take Ferris's $40 million of lease principal off its figure, or add Gannet's lease payments back

questions.onCorrect: Ferris's operating figure is struck before lease principal and Gannet's is struck after its lease payments. Putting both on the same footing is the reader's adjustment, and the standards do not prescribe it.

misconceptions.feedback: Classification differs, and IAS 7 itself lets companies put interest in different places. Printed figures need checking first.
Profit has its own distortions. A reader can adjust the cash figures to a common footing and use both.
Adding the principal moves the figure further from Gannet's. Ferris's lease principal is a cost that sits outside its operating figure, so it comes off.

questions.prompt: Calder Hardware, an invented retailer, reports operating cash flow of $40 million, investing of negative $55 million and financing of positive $20 million, of which new borrowing was $30 million and dividends $10 million. Its cash rose by $5 million. What does the pattern say?
hints: Compare the operating inflow with the investing outflow. Which is larger?
Then ask what the financing section shows about where the shortfall came from.

acceptedIdeas: Operations fall short of its spending on stores, and new borrowing fills the gap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operations fall short of its spending on stores, and new borrowing fills the gap

choices.label: It pays its own way, since the cash balance rose over the year even after the spending
Customers prepaid heavily, since financing shows cash coming in
Operations fall short of its spending on stores, and new borrowing fills the gap
It is returning surplus cash to its owners, since it paid dividends during the year

questions.onCorrect: Operating cash of $40 million falls short of the $55 million spent on investing, and new borrowing of $30 million covers the gap and the dividends. A small rise in cash hides a business that is not yet paying its own way.

misconceptions.feedback: The balance rose only because of new borrowing. Operations alone fell $15 million short of the investing spending.
Prepayments by customers would appear in operating activities. Financing inflows come from lenders and owners.
Dividends of $10 million were paid while the business was also borrowing $30 million. The shortfall is the more important fact.

questions.prompt: These seven lines are based on other parts of Woolworths's cash flow statement for 2026. Which section does each one belong to?
hints: Ask whom the cash moves between. Suppliers, staff and the interest on what the company owes point to operating.
A lease payment has two parts, and only one of them is in financing.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operating: payments to suppliers and employees, net finance costs paid on borrowings and the interest portion of lease payments. Investing: payments to buy businesses and cash from selling subsidiaries and investments. Financing: repayment of borrowings and dividends paid to minority owners.

items.label: Payments to suppliers and employees
items.explanation: Paying for the goods and labour that the business uses is operating.

items.label: Net finance costs paid on borrowings
items.explanation: Woolworths shows interest paid in operating, though IAS 7 would let it use financing.

items.label: Interest portion of lease payments
items.explanation: The interest part of a lease payment sits in operating, and the principal part sits in financing.

items.label: Payments to buy businesses
items.explanation: Buying a business is spending on a long-term asset.

items.label: Cash from selling subsidiaries and investments
items.explanation: Selling long-term holdings brings cash into investing.

items.label: Repayment of borrowings
items.explanation: Paying back lenders is a financing flow.

items.label: Dividends paid to minority owners of subsidiaries
items.explanation: Cash paid to owners is a financing flow, whoever the owner is.

questions.onCorrect: The same logic sorts every line: operations with suppliers, staff and the interest paid, investing with businesses and long-term holdings, and financing with lenders and owners. Interest is the line where IAS 7 leaves a choice.

questions.prompt: Hollis Cafes, an invented chain, reports operating cash flow of $60 million, spending of $35 million on property, plant and equipment, lease principal of $18 million and dividends of $15 million. About how much operating cash is left after stores and leases, and does it cover the dividends?
hints: Both the equipment spending and the lease principal use up operating cash. Take both off.
Compare what is left with the $15 million of dividends.

acceptedIdeas: About $7 million, which does not cover the $15 million of dividends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $7 million, which does not cover the $15 million of dividends

choices.label: About $7 million, which does not cover the $15 million of dividends
About $25 million, which covers the dividends with room to spare
About $42 million, which covers the dividends comfortably
About $60 million, because investing and lease flows are not deducted

questions.onCorrect: Taking $35 million and $18 million off $60 million leaves about $7 million, well short of $15 million. The dividends would have to come from borrowing or from cash on hand.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes off the equipment spending only. The lease principal is also paid from operating cash.
That takes off the lease principal only. The equipment spending is also paid from operating cash.
Operating cash flow is the cash that is available before the investing and lease flows. It is what pays for them.

questions.prompt: Ardent and Birch, two invented retailers, are identical except that Ardent shows its interest paid in operating activities and Birch shows it in financing. According to the source, which has the higher operating cash flow?
hints: Read what the source says IAS 7 allows. Is the place fixed?
A payment shown outside the operating section cannot reduce the operating total.

acceptedIdeas: Birch, because its interest sits outside the operating figure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Birch, because its interest sits outside the operating figure

choices.label: Ardent, because paying interest from operations shows strength
They are equal, because IAS 7 requires interest in operating
Birch, because its interest sits outside the operating figure

extracts.text: IAS 7 allows interest paid to be included in operating activities or financing activities.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Cash flow statement" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: Birch's operating figure is not reduced by the interest, because it shows it in financing. Interest paid is a classification choice, so compare it on the same footing before drawing conclusions.

misconceptions.feedback: Where a company shows interest says nothing about strength. It only changes which section holds the payment.
The source says IAS 7 allows either place, so the requirement is not fixed.

questions.prompt: Harbour Print, an invented printing firm, reports a profit of $48,000, yet its bank balance has fallen over the year. It has repaid no loans and paid no dividends. What is the most likely reason?
hints: Profit counts a sale when the work is delivered. Ask when the cash for it arrives.
Think of the order of events for one job: the materials and wages, the delivery, and the customer's payment.

acceptedIdeas: Its sales grew on credit terms, so cash is tied up in what customers owe and in stock
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its sales grew on credit terms, so cash is tied up in what customers owe and in stock

choices.label: Its profit figure must be wrong, since profit and cash cannot move in opposite directions
Its sales grew on credit terms, so cash is tied up in what customers owe and in stock
Depreciation raised its profit, so the cash it earned was spent on equipment

questions.onCorrect: Profit records a sale when it is made, and cash arrives when the customer pays. A growing firm that sells on credit and holds more stock uses cash even while it makes a profit.

misconceptions.feedback: Profit and cash are measured differently, so they can move in opposite directions in the same year. The next screens show how.
Depreciation lowers profit, and it does not raise it. It is also not cash spent on equipment, which would appear in investing.

questions.prompt: Why is the $100,000 rise in Harbour Print's receivables taken off its profit on the way to operating cash flow?
hints: A receivable is what customers owe the firm. Has that cash arrived?
Profit counts the sale when it is made. Cash counts it when the customer pays.

acceptedIdeas: The firm recorded $100,000 of sales that customers have not yet paid for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The firm recorded $100,000 of sales that customers have not yet paid for

choices.label: Receivables are a cost, so a rise in them reduces profit by the amount owed
Customers owe the firm money, so the firm has a liability of $100,000
The firm recorded $100,000 of sales that customers have not yet paid for

questions.onCorrect: The sales are in profit and the cash is not yet in the bank, so the rise in receivables is taken off to reach cash. The customers' debt is an asset, and it turns into cash when they pay.

misconceptions.feedback: A receivable is an asset, a claim on customers. The sale it came from is already in profit, so the adjustment corrects profit and does not record a cost.
What customers owe the firm is an asset, not a liability. It is subtracted because the cash for those sales has not yet arrived.

questions.prompt: In 2025 Woolworths's profit was $953 million and its operating cash flow was $4,550 million. Its reconciliation lines included depreciation and amortisation of $2,953 million, impairment of non-financial assets of $459 million, a rise in trade payables of $171 million and a rise in other payables of $150 million. Which line does most to lift cash above profit?
hints: Find the largest of the four lines. Each of them raises cash above profit.
Then ask why a line of that kind is added to profit and not subtracted.

acceptedIdeas: Depreciation and amortisation, a charge in profit that needed no cash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Depreciation and amortisation, a charge in profit that needed no cash

choices.label: Depreciation and amortisation, a charge in profit that needed no cash
Impairment of non-financial assets, a write-down that was not a cash cost
The rise in trade payables, because suppliers were owed more at the year end
The rise in other payables, because more bills were outstanding

questions.onCorrect: The largest line is depreciation and amortisation, which lowered profit and sent no cash out, and it makes up more than four fifths of the $3,597 million gap.

misconceptions.feedback: The impairment line also adds cash against profit, but at $459 million it is far smaller than the depreciation line.
A rise in trade payables does raise cash against profit, but at $171 million it is a small part of the gap.
A rise in other payables does raise cash against profit, but at $150 million it is a small part of the gap.

questions.prompt: Larch Furniture, an invented maker, has profit of $60,000 and depreciation of $15,000. What should be done with the depreciation on the way from profit towards cash?
hints: Did cash leave the business when depreciation was charged?
Profit has the charge deducted. To get to cash, ask whether the deduction should be undone.

acceptedIdeas: Add it back, because it lowered profit and no cash left the business
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add it back, because it lowered profit and no cash left the business

choices.label: Add it back, because it lowered profit and no cash left the business
Subtract it, because using assets is a cost of the business
Leave it out, because depreciation does not appear in a reconciliation

questions.onCorrect: Depreciation was deducted in reaching profit, and no cash left the business, so it is added back. The cash for the assets went out when they were bought.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting would deduct a cost twice. It is already deducted in profit and no cash went out.
Depreciation is one of the lines a reconciliation adds back. Woolworths's own table starts with it.

questions.prompt: Larch's stock fell by $10,000 during the year. Which way does that move operating cash flow against profit?
hints: A rise in stock takes cash out of the business. What does a fall do?
Think of the goods sold this year as paid for in an earlier period.

acceptedIdeas: Higher, because goods paid for earlier were sold and less new stock was bought
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Higher, because goods paid for earlier were sold and less new stock was bought

choices.label: Lower, because a fall in stock means the firm now has less of what it owns
Neither, because the stock balance is not a cash item and so is left out of it
Higher, because goods paid for earlier were sold and less new stock was bought

questions.onCorrect: Stock that falls has been turned into sales without new cash being spent to replace it, so operating cash is higher than profit by that amount.

misconceptions.feedback: Having less stock does not use cash. Buying stock uses cash, and a fall means less was bought than was sold.
The cash spent on stock is a real flow. A change in the stock balance is one of the lines that separates profit from cash.

questions.prompt: Putting all of Larch's lines together, how does its operating cash flow compare with its profit of $60,000? Depreciation was $15,000, receivables rose $30,000, stock fell $10,000 and payables rose $5,000.
hints: Sort the four lines into those that add to cash and the one that takes from it.
Add up the three additions and compare them with the one subtraction.

acceptedIdeas: About the same as profit, because the additions and subtractions roughly cancel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About the same as profit, because the additions and subtractions roughly cancel

choices.label: Far above profit, because depreciation and the fall in stock both add a lot of cash
About the same as profit, because the additions and subtractions roughly cancel
Far below profit, because receivables rose and customers have not yet paid

questions.onCorrect: The additions of $15,000, $10,000 and $5,000 add up to $30,000, and the rise in receivables takes the same $30,000 away. Operating cash flow ends at about $60,000, the same as profit.

misconceptions.feedback: Those two lines do add cash, and so does the rise in payables, but the rise in receivables takes the same total away.
The rise in receivables does lower cash, but three other lines add cash and together they offset it.

questions.prompt: Eight things happen at a firm during its year. Does each one make operating cash flow higher than profit, or lower than profit?
hints: Ask whether the item put a cost or a sale into profit before the cash moved, or moved cash before profit recorded it.
A cost counted and not yet paid raises cash against profit. Cash paid out for something already counted lowers it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Higher: depreciation, a fall in stock, a rise in trade payables and a provision not yet paid. Lower: a rise in receivables, a rise in stock, a fall in trade payables and a payment out of an earlier provision.

items.label: A depreciation expense is recorded
items.explanation: It lowered profit and no cash left, so it is added back.

items.label: Stock falls because the firm sold down its shelves
items.explanation: Goods paid for earlier were sold, so less new cash went on stock.

items.label: Trade payables rise because suppliers are paid later
items.explanation: Costs are in profit and the cash has not gone out yet.

items.label: A provision is recognised for a cost and not yet paid
items.explanation: The cost is in profit, and the cash leaves later.

items.label: Receivables rise because customers take longer to pay
items.explanation: Sales are in profit and the cash has not arrived.

items.label: Stock rises because the firm buys ahead of a busy season
items.explanation: Cash went out for goods that are not yet a cost.

items.label: Trade payables fall because suppliers are paid sooner
items.explanation: Cash goes out to settle bills whose costs were counted earlier.

items.label: A payment is made out of a provision recognised last year
items.explanation: The cost was counted last year, and the cash goes out now.

questions.onCorrect: Items where profit counted something before the cash moved make cash higher than profit, and items where cash moved first make it lower. Depreciation is the one that never involves cash at all.

questions.prompt: Orrin Metalworks, an invented firm, reports profit of $60, $70 and $85 thousand in years 1, 2 and 3. Its receivables were $40, $90 and $160 thousand, its stock $50, $120 and $210 thousand, its borrowings $20, $90 and $180 thousand, and its cash $30, $18 and $8 thousand. A bank sees profit rising every year. What should worry it most?
hints: Compare how fast profit grows with how fast receivables and stock grow.
Ask where the cash to buy the extra stock and fund the extra credit has come from.

acceptedIdeas: Receivables, stock and borrowings grow faster than profit while cash falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Receivables, stock and borrowings grow faster than profit while cash falls

choices.label: Profit is rising every year, so there is nothing for the bank to worry about
Cash is falling, so the profit figure must have been overstated by the firm
Stock is rising, which is only a problem if the firm cannot sell it
Receivables, stock and borrowings grow faster than profit while cash falls

questions.onCorrect: Orrin's growth is being funded by borrowing, and the cash is tied up in what customers owe and in stock. A firm in that position can be profitable and still unable to pay its bills when they fall due.

misconceptions.feedback: Profit has risen, and the cash balance has fallen to $8 thousand. A rising profit does not settle whether the firm can pay what it owes.
A falling cash balance beside a rising profit is the usual result of growth funded by credit. It does not show that profit is overstated.
Stock matters here because it is growing together with receivables and borrowings while cash falls. The pattern across all four lines is the concern.

questions.prompt: A manager at Pellam Bus Co, an invented company, says: 'Our $2 million of depreciation each year gives us $2 million of cash to spend on new buses.' What is wrong with that?
hints: Read what the source says depreciation is, and what it is not.
Ask where the cash that pays for new buses comes from.

acceptedIdeas: It is added back only because no cash left, and cash for buses comes from customers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is added back only because no cash left, and cash for buses comes from customers

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since setting aside depreciation builds up a pool of cash for new buses
It is added back only because no cash left, and cash for buses comes from customers
It should be subtracted instead of added, since it measures wear on the buses
It is a cash cost paid into a fund each year, so adding it back counts the cash twice

extracts.text: depreciation is not a direct source of cash, but rather a non-cash expense that is "added back" on the statement of cash flows to reconcile net income with cash from operations.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Depreciation" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The add-back corrects profit for a charge that needed no cash. It does not create cash. The money for new buses has to come from customers, from lenders or from owners.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is set aside when depreciation is charged. The charge is a deduction in profit, and no cash is paid anywhere.
Depreciation is added back, because it lowered profit without cash leaving. Subtracting it would deduct the cost twice.
Depreciation is not a payment to a fund. It is a non-cash charge, so there is no cash to count twice.

questions.prompt: Wren Stores, an invented retailer, records a $3 million provision in June for a court-ordered refund, to be paid in August. For the year to 30 June, how does the provision affect operating cash flow compared with profit?
hints: The cost is deducted in profit this year. When does the cash leave?
Compare Woolworths's increase in provisions of $652 million in its reconciliation.

acceptedIdeas: Operating cash flow is $3 million higher than profit, because no cash has gone out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operating cash flow is $3 million higher than profit, because no cash has gone out

choices.label: Operating cash flow is $3 million higher than profit, because no cash has gone out
Operating cash flow is $3 million lower than profit, because the refund has been paid
Operating cash flow is unchanged, because provisions are not part of the reconciliation
Operating cash flow is lower than profit, because the liability has risen

questions.onCorrect: The cost is in profit and the cash goes out in August, so operating cash flow for the year is $3 million higher than profit. The difference reverses next year when the refund is paid.

misconceptions.feedback: The refund is paid in August, after the year end, so no cash has gone out in the year.
An increase in provisions is one of the lines of Woolworths's reconciliation, added because the cost is in profit and not yet paid.
A liability that has risen without payment means cash has not left. That makes cash higher than profit, not lower.

questions.prompt: Aldous Bakery, an invented company, buys flour on 14-day terms and sells bread to a cafe on 30-day terms. In what order do these happen?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bakery buys the flour on credit first, then delivers the bread and records the sale, then pays the supplier after 14 days, and the cafe pays after 30 days.

items: It buys the flour on credit, so trade payables rise
It delivers the bread and records the sale and the profit
It pays the flour supplier after 14 days, so cash falls
The cafe pays after 30 days, so cash arrives and receivables fall

questions.prompt: Quay Cafes, an invented chain, shows profit of $40 million and operating cash flow of $100 million. Its reconciliation adds depreciation of $30 million, a rise in trade payables of $25 million and a rise in provisions of $10 million, and takes off a rise in stock of $5 million. A friend says the cash flow shows the business is far stronger than its profit. What is a fair reply?
hints: Sort the lines into those that stay in the gap every year and those that reverse when bills are paid.
A rise in payables and provisions means cash is still to go out.

acceptedIdeas: Partly: depreciation recurs, but unpaid bills and provisions still have to be paid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Partly: depreciation recurs, but unpaid bills and provisions still have to be paid

choices.label: Agree, because operating cash flow above profit always shows a stronger business
Disagree, because operating cash flow is unreliable and profit is the only figure to trust
Disagree, because depreciation is a real cash cost and should be subtracted from profit
Partly: depreciation recurs, but unpaid bills and provisions still have to be paid

questions.onCorrect: The depreciation add-back is a feature of the business and repeats each year. The $35 million from payables and provisions comes from costs not yet paid, so part of the boost will reverse when they are.

misconceptions.feedback: A gap can be made of unpaid bills and unpaid provisions, which will take cash out later. Read the lines before judging.
Both figures are useful. The reconciliation shows which lines explain the gap, so each can be weighed.
Depreciation is a non-cash charge, so it is added back and not subtracted.

questions.prompt: A business customer takes delivery of groceries from Woolworths on 20 June and pays on 14 July. Woolworths's year ends on 28 June. In which year's revenue does Woolworths count the sale?
hints: Ask what happened on 20 June, and leave the cash on 14 July aside for the moment.
Woolworths's policy turns on the moment control of the goods passes to the customer.

acceptedIdeas: This year, because the goods were handed over before the year end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This year, because the goods were handed over before the year end

choices.label: Next year, because the cash arrives only after the year has ended
This year, because the goods were handed over before the year end
Both years, shared out by the number of days on each side of the year end

questions.onCorrect: Control passed on 20 June, so the sale is this year's revenue, and the customer's 24 days of credit leave a receivable at the year end.

misconceptions.feedback: The timing of the cash doesn't set the year. Woolworths counts a sale when control of the goods passes to the customer, and that happened on delivery. The 24 days only decide when the cash comes in.
A sale of goods happens once, at the moment control passes, so it belongs wholly to one year. Sharing a price across years is for services delivered over time, which come later in the lesson.

questions.prompt: A yoga studio sells a six-month pass for $600 on 1 May, and its year ends on 30 June. Which part of the $600 is revenue for this year?
hints: Count how many of the six months are over by 30 June.
The price is spread evenly across the six months, and revenue follows the months delivered.

acceptedIdeas: $200, one third, for the two months already delivered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: $200, one third, for the two months already delivered

choices.label: $600, all of it, because the member has paid the whole price
$400, two thirds, for the four months still to come
$200, one third, for the two months already delivered

questions.onCorrect: Two of the six months are delivered, so one third of the price is earned and the other two thirds is still owed to the member.

misconceptions.feedback: Cash received doesn't make revenue. The studio has delivered two of the six months, and only that share of the price is earned.
That is the share still owed to the member. Revenue is the share already delivered, which here is May and June.

questions.prompt: What does the studio's balance sheet show for the rest of the $600?
hints: The member has paid. Who now owes something to whom?
Think of the gym's $900 at 30 June, which was cash for months not yet delivered.

acceptedIdeas: A contract liability, because the studio still owes the member four months
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contract liability, because the studio still owes the member four months

choices.label: A contract liability, because the studio still owes the member four months
A receivable, because the member still owes the studio for the pass
Nothing, because that part becomes revenue only in the following year

questions.onCorrect: Cash received for months not yet delivered sits as a contract liability, and it moves into revenue month by month.

misconceptions.feedback: The member has already paid, so nobody owes the studio anything. It is the studio that owes the member four months of classes.
The cash is already in the studio's bank account, so the balance sheet has to show where it came from. The studio's obligation to deliver is that liability.

questions.prompt: Woolworths describes how it treats the points its customers earn. A shopper earns points on a shop and hasn't redeemed any by the year end. Where does the part of the price allocated to those points sit at the year end?
hints: Read the end of the first sentence: it names the line of the balance sheet.
Is a promise to a shopper something Woolworths owns, or something it owes?

acceptedIdeas: In trade and other payables, as a contract liability until the points are redeemed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In trade and other payables, as a contract liability until the points are redeemed

choices.label: In revenue with the rest of the sale, because the shopper has paid in full at the till
In inventories, because the points will be redeemed for goods from the shelves
In trade and other payables, as a contract liability until the points are redeemed
Nowhere in the accounts, because points are recorded only once they are redeemed

extracts.text: A portion of the transaction price is allocated to the loyalty points awarded to the customer based on its relative stand‑alone selling price and is recognised as a contract liability within trade and other payables until the points are redeemed. Revenue is recognised upon redemption of the points by the customer.
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 2.1, loyalty program policy
extracts.kind: A company's accounting policy, from the notes to its financial statements

questions.onCorrect: The allocated part waits as a contract liability, inside the trade and other payables line, and becomes revenue only when the shopper redeems the points.

misconceptions.feedback: The policy allocates part of the price to the points and holds it back. Revenue arrives only when the shopper redeems the points.
The points are a promise Woolworths has made to the shopper, so they are something it owes. Inventories are goods it owns.
The policy records the obligation when the points are earned, as a contract liability, long before redemption.

questions.prompt: A building firm signs a contract to fit out a shop and to maintain it for a year, for one price. In what order does IFRS 15 have the firm work through its five steps?
hints: Start with what has to exist before anything can be priced.
A price can't be split across promises until you know what the promises are.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Contract first, then the separate promises in it, then the price, then the split of the price across the promises, and last the revenue as each promise is met. Here the fit-out and the year of maintenance are two promises.

items: Identify the contract with the customer
Identify the separate promises in the contract
Allocate the price across the promises
Recognise revenue as each promise is met

questions.onCorrect: Each step needs the one before it: the price can't be split until the promises are known, and revenue can't be counted until each promise is met.

questions.prompt: A firm's year ends on 30 June. Where does each of these items sit at that date: in this year's profit, or on the balance sheet for a later year?
hints: For each item, ask whether the work, the use or the sale had happened by 30 June.
