When the thing hasn't happened by 30 June, whatever was paid for it waits on the balance sheet.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The removalist's job, the June wages and the stock sold in May are this year's. The September deposit, the licence months after 30 June and the unsold stock wait on the balance sheet.

bins.label: Held on the balance sheet for later

items.label: A removalist's job finished on 29 June and invoiced on 5 July
items.explanation: The work was delivered in June, so the revenue belongs to this year and the unpaid invoice is a receivable.

items.label: Wages for the last week of June, paid on 3 July
items.explanation: The work was done in June, so the wages are a cost of this year and the unpaid part is a liability.

items.label: Stock bought in March and sold in May
items.explanation: The sale is this year's revenue, so the cost of the stock goes in the same year.

items.label: A customer's deposit for a kitchen to be built in September
items.explanation: The work is still to be done, so the deposit is a contract liability and the revenue comes later.

items.label: The part of a year's software licence, paid on 1 January, that covers the months after 30 June
items.explanation: The months after 30 June help earn next year's revenue, so that part is a prepayment, an asset.

items.label: Stock bought in June and still on the shelf at the year end
items.explanation: Unsold stock is an asset until it is sold, and its cost joins the revenue then.

questions.onCorrect: An item belongs to the year in which the work, the use or the sale happened. Whatever has been paid or owed ahead of that waits on the balance sheet.

questions.prompt: ASIC described its inquiries into the fee revenue and work in progress of the legal services company Slater and Gordon. When a company's revenue rests on work in progress, what does this statement point a reader to look at first?
hints: Find the two things the statement says the inquiries focussed on.
An estimate can be checked against what actually happened in earlier periods.

acceptedIdeas: The policies and the estimates of work done, tested against what happened before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The policies and the estimates of work done, tested against what happened before

choices.label: Whether ASIC found the revenue overstated, because it asked questions about it
The cash collected in the year, because revenue without matching cash is always suspect
Nothing, because the old standard was replaced by AASB 15 and its estimates no longer matter
The policies and the estimates of work done, tested against what happened before

extracts.text: ASIC’s inquiries on revenue recognition and WIP focussed on the appropriateness of accounting policies adopted and the testing of WIP estimates and assumptions against historical data. Given S+G’s transition to AASB 15, ASIC has not approved or disapproved of S+G’s use of the percentage of completion basis of accounting for fee revenue under accounting standard AASB 118 Revenue in its previous financial reports.
extracts.who: ASIC, media release 16-050MR, "ASIC notes Slater and Gordon's decision to reduce asset values"
extracts.kind: A regulator's statement to the public about a listed company. © Australian Securities & Investments Commission: Reproduced with permission.

questions.onCorrect: ASIC looked at the policies and tested the work in progress estimates against historical data. Where revenue rests on an estimate, that is the place to start.

misconceptions.feedback: The statement says ASIC has neither approved nor disapproved the basis. A question is not a finding, so nothing here says the revenue was wrong.
Revenue earned over time is counted before the cash arrives. ASIC's concern is whether the estimates behind it hold up, which is a different test from cash in the same year.
A new standard changes the rules and not the fact that work in progress rests on estimates. The statement shows where ASIC looked, and those estimates still deserve the same test.

questions.prompt: Two invented firms handle the same $80 order. Firm A buys the goods and sells them on, taking the risk of buying and selling. Firm B only passes the order to the seller and keeps a $12 commission. What revenue should each report, on the principle in the lesson?
hints: Which firm takes the risk of buying and selling the goods?
A firm that only arranges a trade earns a fee for arranging it.

acceptedIdeas: Firm A reports $80 and Firm B reports $12
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Firm A reports $80 and Firm B reports $12

choices.label: Firm A reports $80 and Firm B reports $12
Both report $80, because both handled the same order from the customer
Both report $12, because revenue is always the fee a firm keeps
Firm A reports $12 and Firm B reports $80, because the broker handled the money

questions.onCorrect: The merchant reports the selling price and the agent reports its fee, so the same $80 order gives $80 of revenue in one firm and $12 in the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Handling an order isn't the test. A firm that only arranges the sale reports its fee, because it doesn't take the risk of buying and selling the goods.
A firm that buys and sells the goods itself reports the selling price as revenue and the cost of the goods as a cost. Only an agent reports just its fee.
That turns it round. The firm taking the risk of buying and selling reports the full price, and the broker reports its commission.

questions.prompt: Lovisa sells jewellery that customers can return. Read its policy. When it records the right of return provision at the year end, what happens to its revenue and its cost of sales?
hints: Read the last sentence of the policy: it names two effects.
A provision is made for something that hasn't happened yet, on the strength of an estimate.

acceptedIdeas: Revenue falls by the sales expected to come back and cost of sales falls by the goods expected to be recovered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Revenue falls by the sales expected to come back and cost of sales falls by the goods expected to be recovered

choices.label: Revenue falls and cost of sales is unchanged, because returned goods are worth nothing to Lovisa
Revenue falls by the sales expected to come back and cost of sales falls by the goods expected to be recovered
Both stay as they were until a customer actually returns something, because only a return is recorded
Revenue is delayed until the return period has ended, because a sale isn't final before then

extracts.text: Revenue from the sale of fashion jewellery is recognised when the customer obtains control of the goods. A right of return provision has been recognised in line with the Group’s returns policy and in line with the requirements of AASB 15 along with a right to recover returned goods asset. The right of return provision decreases revenue and the right to recover returned goods decreases cost of sales.
extracts.who: Lovisa Holdings Limited, Annual Report 2026, revenue note, sale of goods policy
extracts.kind: A company's accounting policy, from the notes to its financial statements

questions.onCorrect: The provision takes the expected returns out of revenue, and the right to recover the goods takes their cost out of cost of sales. Both rest on an estimate of returns.

misconceptions.feedback: The policy also records a right to recover the returned goods, and that asset lowers cost of sales. The goods are kept, so their cost isn't lost.
The policy records the provision in advance, at the year end, for the returns it expects. That is an estimate, made before any particular return happens.
The sale is counted when the customer obtains control. The provision then takes off the part expected to come back, and the rest stays in revenue.

questions.prompt: Six invented businesses each report revenue on a sale. Which of them report the full selling price, and which report only their fee?
hints: Ask of each business whether it owns the goods and carries the risk if they don't sell.
A business that only arranges a sale for someone else earns a fee for it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shop, the bakery and the tile wholesaler take the risk of buying and selling and report the full price. The booking site, the broker and the ticket agency only arrange the sale and report their fees.

items.label: A shop buys phones for $400 each and sells them for $550, and bears the loss if they don't sell
items.explanation: It takes the risk of buying and selling, so the selling price is revenue and the $400 is a cost.

items.label: A booking site sells hotel rooms for the hotel, keeps 10% and carries no risk if rooms stay empty
items.explanation: It arranges the sale and carries no risk of buying and selling, so its revenue is the commission.

items.label: A bakery bakes loaves and sells them over the counter
items.explanation: It makes and sells its own goods, so the price of each loaf is its revenue.

items.label: A broker finds a buyer for a landlord's flat and takes a 2% fee
items.explanation: The flat isn't the broker's, so the fee is all the revenue it earns.

items.label: A tile wholesaler buys in bulk and resells, carrying whatever stays unsold
items.explanation: It owns the stock and carries the risk of selling it, so it reports the full price.

items.label: A ticket agency sells concert tickets for the promoter and keeps $5 on each
items.explanation: It sells tickets for someone else and keeps only a fee, so $5 a ticket is its revenue.

questions.onCorrect: Whoever takes the risk of buying and selling reports the full price, and whoever only arranges the sale reports the fee.

questions.prompt: A firm's year ends on 30 June. On 1 May it pays $3,000 for six months of equipment hire, running to 31 October. How much of the $3,000 is a cost of this year, and what is the rest?
hints: Count how many of the six months fall before 30 June.
The firm has already paid in cash. Does it now owe something, or does it hold something?

acceptedIdeas: About $1,000, for May and June, and the other $2,000 is an asset until the hire is used
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $1,000, for May and June, and the other $2,000 is an asset until the hire is used

choices.label: All $3,000, because the firm paid it in this year and the cash has gone
About $1,000, for May and June, and the other $2,000 is a liability to the hire company
Nothing yet, because hire becomes a cost only when the full six months are over
About $1,000, for May and June, and the other $2,000 is an asset until the hire is used

questions.onCorrect: Two of the six months are used, so about $1,000 is this year's cost, and the unused $2,000 is a prepayment that becomes a cost as the months pass.

misconceptions.feedback: Paying the cash doesn't decide the year. A cost belongs to the period whose revenue it helps earn, and the hire after 30 June helps earn next year's.
The firm has already paid, so it owes nothing. The unused hire is something it holds, which is an asset called a prepayment.
The cost follows the months used. May and June are used by the year end, so their share of the price is a cost of this year.

questions.prompt: A machine cost $20,000 and has been depreciated at $3,600 a year for two years. The owner now expects it to last six more years and to be worth $5,000 at the end. What happens to the depreciation charge from now on?
hints: Work out how much of the cost is still to be written off.
Ask whether that remaining amount is now spread over more years or fewer than before.

acceptedIdeas: It falls, because the cost still to be written off is spread over more years
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, because the cost still to be written off is spread over more years

choices.label: It stays at $3,600, because the charge is fixed on the day the machine is bought
Every year is redone, so the two years already charged carry the new amount too
It falls, because the cost still to be written off is spread over more years

questions.onCorrect: The remaining cost is now spread over six years instead of three, so each year carries less, and the first two years aren't redone.

misconceptions.feedback: The charge rests on estimates of life and residual value, and a business re-examines them. When they change, so does the charge, from that date.
A change in estimate applies from the date of the change. The two years already charged stay as they were, and only the years ahead carry the new amount.

questions.prompt: A bakery's oven cost $30,000, was given a five-year life and a $5,000 residual value, and is depreciated at $5,000 a year. After three years its carrying amount is $15,000. The owner now expects it to last only two more years and to be worth nothing. What happens from now on?
hints: The amount left to write off is the carrying amount less the new residual value.
Spread that amount over the years now expected, and set the result beside $5,000.

acceptedIdeas: Profit falls by about $2,500 a year, and the bakery's cash is unaffected
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Profit falls by about $2,500 a year, and the bakery's cash is unaffected

choices.label: Profit falls by about $2,500 a year, and cash falls by the same amount
Profit falls by about $2,500 a year, and the bakery's cash is unaffected
Profit rises by about $2,500 a year, because the oven is now worth less
Nothing changes, because the oven was bought for $30,000 whatever the new estimate says

questions.onCorrect: The remaining $15,000 over two years is $7,500 a year, up from $5,000, so profit falls by about $2,500 a year while cash is untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: Depreciation allocates a cost that was paid when the oven was bought. A change in estimate moves profit and the carrying amount and leaves cash where it was.
A shorter life writes the remaining cost off faster, so the yearly charge rises and profit falls. The worth of the oven is not what sets the charge.
The $30,000 was paid in the past, and the charge for the years ahead is worked out from what is left and from the new estimates.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's depreciation of property, plant and equipment was $1,276 million in 2026, and its EBIT after significant items was $2,407 million. Suppose longer lives cut that depreciation by 10%. What would that do?
hints: Find 10% of the charge that the what-if changes, which is the property, plant and equipment line.
Compare that amount with EBIT, and ask whether any cash moved when the charge was made.

acceptedIdeas: EBIT would rise by about $128 million, around 5%, and cash would be unchanged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: EBIT would rise by about $128 million, around 5%, and cash would be unchanged

choices.label: EBIT would rise by about $128 million, around 5%, and cash would be unchanged
EBIT would rise by about $128 million, around 5%, and cash would rise by the same amount
EBIT would rise by about $13 million, around 1%, and cash would be unchanged
EBIT would rise by about $298 million, around 12%, and cash would be unchanged

questions.onCorrect: A 10% cut in a $1,276 million charge adds about $128 million to EBIT, about 5% of it, and leaves cash exactly where it was.

misconceptions.feedback: Depreciation involves no cash in the year it is charged, so lowering it can't bring cash in. It changes how much of an old payment is counted in this year's profit.
Ten percent of $1,276 million is about $128 million, ten times that figure. Check where the decimal point goes.
That takes 10% of the whole $2,984 million, which also covers lease assets and intangibles. The what-if changes only the property, plant and equipment charge.

questions.prompt: This sentence comes from Lovisa's inventory note. What does it show?
hints: Read the words after 'written down to': what is the lower figure?
Ask when the cash for the stock was spent, and whether a write-down spends any more.

acceptedIdeas: Some stock was expected to sell for less than it cost, and the loss was recognised before the stock was sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Some stock was expected to sell for less than it cost, and the loss was recognised before the stock was sold

choices.label: Cash of about $21 million left the business in 2026, at the moment the stock was written down to the lower value
Stock worth about $21 million was stolen or lost, so it was removed from the books altogether
Sales were overstated by about $21 million and the note records the correction of that mistake
Some stock was expected to sell for less than it cost, and the loss was recognised before the stock was sold

extracts.text: During 2026, inventories of $20,999,000 (2025: $14,929,000) were written down to net realisable value and included in cost of sales.
extracts.who: Lovisa Holdings Limited, Annual Report 2026, note B2 on inventories
extracts.kind: A company's note to its financial statements, written for shareholders

questions.onCorrect: The stock was carried at net realisable value, below cost, and the loss went into cost of sales in 2026, before any of that stock had been sold.

misconceptions.feedback: The cash left when the stock was bought. A write-down changes the stock figure and cost of sales in the year it is recognised, and no cash moves then.
The note says the stock was written down to net realisable value, which means it was still held and expected to sell for less than it cost.
A write-down is a judgement about what stock will fetch, and it goes into cost of sales. It does not correct the sales figure.

questions.prompt: Why does FIFO give the higher profit when the price of frames is rising?
hints: Look at the cost of sales line under each formula.
Ask which batch of frames each formula says was sold.

acceptedIdeas: It charges the cheaper, older frames to cost of sales and keeps the dearer ones
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It charges the cheaper, older frames to cost of sales and keeps the dearer ones

choices.label: It brings in more cash, because the frames it sells go for a higher price to customers
It charges the cheaper, older frames to cost of sales and keeps the dearer ones
It buys the frames at a lower price, because it chooses the cheaper supplier each time

questions.onCorrect: FIFO charges the $100 batch to cost of sales and leaves the $120 batch in stock, so cost of sales is lower and profit and stock are both higher.

misconceptions.feedback: Both formulas sell the same ten frames at $200, so the cash is identical. The formulas differ only in which cost they charge.
The purchases are the same under both formulas. Only the rule for charging them to cost of sales differs.

questions.prompt: A phone-case seller buys its stock at falling prices all year. Compared with the weighted average formula, what will FIFO report?
hints: Under FIFO, which cases are charged to cost of sales first, and what did they cost?
The cases left on the shelf under FIFO are the ones bought most recently.

acceptedIdeas: A lower profit and a lower value for the closing stock, because the older, dearer cases are charged first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A lower profit and a lower value for the closing stock, because the older, dearer cases are charged first

choices.label: A higher profit and a higher value for the closing stock, as when prices rise
The same profit as weighted average, because the cash is the same under both formulas
A lower profit and a lower value for the closing stock, because the older, dearer cases are charged first
A lower profit and a higher value for the closing stock, because the dearer cases stay on the shelf

questions.onCorrect: With costs falling, FIFO charges the dearer old cases first and keeps the cheap new ones, so profit and closing stock are both lower than under weighted average.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rising-price result. When costs fall, FIFO charges the older, dearer cases to cost of sales first, so profit is lower.
The cash is the same, but the profit isn't. A formula decides how much of the buying cost is charged to this year and how much stays in stock.
FIFO leaves the newest cases in stock, and when costs fall those are the cheapest, so the closing stock is valued lower, not higher.

questions.prompt: A retailer's store fit-out has a carrying amount of $300,000. Sales at the store have collapsed, and the retailer now expects to recover only $120,000 from using or selling the fit-out. What does an impairment do?
hints: The write-down is the gap between the carrying amount and the amount the retailer expects to recover.
Ask when the cash for the fit-out was spent, and whether the write-down spends any more.

acceptedIdeas: It writes the fit-out down by $180,000, lowers profit by that amount and takes no cash that year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It writes the fit-out down by $180,000, lowers profit by that amount and takes no cash that year

choices.label: It writes the fit-out down by $180,000, lowers profit by that amount and takes no cash that year
It lowers profit by $180,000 and takes $180,000 of cash out of the bank that year
It writes the fit-out down to $120,000, but profit stays the same until the store is closed
It lowers profit by $300,000, because the whole carrying amount is lost once sales collapse

questions.onCorrect: The fit-out drops from $300,000 to the $120,000 that can be recovered, profit takes the $180,000 loss now, and no cash leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: The cash was spent when the fit-out was built. An impairment is a write-down of what is carried on the balance sheet, so no cash leaves when it is recorded.
The write-down is an expense in the period it is recognised, so profit takes the hit now. The retailer doesn't wait for the store to close.
Only the shortfall is written off. The fit-out is still carried at the $120,000 the retailer expects to recover.

questions.prompt: A company buys a delivery van and also holds some of last season's clothing in stock. Which of these figures in its accounts are judgements, and which are records of what happened?
hints: Ask whether the figure could be checked against a document today, or only against what happens later.
A figure that depends on the future is a judgement even when it is written with a precise number.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The van's life, its end-of-life value and the selling price of old clothing are judgements. The price paid, the stock count and the purchase date are records.

items.label: How many years the van will be used
items.explanation: It is an estimate of the future, and it can be revised.

items.label: The price paid for the van
items.explanation: It is on the invoice and the bank statement, and it can't change.

items.label: What the van will be worth at the end of its life
items.explanation: Nobody knows it until the van is sold, so it is an estimate.

items.label: The number of items in the year-end stock count
items.explanation: It is counted, so it is a record of what was on the shelves.

items.label: What last season's clothing will sell for
items.explanation: It is an expectation about prices that haven't been paid yet.

items.label: The date the van was bought
items.explanation: It happened once and is written down.

questions.onCorrect: The figures that depend on what happens later are judgements, and the ones that happened already are records.

questions.prompt: Source A is two lines from Woolworths's reconciliation of profit to operating cash flow, in $ millions, with 2026 first and 2025 second. Source B is the note to the impairment line. What do the two sources show about the 2025 impairments?
hints: Ask what a reconciliation of profit to cash adds back, and why.
Check whether either source says anything about cash received or paid.

acceptedIdeas: They reduced 2025 profit, and the add-back shows that no cash left in 2025 because of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They reduced 2025 profit, and the add-back shows that no cash left in 2025 because of them

choices.label: They took $459 million of cash out of Woolworths in 2025, which the reconciliation then puts back
They were reversed in 2026, which is why the 2026 figure is only $16 million
They reduced 2025 profit, and the add-back shows that no cash left in 2025 because of them
They were sales of the BIG W, MyDeal and Healthylife businesses, so the $459 million is cash received

extracts.text: Depreciation and amortisation 2.3.3 2,984 2,953 Impairment of non-financial assets1 16 459
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 4.5
extracts.kind: Part of a company's reconciliation of its profit to its operating cash flow

extracts.text: In the prior period, impairment of non-financial assets included the BIG W impairment of $346 million, MyDeal impairment of $45 million and Healthylife impairment of $17 million.
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 4.5, footnote 1
extracts.kind: A note to the same reconciliation, naming what the 2025 figure included

questions.onCorrect: An impairment lowers profit without using cash, so the reconciliation adds it back: $459 million in 2025, including the three named businesses.

misconceptions.feedback: A reconciliation adds back an item that reduced profit without using cash. If the impairments had used cash, there would be nothing to add back.
Nothing in either source says the 2025 charges were reversed. The 2026 column is a separate, much smaller charge for that year.
The note says the 2025 impairment included charges relating to those three businesses. An impairment is a write-down, and a write-down brings in no cash.

questions.prompt: A shoe retailer holds last season's stock that cost $80,000 and is now expected to sell for $50,000 after the costs of selling it. What should its accounts show at the year end?
hints: Compare what the stock cost with what it is now expected to fetch after selling costs.
Stock is carried at the lower of the two, and a write-down is an expense in the period it is recognised.

acceptedIdeas: The stock carried at $50,000, with a $30,000 write-down charged to this year's cost of sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stock carried at $50,000, with a $30,000 write-down charged to this year's cost of sales

choices.label: The stock carried at $50,000, with a $30,000 write-down charged to this year's cost of sales
The stock carried at $80,000 until it is sold, with the $30,000 loss recognised only at the sale
The stock carried at $50,000, with $30,000 of cash recorded as leaving the business this year

questions.onCorrect: Stock is carried at whichever is lower, cost or net realisable value, so it drops to $50,000 and the $30,000 loss goes into this year's cost of sales.

misconceptions.feedback: Stock is carried at whichever is lower, cost or net realisable value, and a write-down is expensed in the period it occurs. The loss can't wait for the sale.
The cash for the stock was spent when it was bought. The write-down lowers profit and the stock figure, and no cash moves.

questions.prompt: At the start of the year a cinema chain extends the useful life of its projectors from eight years to twelve. Compared with what its accounts would have shown without the change, how is each of these affected?
hints: Start with the depreciation charge: does spreading the cost over more years make it larger or smaller?
Cash, past prices and earlier years' reported profit can't be changed by a new estimate.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Profit and the carrying amount are higher, and the depreciation charge is lower. Cash, the price paid and earlier years' profit are unchanged.

items.label: This year's profit
items.explanation: Less of the cost is charged this year, so profit is higher.

items.label: The projectors' carrying amount at the year end
items.explanation: Less has been written off, so more of the cost is still carried.

items.label: This year's depreciation charge
items.explanation: The remaining cost is spread over more years.

items.label: The cash in the bank
items.explanation: A change in estimate moves no cash.

items.label: The price paid for the projectors
items.explanation: It was paid in the past and is a record.

items.label: The profit already reported for earlier years
items.explanation: A change in estimate applies from now on, and earlier years aren't restated.

questions.onCorrect: A longer life lowers the charge, which lifts profit and the carrying amount, while cash, the price paid and past years stay as they were.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's current liabilities are about $6 billion above its current assets. Which reason for that does its own note give?
hints: Read the second sentence of the extract: it opens with what the shortfall is principally due to.
Check each option against the reasons the note lists, and set aside any it doesn't mention.

acceptedIdeas: Stock turns over quickly and suppliers are paid some time after the goods are sold, among other reasons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stock turns over quickly and suppliers are paid some time after the goods are sold, among other reasons

choices.label: The company can't pay its debts as they fall due, so the directors had to explain the shortfall
Stock turns over quickly and suppliers are paid some time after the goods are sold, among other reasons
Customers owe it unusually large receivables that are not due for another twelve months or more
A single wage provision is the only cause, and it will reverse itself in the following year's accounts

extracts.text: The Group’s working capital is in a net current liability position as at 28 June 2026 of $5,995 million (2025: net current liability position of $5,306 million). The net current liability position is principally due to the fast turning nature of inventories, the timing of payments to suppliers, the use of available funds to support investments that are classified as non-current assets, and the Group’s current lease obligations.
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 1.1.2 on going concern
extracts.kind: A company's note to its financial statements, written for shareholders

questions.onCorrect: The note puts the shortfall down to fast-turning stock, the timing of supplier payments, funds used for non-current assets and current lease obligations.

misconceptions.feedback: The note gives reasons that come from how the business trades. The directors' view in the same note is that the group expects to meet its debts when they fall due.
The note lists no such reason, and Woolworths's trade receivables are small because its retail customers pay at the till.
The note gives four reasons and none is a provision. The 2025 figure of $5,306 million shows the shortfall isn't new this year.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia says this about a current ratio below 1, which means current liabilities are higher than current assets. Which of these invented businesses fits the exception it describes?
hints: Look for the business whose cash arrives before its bills do.
Cash received before a service is delivered is a liability, as in the lesson on when revenue counts, and it is already in the bank.

acceptedIdeas: A theatre that sells tickets months ahead and pays its suppliers after each show
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A theatre that sells tickets months ahead and pays its suppliers after each show

choices.label: A wholesaler that holds stock for four months and waits two months for its customers to pay
A builder whose customers pay a year after each job is finished, and who pays its own bills monthly
A manufacturer that makes a profit but pays suppliers in 30 days and collects from customers in 90
A theatre that sells tickets months ahead and pays its suppliers after each show

extracts.text: A current ratio of less than 1 indicates that the company may have problems meeting its short-term obligations. However, if inventory turns into cash much more rapidly than the accounts payable become due, then the firm's current ratio can comfortably remain less than one. Low current ratios can also be justified for businesses that can collect cash from customers long before they need to pay their suppliers.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Current ratio" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The theatre has its customers' cash before it pays suppliers, so its current liabilities can exceed its current assets without strain.

misconceptions.feedback: This business pays out for stock long before the cash comes back, which is the reverse of the exception. Nothing turns its stock into cash faster than its bills fall due.
Customers who pay a year later leave the builder waiting while its own bills fall due, so a shortage of current assets is a real problem here.
Profit doesn't close a timing gap. This business pays suppliers 60 days before it collects, so it needs funding in between.

questions.prompt: Why are the days to pay suppliers taken away when the cash conversion cycle is worked out?
hints: Ask who is funding the stock during the days before a supplier is paid.
The cycle measures how long the business's own cash is out.

acceptedIdeas: Supplier credit means the business has the stock for those days without yet paying
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Supplier credit means the business has the stock for those days without yet paying

choices.label: Paying suppliers is a cost to the business, and costs are always taken away from the totals
The days to pay are a negative number, because payables are a liability
Supplier credit means the business has the stock for those days without yet paying

questions.onCorrect: During the days before a supplier is paid, the supplier is funding the stock, so those days come off the time the business's own cash is tied up.

misconceptions.feedback: The cycle counts days, not dollars, so there is no cost to take away. It is the days of credit that shorten the time cash is out.
Payables are a liability on the balance sheet, but the days to pay are an ordinary count. They are subtracted because they offset the days the business is out of cash.

questions.prompt: Suppliers are paid after 35 days. What does that leave for Dunmore to fund?
hints: Compare the day Dunmore pays suppliers with the day it gets paid.
Whoever pays for the tiles in between is funding the cycle.

acceptedIdeas: About 140 days of tiles and credit, which Dunmore must fund from somewhere else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 140 days of tiles and credit, which Dunmore must fund from somewhere else

choices.label: About 140 days of tiles and credit, which Dunmore must fund from somewhere else
Nothing, because suppliers are paid out of the sales as the sales come in each week
A negative cycle, because suppliers are paid before the customers pay Dunmore

questions.onCorrect: Suppliers are paid on day 35 and Dunmore is paid on day 175, so 140 days of tiles must be funded by its owners or its lenders.

misconceptions.feedback: Dunmore pays suppliers on day 35, but its first sales cash comes in only after 175 days, so the sales can't pay the suppliers.
Suppliers are paid first, so the cash goes out long before it comes back. That is a positive cycle, one that has to be funded.

questions.prompt: Dunmore gives its customers 30-day terms, but on average they take 55 days to pay. What is the best next check?
hints: The average hides how the receivables are spread: some may be on time and some very late.
If part of the balance may never be collected, which figure should already allow for it?

acceptedIdeas: The age of the receivables, and whether the allowance for doubtful accounts still fits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The age of the receivables, and whether the allowance for doubtful accounts still fits

choices.label: Whether customers are hiding something from the auditors, since late payers always are
The age of the receivables, and whether the allowance for doubtful accounts still fits
Nothing, because the terms don't change when customers actually pay
Last year's profit, because collection is decided by profit alone

questions.onCorrect: An average of 55 days against 30-day terms points to some late balances, so the age of the receivables and the allowance for doubtful accounts come next.

misconceptions.feedback: A slow average has many possible causes, including a few large late payers or a looser credit policy. It is a reason to ask, and it proves nothing yet about concealment.
The gap between the terms and the days taken is the signal. Terms say when payment was due, and 55 days against 30 shows many customers are late.
Profit doesn't tell you how old the receivables are. The question is how much is overdue and whether some of it will never be collected.

questions.prompt: An invented pizza chain holds about 5 days of stock, collects at the till, and pays its suppliers after about 25 days, so its cycle is about -20 days. What does that mean?
hints: Add the stock days and the collection days, then compare the total with the days to pay.
Ask which happens first: the customer's cash arriving or the supplier being paid.

acceptedIdeas: Customers pay about twenty days before suppliers must be paid, so supplier credit funds the stock
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Customers pay about twenty days before suppliers must be paid, so supplier credit funds the stock

choices.label: The chain loses money on every pizza it sells, because its cash conversion cycle comes out negative
Customers pay about twenty days late, so the cash from each sale is delayed
Stock sits unsold for about twenty days, so cash is tied up in the freezer for that long
Customers pay about twenty days before suppliers must be paid, so supplier credit funds the stock

questions.onCorrect: Stock plus collection take 5 days and suppliers wait 25, so the chain holds its customers' cash for about 20 days before it must pay.

misconceptions.feedback: The cycle measures timing in days. A negative figure says nothing about whether each sale is profitable.
This chain collects at the till, so customers aren't late. The negative figure comes from supplier terms that are longer than its stock and collection days put together.
The chain holds only about 5 days of stock. A long time in stock would raise the cycle, and this cycle is negative.

questions.prompt: Two invented firms each have current liabilities $2 million above current assets. Aspen Fresh owes mostly trade payables to suppliers, sells its stock in about 10 days and is paid at the till. Brook Supplies owes mostly short-term bank loans, holds its stock for about 120 days and waits 60 days for customers to pay. Which should a reader worry about more?
hints: Compare how long each firm's cash is out of the business, and who is funding it in the meantime.
Short-term loans have to be repaid or renewed, whereas supplier credit is repaid by the cash from the sales.

acceptedIdeas: Brook, because a long cycle funded by loans due soon leaves cash to be found
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Brook, because a long cycle funded by loans due soon leaves cash to be found

choices.label: Aspen, because trade payables are owed to many suppliers and fall due sooner than loans
Both equally, because the same shortfall of $2 million means the same risk
Brook, because a long cycle funded by loans due soon leaves cash to be found
Neither, because a business that reports a profit can always find the cash it needs

questions.onCorrect: Brook's cash is out for about six months and loans fund it, so it must keep finding cash, while Aspen's suppliers fund stock that has sold long before they are paid.

misconceptions.feedback: Aspen's suppliers are funding stock that sells in 10 days and is paid for at the till, so the cash is there before the bills fall due. Its shortfall is a feature of the model.
The size of the gap is the same but its shape isn't. Ask what the cycle looks like and who funds it before judging the gap.
Profit and cash can come apart, as in the lesson on why profit is not cash. A long cycle funded by loans is exactly where a profitable business can run short.

questions.prompt: A firm's cash conversion cycle can be pulled longer or shorter by what it does. Which way does each of these move it?
hints: The cycle is stock days plus collection days less days to pay. Which of those does each item change?
Anything that makes the firm's own cash stay out longer lengthens the cycle.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More stock days, slower customers and quicker payment to suppliers all lengthen the cycle. Deposits, longer supplier terms and faster-turning stock shorten it.

items.label: Holding stock for eleven weeks instead of eight
items.explanation: More days of stock means cash is out for longer before a sale.

items.label: Letting customers pay in 60 days instead of 30
items.explanation: More days to collect lengthens the time before the cash is back.

items.label: Paying suppliers in 20 days instead of 40
items.explanation: Fewer days of supplier credit means the firm funds the stock for longer.

items.label: Taking a deposit before the work starts
items.explanation: The cash arrives before the work is done, which shortens the days to collect.

items.label: Agreeing 60-day terms with suppliers where it was 30
items.explanation: More days of supplier credit means suppliers fund the stock for longer.

items.label: Clearing slow-selling stock so that it turns over in fewer days
items.explanation: Fewer days of stock means cash comes back sooner.

questions.onCorrect: The cycle lengthens with more stock days, slower collection or quicker payment to suppliers, and shortens when any of those moves the other way.

questions.prompt: An invented wholesaler, Merrick Foods, has reached a cycle of -15 days by paying its suppliers after 75 days. Read what Wikipedia says about such a cycle. What risk does it point to?
hints: Read the end of the extract: it says what isn't always sustainable.
Ask who is funding Merrick's stock, and what happens if that funding stops.

acceptedIdeas: That the cycle holds only while suppliers go on supplying on terms this slow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the cycle holds only while suppliers go on supplying on terms this slow

choices.label: That the cycle holds only while suppliers go on supplying on terms this slow
None, because a negative cycle shows that the business is strong and well run
That customers will start paying later, because they notice the slow payment to suppliers
That the firm has too much cash, because a negative cycle means cash is piling up

extracts.text: However, shortening the CCC creates its own risks: while a firm could even achieve a negative CCC by collecting from customers before paying suppliers, a policy of strict collections and lax payments is not always sustainable.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Cash conversion cycle" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: A policy of strict collections and slow payments isn't always sustainable, because suppliers may stop giving long terms and the firm would then have to fund the stock itself.

misconceptions.feedback: A negative cycle can reflect a strong model, but the extract warns that collecting strictly while paying slowly is not always sustainable.
The extract is about suppliers. Nothing in it says customers' behaviour follows the firm's own payment habits.
A negative cycle means suppliers' money is funding the stock. It doesn't mean the firm's own cash is piling up.

questions.prompt: Two invented chains each hold $50 million of stock. Kemp Stores has an annual cost of sales of $600 million and Lyle Stores has $300 million. Which holds more days of stock, and why?
hints: Days of stock is the stock divided by the cost of sales, times 365.
With the same stock, a smaller cost of sales means the stock is used up more slowly.

acceptedIdeas: Lyle, about twice as many, because the same stock lasts through half the sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lyle, about twice as many, because the same stock lasts through half the sales

choices.label: Kemp, because a larger cost of sales means it carries more stock overall
Both the same, because each chain holds exactly $50 million of stock at the year end
Lyle, about twice as many, because the same stock lasts through half the sales

questions.onCorrect: Kemp holds about 30 days of stock and Lyle about 60, so the same $50 million lasts twice as long when the cost of sales is half as big.

misconceptions.feedback: Days of stock divides the stock by the cost of sales, so a larger cost of sales makes the count smaller. Here the stock is the same for both.
The count of days depends on how fast the stock is used. The same $50 million lasts about twice as long at Lyle.

questions.prompt: Woolworths had borrowings of $5,161 million and equity of $4,910 million at 28 June 2026. Lovisa had loans of $87.0 million and equity of $78.0 million. On borrowings alone, how do the two compare against their equity?
hints: Divide each company's borrowings by its own equity, roughly.
Round to easy numbers: about 5 billion over 5 billion, and about 90 million over 80 million.

acceptedIdeas: About the same, with each company's borrowings close to the size of its equity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About the same, with each company's borrowings close to the size of its equity

choices.label: Woolworths borrows far more compared with its equity, because its debt runs to billions
About the same, with each company's borrowings close to the size of its equity
Lovisa borrows far more compared with its equity, because its equity is so small

questions.onCorrect: Each company's borrowings are about one times its equity, so on loans alone they sit close together, which is why the next screens ask what else counts as debt.

misconceptions.feedback: Size isn't the test. Divide each borrowing figure by its equity and each comes to about one times, so against their equity the two borrow about the same.
Lovisa's equity is small, but so are its loans. $87.0 million against $78.0 million is about one times, close to Woolworths's figure.

questions.prompt: Two invented firms each have a current ratio of 1.5. Beech Foods holds mostly cash and receivables, and Cedar Homewares holds mostly slow-selling stock. Which can meet its bills more easily, and which ratio shows it?
hints: Which current assets can be turned into cash quickly, and which have to be sold first?
Ask what the quick ratio drops from the current assets.

acceptedIdeas: Beech, and the quick ratio shows it, because that ratio leaves stock out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Beech, and the quick ratio shows it, because that ratio leaves stock out

choices.label: Beech, and the quick ratio shows it, because that ratio leaves stock out
Cedar, because more stock gives it more to sell when the bills fall due
Neither, because the same current ratio always means the same ability to pay

questions.onCorrect: Beech's current assets are mostly cash and receivables, so its quick ratio stays close to its current ratio, while Cedar's would fall once stock is taken out.

misconceptions.feedback: Stock has to be sold before it becomes cash, and slow-selling stock may not fetch its carrying amount. The quick ratio leaves it out for that reason.
The same ratio can hide very different mixes of assets. That is why the quick ratio, which leaves out stock, is the more conservative test.

questions.prompt: An invented grocery chain, Hallam Stores, has equity of $10 million, bank loans of $10 million and store lease liabilities of $30 million. Which statement about its gearing is best?
hints: Work out debt over equity twice: once with the loans only, and once with the leases added.
Ask whether a promise to pay rent for years ahead is a fixed commitment.

acceptedIdeas: About 1 on loans alone and about 4 with the leases, which counts its fixed commitments
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1 on loans alone and about 4 with the leases, which counts its fixed commitments

choices.label: About 1 times in all, because leases are only rent, and rent is not counted as a debt at all
About 3 times, because the leases are the real debt and the bank loans are too small to count
About 1 on loans alone and about 4 with the leases, which counts its fixed commitments

questions.onCorrect: Loans of $10 million over equity of $10 million is about 1, and adding $30 million of leases makes it about 4, which is the figure that shows the fixed commitments.

misconceptions.feedback: Since IFRS 16 a lessee shows a lease liability, a fixed commitment to pay that is much like a loan. Leaving it out hides most of what Hallam owes.
The loans are as large as the equity, so they count. With the loans and the leases both in, the debt is about four times the equity.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter that about four fifths of Lovisa's finance costs are interest on its leases?
hints: Ask what the finance costs include, and whether a lease is a fixed commitment.
Compare the lease interest with the total finance costs.

acceptedIdeas: Leases carry a fixed cost like loans, so counting them in gearing matches the cover
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leases carry a fixed cost like loans, so counting them in gearing matches the cover

choices.label: Lease interest isn't a real cost, so the cover figure overstates how safe Lovisa is
Leases carry a fixed cost like loans, so counting them in gearing matches the cover
Lovisa pays no interest on its bank loans, so only its leases carry any cost at all

questions.onCorrect: The finance costs already include the lease interest, so counting leases in both gearing and cover treats them as the fixed commitments they are.

misconceptions.feedback: Lease interest is in finance costs because it is a cost of using the stores that has to be paid. It makes the cover a tougher test, so the cover figure is, if anything, cautious.
The finance costs are $24.8 million and the lease interest $19.7 million, which leaves some $5 million for the loans and other costs.

questions.prompt: Source A and Source B come from Wikipedia's account of ABC Learning, an Australian childcare company that went into receivership in November 2008. What do the two sources support together?
hints: Compare the size of the profit in Source A with the size of the debt in Source B.
Ask what profit measures, and what the lenders needed to know instead.

acceptedIdeas: A business can report a high profit and still be unable to service its debt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A business can report a high profit and still be unable to service its debt

choices.label: A business can report a high profit and still be unable to service its debt
The 2004/5 profit was invented, because no profitable company can later fail
A fall in profit explains the failure, because debt only matters once the profit has gone
The share price fell, so the earlier profit must have been overstated

extracts.text: It was a highly profitable company, in the FY2004/5 recording net profit after tax of $52.3 million on total revenues of $292.7 million.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "ABC Learning" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

extracts.text: An unexpected drop of 42 per cent in profit in the second half of 2007 to $37.1 million and its inability to service its $1.8 billion debt triggered a decline in the company's share price.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "ABC Learning" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: Profit tells you what a business earned, and whether it can pay its debt depends on how big the debt is against that profit, as ABC Learning showed.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither source says the profit was invented. Source A calls the company highly profitable, and a profit can be real while debt grows beyond what it can service.
Source B names two things together: a drop in profit and an inability to service the debt. A lender cares whether the debt can be paid, and that depends on its size against the profit.

A falling share price is the market's reaction. Source B says the fall was triggered by a drop in profit and an inability to service the debt, and it says nothing about earlier profit being overstated.

questions.prompt: A reader puts these questions to a company's statements. Which ratio answers each one best?
hints: Ask whether the question is about paying bills soon, about how much is owed overall, or about paying for the borrowing out of profit.
Each ratio answers one question, so match the question to the ratio built to answer it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bills due this year and stock selling slowly are liquidity questions. The share of funding from lenders and the effect of more leases are gearing questions. How far profit could fall and whether profit pays the finance costs are interest cover questions.

items.label: Is there enough cash and receivables to meet the bills due this year?
items.explanation: It asks about paying what falls due soon, which is what the quick ratio tests.

items.label: How much of the funding comes from lenders and landlords rather than owners?
items.explanation: It asks how much the business leans on borrowing and leases.

items.label: How far could operating profit fall before it stopped covering the interest?
items.explanation: That is the question interest cover answers directly.

items.label: Would the company be stuck if its stock sold slowly while bills arrived on time?
items.explanation: The quick ratio leaves stock out to test exactly this.

items.label: If it took on more store leases, how much more would it owe compared with its equity?
items.explanation: Leases add to what is owed, and gearing compares that with equity.

items.label: Is profit large enough to pay the finance costs comfortably?
items.explanation: It compares operating profit with finance costs, which is interest cover.

questions.onCorrect: Liquidity ratios ask about paying what is due soon, gearing asks how much is owed against equity, and interest cover asks whether profit can carry the cost of the borrowing.

questions.prompt: An invented company reports a current ratio of 1.3. It later emerges that $2 billion of debt due within a year was shown as non-current. What did that do to the reported ratio?
hints: Debt due within a year belongs in current liabilities, which is the bottom of the ratio.
What happens to a fraction when its bottom figure is made smaller?

acceptedIdeas: It overstated the ratio, because the current liabilities on the bottom line were left too low
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It overstated the ratio, because the current liabilities on the bottom line were left too low

choices.label: It understated the ratio, because debt that is shown as non-current counts as an asset
It overstated the ratio, because the current liabilities on the bottom line were left too low
It made no difference to the ratio, because the debt was owed whichever line it sat on

questions.onCorrect: Leaving short-term debt out of current liabilities shrinks the bottom of the ratio, so the reported 1.3 looks safer than the true position.

misconceptions.feedback: Debt is never an asset. Moving it out of current liabilities lowers the bottom of the ratio and raises the ratio itself.
The debt was owed either way, but the ratio uses only the current lines. Leaving $2 billion out of the bottom figure makes the ratio look better than the position is.

questions.prompt: Two invented retailers have the same gearing with leases, about 2 times. Quince Foods has a current ratio of 0.7 and an interest cover of 8. Rowe Retail has a current ratio of 1.4 and an interest cover of 1.5. A downturn halves each firm's operating profit. Which is in more trouble with its lenders?
hints: Halve each firm's interest cover, and see what is left.
A cover below 1 means operating profit no longer pays the finance costs.

acceptedIdeas: Rowe, because its cover would fall below 1 even though its current ratio looks safer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rowe, because its cover would fall below 1 even though its current ratio looks safer

choices.label: Quince, because a current ratio of 0.7 means it can't pay its bills when they fall due
Neither, because both firms have the same gearing and so carry the same risk
Rowe, because its cover would fall below 1 even though its current ratio looks safer

questions.onCorrect: Halving the profit halves the cover, so Quince's falls to about 4 and Rowe's to about 0.75, which is below the 1 it needs to pay its finance costs.

misconceptions.feedback: A low current ratio can be part of a business model, as with Woolworths. Quince's cover would still be about 4 after the downturn, so its interest is comfortably paid.
Gearing says how much is owed, and cover says whether profit can pay for it. Halving profit halves each cover, and only Rowe's drops under 1.

questions.prompt: Four invented retailers report these figures in $ millions. In what order do their interest covers run, from the thinnest to the thickest?
hints: Interest cover is operating profit divided by finance costs, so work out each firm's cover roughly.
A firm whose operating profit is smaller than its finance costs has a cover below 1, which is the thinnest of all.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bellis covers its finance costs about 0.75 times, Dover 2 times, Aster 3 times and Cobalt 10 times, so that is the order from thinnest to thickest.

questions.onCorrect: Cover runs from about 0.75 for Bellis, through 2 and 3, to about 10 for Cobalt, so profit is the thinnest cushion where finance costs are largest against it.

questions.prompt: Retailer A keeps 10 cents of profit from every dollar it sells, and Retailer B keeps 2 cents, yet both earn 5% a year on their assets. Both are invented. What must be true of B?
hints: Return on assets is profit divided by assets, and profit is the margin times sales.
If B keeps a fifth as much from each sales dollar, how many more sales dollars must each asset dollar bring in?

acceptedIdeas: Each dollar of its assets produces about five times as many sales dollars as A's
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each dollar of its assets produces about five times as many sales dollars as A's

choices.label: It has about five times as many assets as A, to make up for its thin margin
Its costs are about five times A's, which is why its margin is so much thinner
Each dollar of its assets produces about five times as many sales dollars as A's
One of the two must have misreported, because a thin margin can't match a thick one

questions.onCorrect: A fifth of the margin needs five times the sales from each dollar of assets to reach the same return, which is what asset turnover measures.

misconceptions.feedback: The return on assets is profit divided by assets, so more assets would lower B's return. The thin margin has to be made up in how hard each asset dollar works.
Costs can explain a thin margin, but they don't make up for it. To earn the same 5%, B must produce more sales from each dollar of assets.
Both can be right. The return on assets is the margin times the number of times the assets turn into sales, so very different margins can give the same return.

questions.prompt: An invented firm, Kerr Home, saw its gross margin rise from 40% to 42% while its net margin fell from 8% to 6%. What is the most likely explanation?
hints: Gross margin looks only at the cost of the goods sold, and net margin at everything.
If gross margin rose and net margin fell, the difference lies in the costs deducted after gross profit.

acceptedIdeas: The costs below gross profit, such as wages and rent, grew faster than sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The costs below gross profit, such as wages and rent, grew faster than sales

choices.label: The costs below gross profit, such as wages and rent, grew faster than sales
The cost of the goods sold must have risen, because the margins always move together
Sales must have fallen, because a higher gross margin always comes with falling sales
Interest and tax can't have changed, so the figures must contain an error

questions.onCorrect: The gross margin gain was swallowed by costs further down the statement, so the margins moved apart. Lovisa's own figures show it: gross margin up from 82.0% to 82.6%, operating margin down from 17.4% to 16.9%.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher gross margin means the cost of goods sold fell as a share of sales. Margins at different levels can move in opposite directions.
Nothing ties a higher gross margin to falling sales. The fall in net margin comes from what was deducted after gross profit.
The margins can differ at each level for good reasons. Costs, interest and tax can each move, and the statement can be perfectly correct.

questions.prompt: Three invented retailers report these figures. X has a net margin of 4% and turns its assets 3 times a year, Y has 12% and 0.8 times, and Z has 6% and 1.5 times. Which earns the highest return on its assets?
hints: Return on assets is the net margin times asset turnover, so multiply the two for each firm.
Don't rank by margin alone, since a thin margin can come with a fast turnover.

acceptedIdeas: X, because its fast turnover more than makes up for the thinnest margin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: X, because its fast turnover more than makes up for the thinnest margin

choices.label: Y, because it has the highest margin of the three, at 12 cents per sales dollar
X, because its fast turnover more than makes up for the thinnest margin
Z, because it is in the middle on both margin and turnover, so it is balanced

questions.onCorrect: X earns about 12%, Y about 9.6% and Z about 9%, so the firm with the thinnest margin earns the most on its assets.

misconceptions.feedback: The margin is only one of two parts. Y's 12% times 0.8 turns is about 9.6%, below X's 4% times 3, which is 12%.
Being in the middle on both gives the lowest return here: 6% times 1.5 turns is about 9%, below Y's 9.6% and X's 12%.

questions.prompt: Woolworths turns its assets faster than Lovisa does, and still earns the smaller return on assets. What explains that?
hints: Compare the two margins, then compare the two turnovers, and ask which gap is bigger.
The return is the margin times the turnover, so a big enough gap in one part can outweigh the other.

acceptedIdeas: Its margin is six times thinner, outweighing a turnover only one and a half times faster
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its margin is six times thinner, outweighing a turnover only one and a half times faster

choices.label: Its margin is six times thinner, outweighing a turnover only one and a half times faster
A faster turnover lowers the return, so the faster turnover must be the cause
One company reports in millions and the other in thousands, so the returns can't be compared

questions.onCorrect: Lovisa's margin is about six times Woolworths's, while Woolworths's turnover is about one and a half times Lovisa's, so the margin wins and Lovisa's return is about four times higher.

misconceptions.feedback: Other things equal, a faster turnover raises the return. The margin gap is what more than offsets it here.
A return on assets is a ratio, so the units cancel. It is the same kind of figure for any company.

questions.prompt: Two invented sellers have the same sales, the same products and the same costs. Corry puts its delivery costs inside cost of sales, and Dell reports them in distribution expenses below gross profit. Which statement is true?
hints: Ask which firm has deducted the delivery costs before it reaches gross profit.
By operating profit, every cost above that line has been taken out for both firms.

acceptedIdeas: Dell shows the higher gross margin, and the two show the same operating margin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dell shows the higher gross margin, and the two show the same operating margin

choices.label: Corry shows the higher gross margin, because it has counted more costs in the sum
Dell shows the higher gross margin, and the two show the same operating margin
The two show the same gross margin, because delivery is a cost for both
Dell shows the higher gross margin and also the higher operating margin

questions.onCorrect: Where a cost sits changes the gross margin and leaves the operating margin alone, so operating margin is the safer line for comparing companies.

misconceptions.feedback: Deducting more costs above gross profit lowers the gross margin. Corry deducts the delivery costs there, so its gross margin is the lower one.
The delivery cost is the same, but it is deducted at different lines. Gross profit comes before distribution expenses, so Dell's is higher.
By the time you reach operating profit, both firms have deducted the same costs in all. The operating margins match.

questions.prompt: An invented firm, Laurel Foods, reports 'one-off' restructuring costs of $20 million, $25 million and $22 million in its last three years, on revenue of about $1,000 million a year. How should a reader treat its margin before those costs?
hints: Work out roughly what share of revenue the restructuring costs are each year.
Ask whether costs that appear every year can fairly be called one-off.

acceptedIdeas: As a best case, because costs of about 2% of revenue came up in all three years
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a best case, because costs of about 2% of revenue came up in all three years

choices.label: As the normal margin, because the company itself calls the costs one-off each year
As a best case, because costs of about 2% of revenue came up in all three years
As meaningless, because any margin reported before some costs is an invention

questions.onCorrect: Costs of about 2% of revenue in each of three years are part of how the firm has really performed, so the margin before them is a best case.

misconceptions.feedback: A label doesn't make a cost unusual. Three years running at about 2% of revenue is a pattern, and the margin before them leaves a real cost out.
A margin before such items still shows the business without them. The mistake is treating it as the whole story when the items keep returning.

questions.prompt: Woolworths reports its margins before significant items, with 2026 first, 2025 second and the change in basis points third (100 basis points is one percentage point). Why did its EBIT margin rise by more than its gross margin?
hints: Read the three changes in basis points, and see which two roughly add up to the third.
Look at the line that sits between the gross margin and EBIT, and see what it did.

acceptedIdeas: Its cost of doing business fell as a share of sales, adding to the gain in gross margin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its cost of doing business fell as a share of sales, adding to the gain in gross margin

choices.label: Revenue grew faster than costs, and that always lifts the operating margin more than the gross margin
Significant items were smaller, which lifted EBIT without lifting the gross margin
The NPAT margin rose, and net profit feeds back into the EBIT figure
Its cost of doing business fell as a share of sales, adding to the gain in gross margin

extracts.text:
Gross margin (%) 27.4 27.2 12 bps
Cost of doing business (CODB) (%) 23.0 23.3 (24) bps
EBIT (%) 4.3 4.0 35 bps
NPAT (%) 2.2 2.0 23 bps
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, margins before significant items
extracts.kind: A table in a company's annual report, written for shareholders

questions.onCorrect: Gross margin rose 12 basis points and the cost of doing business fell 24, which together come to about the 35 basis points gained at EBIT.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing makes the operating margin move more than the gross margin as a rule. Here the table shows the reason: a second line fell.
The table is before significant items, so they can't explain a change in it. Look at the line between gross margin and EBIT.
Net profit comes after EBIT, so it can't feed back into it. The cost of doing business sits between the gross margin and EBIT.

questions.prompt: A reader looks only at a company's margins. Which of these can the margins show, and which can't they show?
hints: A margin divides a profit by revenue, so ask what that division leaves out.
Anything that needs the assets, or the lines inside a cost, is beyond a margin.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A margin shows what is left of each sales dollar at the gross, operating and net levels. It can't show the return on assets, the asset turnover or how a rival classifies its costs.

items.label: How much of each sales dollar is left after the cost of the goods sold
items.explanation: That is the gross margin.

items.label: How much of each sales dollar is left after running costs, before interest and tax
items.explanation: That is the operating margin.

items.label: How much of each sales dollar is left after all costs, interest and tax
items.explanation: That is the net margin.

items.label: How much profit each dollar of assets earns
items.explanation: It needs the assets, which a margin leaves out. Margin times turnover gives it.

items.label: How many sales dollars each dollar of assets produces
items.explanation: That is asset turnover, which uses assets and not profit.

items.label: Whether a rival puts the same costs inside cost of sales
items.explanation: That is in the notes and the cost lines of each statement, and a margin hides it.

questions.onCorrect: A margin is a share of sales at one level. It can't show the assets behind the profit or where a company puts its costs.

questions.prompt: A note in Woolworths's report shows where its depreciation and amortisation of $2,984 million was charged, in $ millions for 2026 and 2025. Lovisa reports its depreciation on a separate line below gross profit. What follows for comparing the two companies' gross margins?
hints: Find the line of the note that sits inside cost of sales, and the line that sits below gross profit.
A cost deducted above gross profit lowers the gross margin. A cost deducted below it doesn't.

acceptedIdeas: Woolworths's gross margin is lowered by $414 million of depreciation, so compare operating margins
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Woolworths's gross margin is lowered by $414 million of depreciation, so compare operating margins

choices.label: Nothing, because depreciation is a non-cash cost and gross margins ignore non-cash costs altogether
Lovisa's gross margin is the lower one, because depreciation is a cost and Lovisa shows more of it
Woolworths's gross margin is lowered by $414 million of depreciation, so compare operating margins

extracts.text:
Cost of sales 414 379
Branch and administration expenses 2,570 2,574
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 2.3.3 on depreciation and amortisation
extracts.kind: Part of a company's note to its financial statements, written for shareholders

questions.onCorrect: Woolworths deducts $414 million of depreciation inside cost of sales and Lovisa deducts none there, so the operating margin is the like-for-like line.

misconceptions.feedback: Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales, and cost of sales can include depreciation. The $414 million is in Woolworths's cost of sales, so it lowers its gross margin.
Lovisa's depreciation is below gross profit, so its gross margin doesn't carry it at all. It is Woolworths that has some inside cost of sales.

questions.prompt: Maya puts $100,000 of her own money into a shop and borrows another $400,000 from a bank. After the bank's interest is paid, the shop earns $50,000 in the year. Which figure says what Maya earned on her own money?
hints: Whose money is the profit left over for, once the bank has been paid?
Compare the $50,000 with the amount Maya herself put in.

acceptedIdeas: About 50%, because $50,000 is half of the $100,000 she put in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 50%, because $50,000 is half of the $100,000 she put in

questions.onCorrect: Profit left after the lender's interest belongs to the owner, so it is set against the owner's own money: $50,000 over $100,000.

choices.label: About 10%, because the shop holds $500,000 of assets
About 50%, because $50,000 is half of the $100,000 she put in
About 12%, because $50,000 is an eighth of the $400,000 borrowed

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by everything the shop holds, which is a return on assets. Maya's own money is the $100,000, and the question is what that money earned.
That divides by the bank's money. The bank has been paid its interest already, so the $50,000 that is left belongs to Maya and is set against what she put in.

questions.prompt: Linden Foods and Marsh Foods are two invented grocers. Linden's return on equity is 32% and Marsh's is 12%. Linden's equity is a tenth of its assets, while Marsh's is half. The extract is Wikipedia's description of the ratio. What is the fairest reading of the two figures?
hints: What does each ratio divide by, and how different are the two amounts?
Linden's equity is a tenth of its assets and Marsh's is half. What does a small denominator do to a ratio?

acceptedIdeas: The two ratios divide by very different amounts of equity, so the gap does not show which grocer is better
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two ratios divide by very different amounts of equity, so the gap does not show which grocer is better

questions.onCorrect: A ratio is only as comparable as its denominators. Next we split return on equity into parts, to see how much of a gap comes from the trading and how much from the equity.

choices.label: Linden is the better business, since its owners' money is working more than twice as hard as Marsh's
Marsh is a poor business, because its 12% falls below the range given in the extract and Linden's is above it
Neither ratio tells us anything, because the equity of the two grocers differs so much
The two ratios divide by very different amounts of equity, so the gap does not show which grocer is better

misconceptions.feedback: A high ratio can come from a thin equity base as well as from good trading. Linden's equity is a tenth of its assets, so a modest profit can look large against it.

The extract gives 15 to 20% as a general rule of thumb and says the ratio is used mostly between companies in the same industry. A figure below the range is a reason to look closer and does not settle quality.
Each ratio does say what its owners' money earned. The difficulty is that the denominators differ, which is a reason to explain the gap before comparing the grocers.

extracts.text: ROE is especially used for comparing the performance of companies in the same industry. As with return on capital, an ROE is a measure of management's ability to generate income from the equity available to it. ROEs of 15–20% are generally considered good.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Return on equity" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: On average figures Lovisa's net margin is 10.2%, its asset turnover 1.35 and its assets over equity 8.9, which gives a return on equity of about 122%. Woolworths's are 1.6%, 2.1 and 7.0, which give about 24%. Which statement about the gap do the three factors support?
hints: Divide Lovisa's figure by Woolworths's for each factor and see which result is the largest.
A factor that is lower for Lovisa cannot be what lifts its return above Woolworths's.

acceptedIdeas: Most of it comes from Lovisa's net margin, which is more than six times Woolworths's, while its turnover is lower
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of it comes from Lovisa's net margin, which is more than six times Woolworths's, while its turnover is lower

questions.onCorrect: Lovisa's figure over Woolworths's is about 6.4 for margin, 0.64 for turnover and 1.3 for assets over equity, and the three multiply to the five-fold gap in return on equity.

choices.label: All three factors favour Lovisa about equally, so none of them stands out as the cause of the gap
Most of it comes from Lovisa's thinner equity, since its assets over equity is the higher of the two
Most of it comes from Lovisa's net margin, which is more than six times Woolworths's, while its turnover is lower
Most of it comes from Lovisa turning its assets over faster, which is how a jewellery chain would earn a high return

misconceptions.feedback: Lovisa's figure divided by Woolworths's is about 6.4 for net margin, 0.64 for turnover and 1.3 for assets over equity. They are far from equal, and turnover goes the other way.
Assets over equity is higher for Lovisa, but only about 1.3 times as high, 8.9 against 7.0. Its net margin is more than six times as high, which is a far larger part of the gap.
Lovisa's turnover is 1.35 against 2.1 for Woolworths, so its assets turn over more slowly. A factor that is lower for Lovisa cannot explain a higher return.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's profit was $95.6 million on average equity of about $78 million. Which explains a return on equity above 100%?
hints: A return above 100% means the profit is bigger than the equity it is divided by. What could keep equity small?
Look at what happened to the profit after it was earned, and at the reserve line.

acceptedIdeas: Its equity is smaller than one year's profit, since most profit is paid out and a reserve cancels its capital
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its equity is smaller than one year's profit, since most profit is paid out and a reserve cancels its capital

questions.onCorrect: Equity of $78.0 million sits against profit of $95.6 million because 93% of the profit was paid out and the reserve cancels nearly all of the share capital.

choices.label: Its equity is smaller than one year's profit, since most profit is paid out and a reserve cancels its capital
Its profit was ten times what it was last year, which pushed the ratio past 100% in a single year
It has no debts, so all of its profit belongs to the equity holders and none goes to lenders
Its shops are ten times as profitable as Woolworths's, which is exactly what a return of more than 100% means for a retailer

misconceptions.feedback: Profit rose from $86.3 million to $95.6 million, which is about 11%. A return above 100% means equity is smaller than a year's profit, whatever happened to profit.
Lovisa does have debts, with loans of $87.0 million and lease liabilities of $419.0 million, and its profit is already after the interest on them.
Lovisa's net margin is about six times Woolworths's, not ten times. A return above 100% needs equity that is smaller than a year's profit, however good the shops are.

questions.prompt: The second retailer's net margin is 2%, against 10% for the first, and both earn 20% on equity with assets twice their equity. Why must the second turn its assets over so much faster?
hints: Both retailers need margin times turnover to come to 10%.
If the margin is five times smaller, what must happen to the other factor?

acceptedIdeas: With a margin five times thinner, each dollar of assets must be used five times as often
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With a margin five times thinner, each dollar of assets must be used five times as often

questions.onCorrect: Margin times turnover must make 10% for both, so a margin one fifth the size needs five times the turnover.

choices.label: A thin margin means the retailer holds fewer assets, which raises its turnover on its own
