Turnover is always five times the margin when a retailer's assets are twice its equity
With a margin five times thinner, each dollar of assets must be used five times as often

misconceptions.feedback: Turnover is sales divided by assets, and a thin margin says nothing about how many assets a retailer holds. The retailer must sell more for each dollar of assets, whatever it holds.
There is no such rule. The needed turnover came from setting margin times turnover equal to 10%, which happens to give 5 for a 2% margin.

questions.prompt: A retailer that rents all its shops is being compared with one that owns its shops and borrowed to buy them. Why does a return on capital that counts lease liabilities give a fairer comparison than return on equity?
hints: Which part of each company's funding is different: the shops, or how the shops were paid for?
Think about what each ratio puts on top, and what it puts on the bottom.

acceptedIdeas: It counts shareholder and lender funding together, starting from operating profit, so financing choices do not change it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It counts shareholder and lender funding together, starting from operating profit, so financing choices do not change it

questions.onCorrect: Starting from operating profit and counting equity, borrowings and lease liabilities together means that renting, borrowing and owning outright can be compared on one footing.

choices.label: It leaves leases out of the calculation altogether, which makes a renting retailer and an owning retailer look much alike
It always gives a higher figure than return on equity, which makes the comparison easier to read
It uses market values in place of book values, which removes the effect of leasing
It counts shareholder and lender funding together, starting from operating profit, so financing choices do not change it

misconceptions.feedback: This version counts lease liabilities as capital. That is what puts the renting retailer's shops on the same footing as the owner's, whose borrowing already sits in its capital.
Return on capital came out lower than return on equity for both companies in the lesson. Its advantage is that funding does not move it, whatever level it reaches.
The version in the lesson uses book values from the balance sheet. Leasing is dealt with by counting the lease liabilities as capital.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Cafés has equity of $8 million, borrowings of $6 million, lease liabilities of $9 million and cash of $4 million. Which total is its capital for this ratio, and why?
hints: Capital here is equity plus borrowings plus lease liabilities, less cash.
Add the first three before you take anything off.

acceptedIdeas: $19 million, because cash in the bank funds nothing and comes off
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: $19 million, because cash in the bank funds nothing and comes off

questions.onCorrect: Equity of 8, borrowings of 6 and leases of 9 make 23, and taking off cash of 4 leaves 19.

choices.label: $10 million, because leases are only rent and the cash comes off
$19 million, because cash in the bank funds nothing and comes off
$23 million, because equity, borrowings and leases all count
$27 million, because cash in the bank is funding as well

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the $9 million of lease liabilities. The cafés' leased premises are funded by the landlord, and the ratio counts that funding.
That adds equity, borrowings and leases and forgets to take off the $4 million of cash.
That adds the cash. Cash sitting in the bank is not being used to run the cafés, so it comes off.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Cafés earns an after-tax operating profit of $3.15 million on capital of $19 million. Which return on capital is right, and why?
hints: Divide the after-tax operating profit by the capital you have just found.
Tax has already been taken off the top, in the first line.

acceptedIdeas: About 17%, because profit after tax is set against all the capital
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 17%, because profit after tax is set against all the capital

questions.onCorrect: A profit of $3.15 million on $19 million of capital is about 17 cents on each dollar, whoever supplied the dollar.

choices.label: About 12%, because the cash belongs in the capital too
About 17%, because profit after tax is set against all the capital
About 24%, because the profit before tax is what the capital earned
About 39%, because the owners' equity is the money that earned it

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by $27 million, which means the cash was added to the capital.
That is the operating profit before tax, $4.5 million, over $19 million. The ratio uses profit after tax.
That divides by the equity alone. Return on capital divides by everything that funds the business.

questions.prompt: Two invented chains report these figures. Ash Co has a return on equity of 40%, equity of a tenth of its assets and a return on capital of 6%. Elm Co has a return on equity of 15%, equity of half its assets and a return on capital of 11%. Which statement is best supported?
hints: Which of the two returns is not changed by how a business is funded?
Ash's equity is a tenth of its assets. What does that do to its return on equity?

acceptedIdeas: Elm's shops earn more on the money in them, and Ash's return on equity is lifted by how little equity it has
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Elm's shops earn more on the money in them, and Ash's return on equity is lifted by how little equity it has

questions.onCorrect: On return on capital Elm earns 11% against Ash's 6%, and Ash's 40% on equity reflects its thin equity more than its trading.

choices.label: Elm's shops earn more on the money in them, and Ash's return on equity is lifted by how little equity it has
Ash is the stronger business, because its return on equity is more than twice Elm's and so its owners earn far more
Elm is the weaker business, because its return on equity is the lower of the two and Ash's is much higher
The two cannot be compared at all, because their equity bases differ so much from one chain to the other

misconceptions.feedback: Ash's return on equity is lifted by having equity of only a tenth of its assets. On the money that funds it, Ash earns 6% against Elm's 11%.
Return on equity is the figure that funding distorts. Elm's return on capital is the higher of the two, so on the money in the business it does better.
Return on capital is built for this comparison. It does not depend on the equity base, so it can be set side by side.

questions.prompt: Harrow Ltd is invented. It earns an after-tax operating profit of $10 million on capital of $100 million, funded by $60 million of equity and $40 million of borrowings. It borrows another $30 million at 5% a year before tax and uses the money to buy back $30 million of its own shares. What happens to its return on equity and its return on capital?
hints: Add equity and borrowings before and after the buyback. Has the total capital changed?
Profit for the owners is divided by equity, which has halved. Is the extra interest large enough to outweigh that?

acceptedIdeas: Return on equity rises, and return on capital stays about the same because capital is unchanged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Return on equity rises, and return on capital stays about the same because capital is unchanged

questions.onCorrect: The buyback swaps equity for debt, so the owners' return rises while capital and operating profit stay where they were.

choices.label: Return on equity falls, because the new loan adds interest to the company's costs
Return on equity stays the same and return on capital falls, because the new loan costs interest
Both rise, because the business now earns its profit on a smaller amount of equity than before
Return on equity rises, and return on capital stays about the same because capital is unchanged

misconceptions.feedback: The extra interest is $1.5 million a year before tax, and the equity that was bought back had been earning the owners far more than that. Replacing equity with cheap debt raises the owners' return.
Interest is paid after operating profit, so it does not enter return on capital, and equity shrinking raises return on equity.
Return on capital divides by equity and borrowings together, which are $100 million before and after the buyback. Operating profit has not changed, so neither has the return on capital.

questions.prompt: Six situations call for a return on equity or a return on capital. Which measure answers each one?
hints: Ask which ratio changes when the mix of borrowing and equity changes.
A question about the owners' own money points to one ratio, and a question about all the funding points to the other.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Return on equity: profit per dollar of the owners' money, the effect of a buyback and the effect of the debt and equity mix. Return on capital: the bank-funded chain against the landlord-funded one, the use of all the funding, and the borrowed company against the debt-free one.

questions.onCorrect: Return on equity answers questions about the owners' money, and return on capital answers questions about the whole business.

items.label: How much profit each dollar of the owners' own money earned after the lenders were paid
items.explanation: It sets the profit left after interest against the owners' equity alone.

items.label: Which of two chains runs its shops better, when a bank funds one and its landlords fund the other
items.explanation: Counting equity, debt and leases together removes the difference in who supplied the money.

items.label: What happens to the owners' return when a company borrows to buy back its shares
items.explanation: The shares bought back leave equity smaller, which changes the denominator of this ratio.

items.label: How well a business uses everything shareholders and lenders have put into it
items.explanation: It starts from operating profit and sets it against all the funding.

items.label: How the mix of debt and equity changes what the owners earn
items.explanation: The profit left after interest and the size of the equity both move with the mix.

items.label: How two companies compare when one is heavily borrowed and the other has no debt
items.explanation: Operating profit and total capital do not change with the amount borrowed.

questions.prompt: Fenn Ltd is invented. Its return on equity was 12% last year and is 18% this year, and its profit is the same in both years. What is the best next question?
hints: Profit did not change, so which part of the ratio did?
What could make a company's equity fall without the business changing?

acceptedIdeas: Why equity fell, since a smaller equity base raises the ratio without any gain in trading
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Why equity fell, since a smaller equity base raises the ratio without any gain in trading

questions.onCorrect: The same profit over a third less equity gives a ratio a half higher, so the question is what shrank the equity.

choices.label: Why equity fell, since a smaller equity base raises the ratio without any gain in trading
Why the business improved, since a rise from 12% to 18% shows that its trading has got better
Why profit did not rise, since the ratio can only go up in a year when profit goes up
Why the ratio passed the range of 15 to 20%, since a figure as high as that must be an error

misconceptions.feedback: With the same profit, trading has not changed. A rise in the ratio has to come from the denominator.
A ratio can rise when its denominator falls. Here the same profit sits on less equity.
A figure of 18% is inside that range, and in any case a high figure is a reason to ask questions and not a sign of an error.

questions.prompt: You want to know when Woolworths counts a sale as revenue. Where should you look first?
hints: The line on the income statement has a small number beside it. What does that number point to?
Which part of the report explains how a figure was worked out, and not just what it came to?

acceptedIdeas: The accounting policy for revenue, which sits in the notes to the statements
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The accounting policy for revenue, which sits in the notes to the statements

questions.onCorrect: A policy for counting revenue is a note, and the small number beside a statement line is the way to it.

choices.label: The accounting policy for revenue, which sits in the notes to the statements
The cash flow statement, because revenue is counted when the cash arrives
The auditor's report, because auditors decide when revenue is recognised
The income statement itself, because the revenue line states its own timing

misconceptions.feedback: The cash flow statement shows cash received, and a sale can be counted as revenue before or after the cash comes in. The timing rule is a policy, and policies are set out in the notes.
The company decides how it recognises revenue, within the accounting standards. The auditor gives an opinion on the result, and does not set the policy.
The revenue line gives one total and a note number. The rule for when a sale is counted is explained in the note it points to.

questions.prompt: Pelham Ltd is invented. Its balance sheet shows cash of $40 million, and a note says that $12 million of it is money due from card payments, which the company will report as receivables from next year. What does the note change about how you read the $40 million?
hints: A receivable is money owed to the company. Who owes it here?
If $12 million of the $40 million is still to come in, how much is already there?

acceptedIdeas: It tells you that $12 million of the cash is money still due to Pelham, so $28 million is in the bank
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It tells you that $12 million of the cash is money still due to Pelham, so $28 million is in the bank

questions.onCorrect: The note splits the line: $28 million is cash in the ordinary sense and $12 million is money Pelham is still waiting to receive.

choices.label: The cash figure is wrong, and the statements must be corrected before anyone relies on them for a decision
It tells you that $12 million of the cash is a debt that Pelham owes to the card companies it uses
Notes only explain accounting policies and never change how a figure on a statement should be read
It tells you that $12 million of the cash is money still due to Pelham, so $28 million is in the bank

misconceptions.feedback: A note that explains what a line contains is part of the statements and does not signal an error. It tells you how to read the figure.
A receivable is an amount owed to the company. Money due from card payments is something Pelham is waiting to receive and not something it has to pay.
Notes also break lines down. This one shows that part of the cash is money still due, which changes how much is in the bank.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's balance sheet shows trade and other receivables of $29,682 thousand. Its note lists trade receivables of $3,177 thousand, deposits of $4,397 thousand, prepayments of $13,953 thousand and other receivables of $8,155 thousand. About what share of the line is money that customers owe?
hints: Only one of the four lines is trade receivables. How does it compare with the total?
A tenth of 29,682 would be about 2,968, and trade receivables are 3,177.

acceptedIdeas: About a tenth, since trade receivables are 3,177 out of the line's 29,682
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About a tenth, since trade receivables are 3,177 out of the line's 29,682

questions.onCorrect: Trade receivables are $3.2 million of $29.7 million, about 11%. The rest of the line is made up of other things.

choices.label: About a tenth, since trade receivables are 3,177 out of the line's 29,682
About a third, since deposits and trade receivables are both money owed
About a half, since prepayments are the largest part of the line
Nearly all of it, since the line is called trade and other receivables

misconceptions.feedback: Deposits are listed separately from trade receivables, so the note does not call them customer debts. Even adding them, the two lines come to about a quarter of the total.
Prepayments are close to half of the line, 47%, but they are costs paid in advance and not money customers owe.
That takes the label at its word. The note shows that the line also holds deposits, prepayments and other receivables.

questions.prompt: In the year to June 2026 Woolworths set aside an extra $710 million for wages it may have underpaid, though the final amount is not yet settled. Which of its three critical estimates would you read first, to see how an amount like that was judged?
hints: What kind of figure is an amount set aside for a payment that has not yet been made?
Match that kind of figure with the three notes the company names: leases, impairment and provisions.

acceptedIdeas: Note 3.12 on provisions, since the amount is an estimate of what is still to be paid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Note 3.12 on provisions, since the amount is an estimate of what is still to be paid

questions.onCorrect: An amount set aside for a cost still to be settled is a provision, and how much to set aside is a judgement the company discloses in its note.

choices.label: Note 3.5 on leases, since the wages relate to the stores it rents
Note 3.12 on provisions, since the amount is an estimate of what is still to be paid
Note 3.9 on impairment, since a large charge in profit signals that assets have lost value
None of the three, since a provision is a fact and not an estimate

misconceptions.feedback: Leases are about the right to use a property and the payments for it. A provision for wages is a different kind of estimate.
Impairment is a write-down of the value of an asset. A provision records an amount the company expects to pay, which is a separate estimate.
A provision is an amount set aside for a cost that is still to be settled, so how much to set aside is a judgement. That is why provisions are among the estimates Woolworths names.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's going concern note says the directors are satisfied that cash reserves, expected cash flows from operations and available facilities will let the group pay its debts as they fall due. What does that sentence commit the directors to?
hints: Whose view is the note, and as at what date was it formed?
Does the note say that debts will be paid, or that the directors expect them to be?

acceptedIdeas: A view, formed when they approved the report, that the debts can be paid, with their reasons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A view, formed when they approved the report, that the debts can be paid, with their reasons

questions.onCorrect: The note records the directors' judgement at the date they approved the report, and the reasons they give are what a reader can check it against.

choices.label: A promise to lenders that every one of the group's debts will be paid on the day it falls due
A forecast of next year's profit, which the directors must answer for if the forecast is missed
A view, formed when they approved the report, that the debts can be paid, with their reasons
A plan to remove the net current liability of $5,995 million within the next twelve months

misconceptions.feedback: The note is a statement of the directors' view and what it rests on. It is not a promise to any lender, and it does not guarantee the outcome.
The note is about whether the group can pay its debts, not about how much profit it will make.
The note explains why the net current liability exists, in terms of fast-turning inventories and supplier timing. It does not commit the directors to removing it.

questions.prompt: A shareholder says: "The accounts were audited, so the business must be sound." Which reply fits what an audit gives a reader?
hints: What is an audit an opinion about: the statements or the business?
Is reasonable assurance the same as a guarantee?

acceptedIdeas: An audit gives reasonable assurance that the statements are not materially misstated, which is not a verdict on the business
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An audit gives reasonable assurance that the statements are not materially misstated, which is not a verdict on the business

questions.onCorrect: An audit gives reasonable assurance about the statements. It is not a verdict on the business, and it is not a guarantee.

choices.label: An audit guarantees that the statements are free of every error, because the auditor tests each transaction in the year
An audit approves the directors' plans for the year, since the auditor reviews strategy as well as figures
An audit confirms that the company will be able to pay all of its debts over the next twelve months, as the directors expect
An audit gives reasonable assurance that the statements are not materially misstated, which is not a verdict on the business

misconceptions.feedback: An audit seeks reasonable assurance and not certainty. It does not promise that no error exists.
The audit looks at whether the statements and internal controls are reliable. It is not a review of strategy.
The audit is about the statements as prepared, not about what happens next. Ability to pay is the subject of the going concern note, where the directors give their own view.

questions.prompt: Tern Foods is invented. Its going concern note says the company made a loss of $3.4 million this year and its current liabilities exceed its current assets by $2.1 million. The directors expect it to keep trading because its main lender has agreed in writing to extend its $4 million facility for the next twelve months. What is the most useful thing to read next?
hints: What do the directors say their view depends on?
Which note would describe the facility and its conditions?

acceptedIdeas: The terms of the lender's agreement and the borrowings note, since the directors' view rests on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The terms of the lender's agreement and the borrowings note, since the directors' view rests on them

questions.onCorrect: The directors' view rests on the lender's agreement, so the agreement and the terms of the facility are what to read.

choices.label: The auditor's name, since a large audit firm guarantees that the company will keep trading afterwards
The terms of the lender's agreement and the borrowings note, since the directors' view rests on them
The dividend history, since a company that has paid dividends will always be able to pay its debts
Nothing more, since a statement from the directors settles whether the company is a going concern or not

misconceptions.feedback: No audit firm guarantees that a company will keep trading, and the name tells you nothing about this lender.
Past dividends say nothing about whether the lender will extend the facility now. The directors have named the lender as the basis for their view, so that is what to check.
The statement is the directors' judgement and what it rests on. The point of reading it is to see what the judgement depends on, and here it depends on the lender.

questions.prompt: Mercer Ltd is invented. An analyst adds its trade and other receivables of $18.0 million to its cash to see whether it can pay its bills next month. The note splits the line into trade receivables of $5.4 million and prepayments of $12.6 million. What is the best correction?
hints: Which of the two parts is money that someone owes the company?
A prepayment is a cost paid in advance. Does it bring cash in?

acceptedIdeas: Use only the $5.4 million of trade receivables, since prepayments are costs already paid and bring no cash in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use only the $5.4 million of trade receivables, since prepayments are costs already paid and bring no cash in

questions.onCorrect: Only the trade receivables are owed by customers, so only they belong in a test of paying bills next month.

choices.label: Use the whole $18.0 million, since the label says receivables and the statements have been audited by an independent firm
Leave the receivables out of the test altogether, since a receivable is never as good as cash in the bank
Use only the $5.4 million of trade receivables, since prepayments are costs already paid and bring no cash in
Use only the $12.6 million of prepayments, since that is the larger of the two parts of the line

misconceptions.feedback: A label names a group and the note says what is in it. Prepayments are not amounts anyone owes the company, whatever the line is called.
Trade receivables are money customers owe and will pay, so they belong in the test. The correction is to remove the prepayments, not all of the line.
A prepayment is a cost paid in advance. It will become an expense as it is used, and it brings no cash in.

questions.prompt: Where in an annual report would you expect to find each of these?
hints: Totals and subtotals sit on the face of the statements.
Ask whether the item explains how a figure was built, or gives an opinion about the statements.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Statements: total non-current assets and the net increase in cash. Notes: the revenue policy, the split of borrowings and the assumptions behind a provision. Auditor's report: the independent opinion.

questions.onCorrect: Totals are in the statements, explanations of how they were built are in the notes, and the independent opinion is the auditor's.

items.label: Total non-current assets
items.explanation: A total on the face of the balance sheet.

items.label: The policy for when a customer is treated as having taken control of the goods
items.explanation: Accounting policies are set out in the notes.

items.label: An independent examiner's opinion on whether the statements are materially misstated
items.explanation: The opinion on the statements is the auditor's report.

items.label: A table splitting borrowings into current and non-current amounts
items.explanation: A breakdown of a line is a note.

items.label: The net increase in cash for the year
items.explanation: A total on the face of the cash flow statement.

items.label: The assumptions behind an amount set aside as a provision
items.explanation: Estimates and their assumptions are explained in the notes.

questions.prompt: The directors of Bram Pty Ltd, an invented company, say they need not check a difficult estimate closely, because the auditor will catch any error. What does ASIC's description of who is responsible for a financial report suggest?
hints: Who does ASIC say is primarily responsible for the quality of a financial report?
What does an audit seek: certainty, or reasonable assurance?

acceptedIdeas: Directors are primarily responsible for the report, and an audit gives reasonable assurance, not certainty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Directors are primarily responsible for the report, and an audit gives reasonable assurance, not certainty

questions.onCorrect: Directors are primarily responsible for their financial report. An audit seeks reasonable assurance, so it is a check on the directors' work and does not replace it.

choices.label: Directors are primarily responsible for the report, and an audit gives reasonable assurance, not certainty
The auditor is primarily responsible, because the audit examines the statements independently of the directors
Responsibility is shared equally between them, so each can rely on the other to find any error in the statements
No one is responsible for an estimate, because an estimate is only a judgement and cannot be wrong

misconceptions.feedback: ASIC puts the main responsibility for the report on the directors. The auditor gives an independent opinion and does not take over that responsibility.
ASIC puts the primary responsibility on the directors. An audit gives reasonable assurance and not certainty, so the directors cannot treat it as a safety net.

ASIC names estimates and areas such as asset values and provisions as the difficult parts that need appropriate expertise and documented judgements. Estimates can be wrong, and the directors answer for them.

questions.prompt: Alder's revenue over three years was 100, 130 and 170, its profit 10, 15 and 21, its operating cash flow 9, 6 and negative 3, and its receivables 12, 28 and 52. Which is the strongest warning sign?
hints: Look at what happened to profit and to operating cash flow over the three years.
Compare how fast receivables grew with how fast revenue grew.

acceptedIdeas: Profit rising while operating cash flow falls and receivables grow far faster than revenue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Profit rising while operating cash flow falls and receivables grow far faster than revenue

questions.onCorrect: Profit and cash moved in opposite directions while receivables outran revenue. Together those patterns call for questions.

choices.label: Revenue growing by about 30% a year, which is too fast to be believable
Profit rising every year, which shows that the numbers have been smoothed
Operating cash flow of negative 3 in year three, because a negative figure always means fraud
Profit rising while operating cash flow falls and receivables grow far faster than revenue

misconceptions.feedback: Fast growth on its own is not a warning sign. Many businesses grow at that rate, and growth is a reason to look at how the cash is coping, which is what the other figures show.
Rising profit is not a sign of smoothing. What matters is whether the profit is matched by cash.
A negative operating cash flow is a reason to ask what absorbed the cash. It does not prove fraud, and a warning sign is a reason for a question and not a verdict.

questions.prompt: A company's receivables rise 80% while its sales rise 10%, and its allowance for doubtful accounts is unchanged. What is the best next check?
hints: Receivables are growing faster than sales. What might that mean for customers' payments?
The allowance is the company's estimate of what it will not collect. Has it kept pace?

acceptedIdeas: How old the receivables are, and whether the allowance still fits them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How old the receivables are, and whether the allowance still fits them

questions.onCorrect: Ageing shows whether the older receivables are building up, and the allowance has to cover what is unlikely to be collected.

choices.label: How old the receivables are, and whether the allowance still fits them
Nothing, since receivables are an asset and a larger asset is good news
The dividend, since a rising dividend shows that customers are paying
The share price, since the market already knows about the collections

misconceptions.feedback: A receivable is only worth what customers pay. Receivables growing much faster than sales can mean customers are paying more slowly or less reliably.
A dividend is paid from cash and says nothing about whether customers are paying the company.
A share price reflects what buyers expect and does not show how old a company's receivables are. The ageing of receivables is the direct check.

questions.prompt: These are two sentences from ASIC's media release on Slater and Gordon. What should a reader conclude about the firm's earlier revenue figures?
hints: Read the second source carefully. Does it say the revenue basis was approved, disapproved, or neither?
What does it mean for a regulator to discontinue an inquiry without giving a view?

acceptedIdeas: ASIC ended its inquiries without a view on the earlier revenue basis, so the closure is not an endorsement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ASIC ended its inquiries without a view on the earlier revenue basis, so the closure is not an endorsement

questions.onCorrect: ASIC discontinued its inquiries without approving or disapproving the earlier revenue basis, so reading the closure as a clean bill goes further than the release does.

choices.label: ASIC ended its inquiries, which shows that the earlier revenue figures were accepted as correct by the regulator
ASIC ended its inquiries because it found that the firm had broken the accounting standards
ASIC ended its inquiries without a view on the earlier revenue basis, so the closure is not an endorsement

misconceptions.feedback: The second source says ASIC had not approved the earlier revenue basis. Ending an inquiry is not the same as approving what was inquired into.
Neither source says so. The first records that the inquiries were discontinued, and the second that ASIC had neither approved nor disapproved the earlier basis.

questions.prompt: ABC Learning reported a net profit of $52.3 million on revenue of $292.7 million in 2004/5. Besides profit, which facts would have told a reader most about the risk to the company?
hints: Profit says how the year went. What says what the company owes, and when?
Which figures would tell you whether profit could pay the interest?

acceptedIdeas: How much it owed, how much of that fell due soon, and whether its profit covered the interest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much it owed, how much of that fell due soon, and whether its profit covered the interest

questions.onCorrect: Profit says nothing about how much is owed. The debt, when it falls due and whether profit covers the interest show the risk.

choices.label: How fast the number of its centres was growing, since faster growth means a lower chance of failure
How much it owed, how much of that fell due soon, and whether its profit covered the interest
How high its margin was on each centre, since a high margin means that debt cannot matter
How large its market value was, since a large market value shows that the debt can be repaid

misconceptions.feedback: Growth is a reason to look at how it was funded. It does not lower the chance of failure, and ABC Learning's growth came with a large debt.
A high margin helps profit and does not remove the debt. The company could not service its $1.8 billion of debt when profit fell.
A market value is what buyers will pay for the shares, and it fell sharply when profit dropped. It does not show that debts can be repaid.

questions.prompt: The extract describes how one company recorded income from long-term projects. What would a careful reader of its statements most likely have seen, year after year?
hints: The extract says income could be recorded although the firm might never have received the money. Which would be larger in the statements: profit or cash?
Which statement would show the money arriving?

acceptedIdeas: Reported profit far above operating cash flow, since income was recorded before any cash arrived
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reported profit far above operating cash flow, since income was recorded before any cash arrived

questions.onCorrect: Income recorded before the money arrives lifts profit above operating cash flow, which is the gap the cash flow statement shows.

choices.label: Reported profit far above operating cash flow, since income was recorded before any cash arrived
Operating cash flow far above reported profit, since cash arrived long before any income was recorded
Revenue falling every year while profit kept rising, since projects became less common
No difference between profit and cash, because both were audited and agreed

misconceptions.feedback: Under the method described, income was recorded before the money arrived, so the profit would run ahead of cash and not behind it.
The extract says income could be recorded on projects that had not brought in cash, which points to profit running ahead of cash and says nothing about revenue falling.
An audit does not make profit and cash the same. Profit counts income when it is recorded, and cash counts when money arrives.

extracts.text: Under this method, income from projects could be recorded, although the firm might never have received the money, with this income increasing financial earnings on the books.

questions.prompt: Brindle's profit over the three years is 71 and its operating cash flow is 75. What does the first check show?
hints: Compare 71 with 75.
Which way did cash move from year to year?

acceptedIdeas: Cash is a little above profit, so there is no gap to be explained
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cash is a little above profit, so there is no gap to be explained

questions.onCorrect: Cash of 75 against profit of 71 means Brindle's profit is turning into cash, so the first check raises no question.

choices.label: Cash is far below profit, so the first check raises a warning
Cash is falling while profit rises, so the first check raises a warning
The check cannot be done unless the balance sheet is also available
Cash is a little above profit, so there is no gap to be explained

misconceptions.feedback: Cash of 75 against profit of 71 is a little above profit, not below it.
Brindle's operating cash flow rose each year, 22, 25 and 28, along with its profit.
The check compares two lines of the income statement and the cash flow statement, and it needs no balance sheet figure.

questions.prompt: Brindle's days of sales in receivables come out at about 55, 54 and 54. What do they show?
hints: Compare the three figures with one another.
What was the pattern for Alder's days, and is Brindle's the same?

acceptedIdeas: Steady at about 54 days, so customers pay at the same pace as they did
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Steady at about 54 days, so customers pay at the same pace as they did

questions.onCorrect: Days that stay near 54 mean receivables are growing in step with sales, which is what a healthy pattern looks like.

choices.label: Rising fast, so customers are taking much longer to pay than they were
Steady at about 54 days, so customers pay at the same pace as they did
Falling fast, so the company is collecting its money much more quickly
Too few years to say anything at all about how customers are paying

misconceptions.feedback: The days are steady, not rising. A rise such as Alder's from 44 to 112 would be the warning.
The days are steady, not falling, at about 54 in each year.
Three years of days at about 54 show that customers are paying at a steady pace, even if more years would add confidence.

questions.prompt: Corvid Ltd is invented. In year three it lengthened the useful life of its equipment from five years to eight. Depreciation fell by $11 million, profit rose by 15% and operating cash flow was unchanged. What is the best next check?
hints: Depreciation is a non-cash charge against profit. What does a smaller charge do to profit, and to cash?
Which part of the profit rise came from the change in estimate and not from the business?

acceptedIdeas: Whether the equipment really lasts eight years, and how much of the profit rise comes from the longer lives
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether the equipment really lasts eight years, and how much of the profit rise comes from the longer lives

questions.onCorrect: A change in estimate can lift profit without bringing in cash, so the next check is how much of the rise it explains and whether the new lives are sound.

choices.label: Whether the rise in profit is real, since a change in estimate always means the profit has been manipulated
Nothing, since depreciation is not cash and so it has no effect on profit
Whether the equipment really lasts eight years, and how much of the profit rise comes from the longer lives
Whether operating cash flow should be restated, since it should have risen along with profit

misconceptions.feedback: A change in estimate can be a sound judgement. The check is how much of the profit rise comes from the change and whether the new lives are reasonable.
Depreciation is charged against profit even though no cash leaves, so a lower charge lifts profit. It has no effect on cash.
Depreciation is not a cash cost, so a lower charge raises profit and leaves cash where it was. The unchanged cash flow is what you would expect.

questions.prompt: Dunlin Ltd is invented. Over three years its profit was 33, 37 and 42, its operating cash flow 31, 17 and 5, its inventory 45, 75 and 115, and its borrowings due within a year 24, 61 and 97. Which reading is best supported?
hints: Which figures are rising, and which is falling to almost nothing?
What is the company using to pay for the extra inventory?

acceptedIdeas: Profit is rising, but stock is absorbing the cash and short-term borrowing is paying for it, so check liquidity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Profit is rising, but stock is absorbing the cash and short-term borrowing is paying for it, so check liquidity

questions.onCorrect: Profit is up while operating cash has fallen from 31 to 5, and short-term borrowing has grown to pay for stock. The questions are about liquidity and about whether the stock will sell.

choices.label: Profit is rising, but stock is absorbing the cash and short-term borrowing is paying for it, so check liquidity
The business has been overstating its profit, since inventory that rises year after year always means the accounts are false
The rise in borrowings is ordinary financing for a growing business, so there is nothing that needs checking
Profit is rising every year while the company grows, which shows that the company is healthy

misconceptions.feedback: Rising inventory is not proof of anything. It does show cash being used up, which is where the next questions lie.
Growth is a reason to look more closely at how it is funded. Operating cash has fallen to 5 while short-term borrowing has risen to 97, which raises a question about paying for it.
Profit is rising while cash from operations falls to nearly nothing. A company can report a profit and still be short of the cash it needs.

questions.prompt: Six patterns appear in statements. Which ones need a question, and which may be normal for the business?
hints: A pattern that comes with a reason that fits the business, and reverses, may be normal.
A pattern that grows year after year, or that the notes seem to contradict, needs a question.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Needs a question: stock doubling against a tenth of sales growth, a late heavy write-down and borrowings classed differently in the notes. May be normal: the café chain's explained net current liability, the one-year cash gap from new-shop stock and the dip from the new factory.

questions.onCorrect: A pattern that comes with a fitting reason may be normal, while one that grows or that the notes seem to contradict needs a question.

items.label: Inventory has doubled in two years while sales are up a tenth
items.explanation: Stock growing much faster than sales needs an explanation, such as slow sales or a build-up before an opening.

items.label: An asset carried at the same value for years is written down heavily in one half-year
items.explanation: A late, large write-down raises the question of why the earlier values were held.

items.label: Borrowings are shown as long-term on the balance sheet while the notes list amounts due within twelve months
items.explanation: A mismatch between classification and the notes calls for a closer look at how the debt is classed.

items.label: A café chain's current liabilities exceed its current assets, and its notes explain that customers pay at the till while suppliers are paid in thirty days
items.explanation: The pattern comes with a stated reason that fits how the business works.

items.label: A retailer's operating cash flow is below profit in a year when it built up stock for new shops, and above profit the next year
items.explanation: The gap has an explanation and reverses once the new shops are trading.

items.label: A manufacturer's profit dips in the year it spends heavily on a new factory, and its notes describe the spending
items.explanation: The dip has a disclosed cause that fits the business, so it is a reason to read the note and not a warning.

questions.prompt: In a year when bonuses depend on profit, Hana, a manager in an invented company, delays writing down a failing store so that profit looks steady. Ravi, in another, shortens the life of a machine because a breakdown shows it wears out faster than he thought. Using the extract, which choice is an example of earnings management?
hints: What is each manager's judgement based on, and what is it used for?
The definition mentions influencing contractual outcomes that depend on reported numbers. Which case fits?

acceptedIdeas: Hana's, because she uses judgement to alter reported profit in a year when a bonus depends on it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hana's, because she uses judgement to alter reported profit in a year when a bonus depends on it

questions.onCorrect: Hana's delay uses judgement to alter reported results in a bonus year, while Ravi's follows evidence. The purpose and the evidence separate them.

choices.label: Both, because both choices change the profit that the company reports to its owners
Ravi's, because shortening the life of a machine lowers the profit that is reported
Neither, because both choices are judgements and the accounting rules allow judgements like these
Hana's, because she uses judgement to alter reported profit in a year when a bonus depends on it

misconceptions.feedback: A choice that changes profit is not enough. The definition turns on what the judgement is used for, and Ravi's follows evidence about the machine.
Ravi's change reflects evidence, the breakdown, and lowers profit. The definition is about judgement used to mislead or to influence a contractual outcome.
A judgement can be allowed by the rules and still be used to alter reported results. Creative accounting follows the letter of the rules.

extracts.text: Earnings management occurs when managers use judgment in financial reporting and in structuring transactions to alter financial reports to either mislead some stakeholders about the underlying economic performance of a company or influence contractual outcomes that depend on reported accounting numbers.

questions.prompt: Between 2024 and 2026 Lovisa's earnings per share rose from 75.4 to 86.3 cents while its share price fell from $32.87 to $23.25. What happened to the price buyers paid for each dollar of earnings?
hints: Divide each year's price by that year's earnings per share, in dollars.
A smaller price over larger earnings gives a smaller or a larger figure?

acceptedIdeas: It fell from about 44 times earnings to about 27, so buyers pay less for each dollar of profit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fell from about 44 times earnings to about 27, so buyers pay less for each dollar of profit

questions.onCorrect: The price per dollar of earnings went from about 44 to about 27, because the price fell while earnings rose.

choices.label: It rose, since earnings went up while the price had already been set at the earlier level
It fell, which shows that the shares are now cheap and so should be bought by an investor
It fell from about 44 times earnings to about 27, so buyers pay less for each dollar of profit
It stayed about the same, since the rise in earnings and the fall in price cancel each other out

misconceptions.feedback: The price did not stay fixed. It fell by about 29% while earnings rose by about 14%, so the price per dollar of earnings fell.
The price per dollar of earnings did fall, but that alone does not show the shares are cheap. Buyers may expect less growth or doubt the earnings more.
A price that falls while earnings rise does not leave the ratio unchanged. Dividing a smaller price by larger earnings gives a smaller figure.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's closing share price was $40.24 and its basic earnings per share were 93.2 cents. About what is its price-to-earnings ratio?
hints: Put the earnings per share into dollars first.
The ratio is the price divided by the earnings per share.

acceptedIdeas: About 43, from dividing $40.24 by $0.932
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 43, from dividing $40.24 by $0.932

questions.onCorrect: Dividing $40.24 by $0.932 gives about 43, so a buyer pays for about 43 years of this year's earnings.

choices.label: About 0.4, from dividing $40.24 by 93.2
About 2.3, from dividing 93.2 cents by $40.24
About 31, from using earnings before significant items
About 43, from dividing $40.24 by $0.932

misconceptions.feedback: That divides dollars by cents. Earnings of 93.2 cents are $0.932, and $40.24 over $0.932 is about 43.
That turns the ratio upside down and also mixes cents with dollars. The ratio is the price over earnings per share.
That uses 130.9 cents, the earnings per share before significant items. The question gives basic earnings per share of 93.2 cents.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's operating cash flow was $232.8 million. It spent $58.5 million net on investing, after $10.5 million that landlords contributed to fit-outs, and $89.2 million on lease payments, which leaves about $85 million. It paid $88.6 million in dividends and drew $10 million on its borrowing facility. What does this show?
hints: Compare free cash flow of about $85 million with dividends of $88.6 million.
What was the $10 million drawn on the facility?

acceptedIdeas: Dividends were a little more than free cash flow, so borrowing helped to fill the gap in the payout
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dividends were a little more than free cash flow, so borrowing helped to fill the gap in the payout

questions.onCorrect: Dividends of $88.6 million were a little above free cash flow of about $85 million, and the $10 million of borrowing was available to fill the gap.

choices.label: Dividends were a little more than free cash flow, so borrowing helped to fill the gap in the payout
Dividends were well covered by free cash flow, so the borrowing was for some other purpose entirely
There was no free cash flow at all, since lease payments are not a cash cost to the company
Free cash flow is the same as profit, so the dividend was covered by the year's earnings in full

misconceptions.feedback: Free cash flow of about $85 million was less than the $88.6 million paid, so the dividend was not covered by the year's cash after shops and leases.
Lease payments are cash leaving the business, and they are the cost of keeping the shops. Treating them as a cost leaves about $85 million.
Profit was $95.6 million and free cash flow about $85 million, which are not the same. Profit covered the dividend but the year's free cash did not quite do so.

questions.prompt: Quarry Ltd is invented. Its equity is $50 million, it has 25 million shares and its share price is $18, which is nine times its equity per share of $2. A reader says the shares must be overpriced for that reason. What is the best reply?
hints: What does a balance sheet record: cost, or earning power?
What would you want to know about earnings before judging a price of $18?

acceptedIdeas: The price may be fair, since the balance sheet leaves out earning power, so ask what $18 assumes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price may be fair, since the balance sheet leaves out earning power, so ask what $18 assumes

questions.onCorrect: Equity per share records cost and leaves out earning power, so a large gap with the price is a reason to ask what earnings and growth the price assumes.

choices.label: A share price should always stay close to equity per share, so $18 is far too high for Quarry
The price may be fair, since the balance sheet leaves out earning power, so ask what $18 assumes
The comparison shows nothing, because equity per share is simply an accounting error and not a real figure
The price must fall to $2, because book value is what the company would fetch if it were sold

misconceptions.feedback: A balance sheet records assets at cost and leaves out earning power, so there is no reason for a price to stay close to equity per share.
Equity per share is a correct division of recorded equity by shares. It measures what the balance sheet records, which is a different thing from what buyers expect.
Book value is recorded at cost and changes in market value are generally not recorded, so it is not what the company would fetch if sold.

questions.prompt: Heron Ltd is invented. Two analysts forecast the same cash flows for it. One discounts at 8% and values the business at $900 million, and the other discounts at 10% and gets $750 million. Which explains the gap?
hints: What does a higher discount rate do to cash that arrives in year 25?
Where in a forecast does most of the value usually sit?

acceptedIdeas: Much of the value comes from cash far in the future, which is very sensitive to the discount rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Much of the value comes from cash far in the future, which is very sensitive to the discount rate

questions.onCorrect: Terminal value is often a large share of the total and is very sensitive to the discount rate and growth, so a small change in either moves the value a good deal.

choices.label: One analyst has made an arithmetic error, since the same forecast must always give the same value
Much of the value comes from cash far in the future, which is very sensitive to the discount rate
A discounted cash flow cannot be used for a listed company, so the two values are not comparable
The discount rate does not affect value at all, because only the forecast cash flows count

misconceptions.feedback: The same forecast gives different values at different discount rates, so the gap does not need an error to explain it.
Discounted cash flow is used for securities, projects, companies and assets alike, and the question is why a small change in one assumption moves the value.
Discounting reduces the value of each year's cash, and the further away the cash is, the more a higher rate reduces it.

questions.prompt: Moss Ltd has no debt and a market capitalisation of $500 million. Sedge Ltd, which is heavily borrowed, has a market capitalisation of $300 million and debt of $200 million. Neither holds any cash. A reader says Moss is worth more than Sedge. What is the best reply?
hints: Who else, besides the shareholders, has a claim on Sedge?
What would you have to pay to buy the whole of each business?

acceptedIdeas: Compare enterprise values: $300 million plus $200 million of debt puts Sedge level with Moss at $500 million
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compare enterprise values: $300 million plus $200 million of debt puts Sedge level with Moss at $500 million

questions.onCorrect: Enterprise value adds the lenders' claims to the shareholders', so the two companies are compared on the same footing.

choices.label: Moss is worth more, since a company's market capitalisation is the value of the whole company and Sedge's is smaller
Sedge's debt makes it worth less than Moss, since debt always reduces the value of any company that has to carry it
Compare enterprise values: $300 million plus $200 million of debt puts Sedge level with Moss at $500 million
Market capitalisation is the better measure, because debt is only a promise and not a claim on the business

misconceptions.feedback: A market capitalisation counts only the shareholders' claim. Sedge's lenders have a claim of $200 million that the figure leaves out.
Debt is one of the ways a business is funded. It adds to what must be paid to buy the whole business, and it is not a reason by itself to value the business less.
Lenders have a claim on the business, and enterprise value counts creditors as well as shareholders.

questions.prompt: Two invented companies have price-to-earnings ratios of 8 and 35. Which statement is best supported?
hints: What does the ratio measure: the value of the business, or what is paid for this year's earnings?
What would make a buyer willing to pay 35 years of earnings?

acceptedIdeas: The ratio shows what is paid for current earnings, so ask about growth, risk and the cash behind the profit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ratio shows what is paid for current earnings, so ask about growth, risk and the cash behind the profit

questions.onCorrect: A P/E shows the price paid for current earnings, so whether it is high or low depends on expected growth, risk and how much of the profit arrives as cash.

choices.label: The ratio shows what is paid for current earnings, so ask about growth, risk and the cash behind the profit
The one at 8 is the better buy, since a lower ratio always means that the shares are better value
Neither ratio tells us anything, since a share price cannot say anything at all about a business
The one at 35 must contain an error, since no real company can have a ratio above 20 for long

misconceptions.feedback: A low ratio can mean that buyers expect earnings to shrink or doubt them. It shows what is paid for current earnings, and growth and risk differ between companies.
A ratio does say what buyers pay for current earnings, which is the starting point for asking what the price assumes.
Wikipedia's range of 10 to 20 is a general view that depends on sector and business. Ratios above it are common, and Lovisa's was above it in each of five years.

questions.prompt: Harlan Ltd is invented. Its profit was $40 million, its operating cash flow $55 million, its spending on property, plant and equipment $60 million and its lease principal $8 million. What does its free cash flow show?
hints: Subtract the spending on property, plant and equipment and the lease principal from operating cash flow.
Is the result positive or negative, and what could explain it?

acceptedIdeas: Free cash flow is negative, so ask whether the spending is for growth and how it is funded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free cash flow is negative, so ask whether the spending is for growth and how it is funded

questions.onCorrect: 55 less 60 less 8 is negative 13, so the business spent more than it brought in. The question is whether the spending is growth and how it is funded.

choices.label: A profit of $40 million shows that the business can pay a dividend of $40 million this year
Free cash flow is negative, so ask whether the spending is for growth and how it is funded
Operating cash flow above profit means that free cash flow must therefore be a positive number
Negative free cash flow shows that the accounts are wrong and that the profit it reports is false

misconceptions.feedback: Free cash flow is about negative $13 million, so a dividend of that size would have to be funded from borrowing or savings.
Free cash flow is what is left of operating cash flow after spending on property, plant, equipment and leases, and here that spending is larger than the cash from operations.
Negative free cash flow is a reason to ask where the cash went. A business that is investing in growth can have one without any error in its accounts.

questions.prompt: Which measure answers each of these questions about a business?
hints: Ask whether the question is about a price, a cash amount, the claims of everyone who funds the business, or a forecast.
A question about a forecast discounted to today points to one measure.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Price-to-earnings: the years of earnings paid for and the two shares at $20. Free cash flow: the cash free to lenders and owners and the dividend cover. Enterprise value: the cost of the whole business and the debt-free against the borrowed company. Discounted cash flow: the value today of forecast cash and its sensitivity to far-off growth.

questions.onCorrect: Each measure answers one kind of question: what is paid for earnings, what cash is free, who has a claim, and what forecast cash is worth today.

items.label: How many years of this year's earnings a buyer pays for one share
items.explanation: A ratio of the share price to earnings per share.

items.label: Why a share at $20 earning $2 and a share at $20 earning $1 are priced differently
items.explanation: The two have ratios of 10 and 20, and the ratio is what compares them.

items.label: How much cash could go to lenders and owners without harming operations
items.explanation: Operating cash flow after the spending needed to carry on.

items.label: Whether a dividend was covered by the year's cash after spending on shops and leases
items.explanation: Free cash flow is set against what is paid out.

items.label: What it would cost to buy the whole business, settling with lenders as well as shareholders, less its cash
items.explanation: The sum of all claims, less the cash a buyer would get.

items.label: How a debt-free company and a heavily borrowed one compare on the same footing
items.explanation: It counts the lenders' claims as well as the shareholders'.

items.label: What a business is worth today if its forecast cash is discounted for the time value of money
items.explanation: It discounts each year's forecast cash back to today.

items.label: Why a value moves a great deal when the assumed growth in the far future changes
items.explanation: A large share of the value is terminal value, which is sensitive to growth and the discount rate.

questions.prompt: Alpine Ltd is invented. Its earnings were $1 a share in each of two years, and its share price was $12 in the first year and $36 in the second. What changed?
hints: Divide the price by earnings in each year.
If earnings did not change, what must have changed in how buyers see the business?

acceptedIdeas: Buyers now pay 36 years of earnings instead of 12, so they expect more growth or worry less about risk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers now pay 36 years of earnings instead of 12, so they expect more growth or worry less about risk

questions.onCorrect: The ratio moved from 12 to 36 on the same earnings, so buyers' expectations or their view of the risk changed, and the business did not.

choices.label: Alpine became three times as profitable, since its share price rose to three times what it was
Earnings per share must have tripled, since a share price cannot rise unless earnings have risen too
Nothing changed, since a share price and a profit are separate things that have no link between them
Buyers now pay 36 years of earnings instead of 12, so they expect more growth or worry less about risk

misconceptions.feedback: Earnings were $1 a share in both years, so the business earned the same. The price changed, and so did what buyers pay for each dollar of earnings.
The question gives earnings of $1 a share in both years. Prices can rise on expectations alone.
The ratio of the two is what moved, from 12 to 36, and it measures what buyers are paying for each dollar of earnings.

flashcards.front: What is the name for what is left of a company's assets after all its liabilities are taken away?
flashcards.back: Equity, also called net assets or net worth. It is a recorded difference at cost, which says little about cash on hand or sale price.

flashcards.front: A company leases a store for ten years. Which two lines show it on the balance sheet?
flashcards.back: A right-of-use asset for the right to use the store and a lease liability for the payments it must make.

flashcards.front: Why can't a balance sheet tell you how much profit a company made during the year?
flashcards.back: It shows one date only. Profit covers a period, so it comes from the income statement.

flashcards.front: What name is given to assets = liabilities + equity, which every entry keeps in balance?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The accounting equation. Every transaction changes at least two things so that it still holds.

flashcards.front: Why does borrowing $50,000 not change a firm's profit?
flashcards.back: Cash and the loan both rise by $50,000. Profit changes only when revenue or a cost is recorded.

flashcards.front: A company records a provision for wages it owes. What two things change on the day?
flashcards.back: A liability rises and profit falls by the same amount. Cash goes out later, as payments are made.

flashcards.front: What do the letters EBIT stand for?

flashcards.front: Why read a profit before significant items beside the profit after them?

flashcards.front: Why can earnings per share fall in a year when profit rises?
flashcards.back: Earnings per share divides profit by the number of shares. If the share count grows by more than profit, each share's slice gets smaller.

flashcards.front: In which section of the cash flow statement do Woolworths and Lovisa report dividends paid and lease principal?

flashcards.front: What three questions would you ask of any cash flow statement?

flashcards.front: Why can a company's cash rise only a little in a year when its operating cash flow is large?
flashcards.back: The operating cash can be spent on stores, lease payments and dividends, so the balance reflects what is left. The size of the rise says little by itself.

flashcards.front: What is the table called that starts from profit and ends at operating cash flow?

flashcards.front: Why is depreciation added back in the reconciliation, and why is it not a source of cash?
flashcards.back: It is deducted in profit and no cash leaves, so it is added back to reach cash. The cash that pays for the business still comes from customers.

flashcards.front: Why can a growing, profitable business run short of cash?
flashcards.back: Sales are counted when made, while cash arrives later. Receivables and stock grow first, so the firm must fund the gap from its own cash, suppliers or lenders.

flashcards.front: When does a business recognise revenue from selling goods?

flashcards.front: How should a reader treat items a company calls significant when they appear every year?

flashcards.front: What is the name for the third factor of the DuPont split, total assets divided by equity?

flashcards.front: A company's return on equity is far above 100%. What do you check first, and why?
flashcards.back: Its equity. A return above 100% means equity is smaller than a year's profit, which can come from heavy payouts or from a negative reserve, and the business may be no better for it.

flashcards.front: Why is return on capital a fairer way than return on equity to compare companies that are funded differently?
flashcards.back: It starts from operating profit and divides by equity, borrowings and lease liabilities together, so swapping debt for equity changes neither the top nor the bottom.

flashcards.front: A statement line is labelled trade and other receivables. Where do you look to see what it contains, and why?
flashcards.back: In the note whose number sits beside the line. The label names a group and the note breaks it down, so a line can hold items that are not what the label suggests.

flashcards.front: What does an audit give a reader of the statements?

flashcards.front: What does a going concern note commit the directors to, and what should you look for in it?
flashcards.back: A view, formed when they approved the report, that the company can pay its debts as they fall due. Look for what the view rests on, such as cash, expected cash flows and facilities, and for the reasons given for anything that looks alarming.

flashcards.front: What does it suggest when profit rises for years while operating cash flow falls?
flashcards.back: Profit is not turning into cash, and the gap usually sits in receivables, stock or estimates. It is a reason to ask what absorbed the cash, and it does not prove anything wrong.

flashcards.front: Which term names the use of judgement in reporting to alter results, either to mislead some stakeholders or to influence outcomes that depend on reported numbers?

flashcards.front: How does this course build free cash flow from the statements?
flashcards.back: Operating cash flow, less spending on property, plant, equipment and intangibles, less lease principal. The lease step is the reader's adjustment.

flashcards.front: What is the sum of the claims of creditors and shareholders on a business, which is wider than its market capitalisation?
